title: What Is a Home Appraisal? | Your Realty Link
meta: A home appraisal is a lender-ordered estimate of a home's market value. Learn how the appraisal process works for buyers and sellers in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: An independent check on what a home is really worth — and a key step in almost every financed purchase.
definition: A home appraisal is an independent, professional opinion of a property's market value, prepared by a state-licensed appraiser. Mortgage lenders order one to confirm a home is worth the amount being borrowed.
qa_lead: When you finance a home, your lender orders an appraisal so it doesn't lend more than the property is worth. A licensed appraiser inspects the home and compares it to recent nearby sales to reach a value. If the appraisal comes in below your agreed price, you may face an appraisal gap to solve before closing.
sections: Why Lenders Require an Appraisal

A mortgage is secured by the home itself, so the lender needs to know the property is worth at least what it's lending. The appraisal is that safeguard. It protects the bank from over-lending and, indirectly, protects you from overpaying.
Even a strong offer can hinge on the appraisal. If you're paying cash you can waive it, but most financed purchases in Central Indiana include an appraisal step tied to loan approval.
How an Appraiser Determines Value

Most appraisers use the sales comparison approach: they look at recently sold homes nearby that are similar in size, age, and condition, then adjust for differences like an extra bath, a finished basement, or a larger lot. The result is a supported opinion of value, not a guess.
This differs from a comparative market analysis your agent prepares. An appraisal is a formal, licensed valuation used by the lender, while a market analysis helps set a listing or offer price.
When the Appraisal Comes in Low

Sometimes an appraisal lands below the contract price. When that happens you generally have options: the buyer can cover the difference in cash, the parties can renegotiate the price, or the buyer can walk away if the contract includes the right contingency.
This shortfall is called an appraisal gap. Knowing how you'd handle one before you write an offer keeps a low number from derailing your purchase.
faqs: How long does a home appraisal take?
The on-site visit is often under an hour, but the written report usually takes several days to a week to reach your lender.
Is an appraisal the same as a home inspection?
No. An appraisal estimates value for your lender, while an inspection evaluates the home's condition for you as the buyer.
Can I use my own appraisal?
For a mortgage, the lender orders the appraisal through an approved appraiser, so you generally can't substitute one you ordered yourself.

title: What Is a Home Inspection? | Your Realty Link
meta: A home inspection is a professional review of a home's condition before you buy. Learn what inspections cover and why they matter for Central Indiana buyers.
hero_sub: Your independent look under the hood before you commit to a home.
definition: A home inspection is a professional, top-to-bottom review of a home's condition, performed by a qualified inspector so a buyer understands what they're purchasing before closing.
qa_lead: A home inspection is your chance to learn a property's real condition before you're locked in. You hire a qualified inspector who examines the home's major systems and structure, then gives you a written report. Most Central Indiana buyers keep an inspection contingency in their offer so they can renegotiate or walk away if something serious turns up.
sections: What a Home Inspection Covers

A general inspection looks at the home's big-ticket systems: roof and structure, foundation, HVAC, electrical, plumbing, water heater, windows, and visible signs of moisture or pests. The inspector documents what's working, what's worn, and what may need attention soon.
It's not a pass-or-fail test and not a code inspection. Think of it as a detailed snapshot of condition so you can make an informed decision.
Why It Matters in Central Indiana

Indiana law requires most sellers to complete a residential seller's disclosure, but that reflects the seller's knowledge, not an expert's. An inspection is your own due diligence, and it often pays for itself by catching issues early.
Radon is worth a special mention: much of Central Indiana sits in a higher-radon region, so many buyers add a radon test to their inspection. It's an easy, affordable safeguard.
Using Inspection Results

Your report becomes a negotiating tool. Depending on your contract, you can ask the seller to make repairs, offer a credit, adjust the price, or, for major problems, cancel under your inspection contingency.
The goal isn't a perfect house — no home is flawless. It's making sure there are no expensive surprises you didn't sign up for.
faqs: Is a home inspection required in Indiana?
It isn't legally required, but it's strongly recommended and is a standard part of most purchase agreements as a contingency.
How much does a home inspection cost?
Costs vary with the home's size and age and any add-ons like radon or a sewer scope; your agent can point you to fair local pricing.
What if the inspection finds problems?
You can typically request repairs, a credit, or a price change — or, for serious issues, exercise your inspection contingency to exit the deal.

h1: Pre-Approval vs. Pre-Qualification: What's the Difference?
title: Pre-Approval vs. Pre-Qualification | Your Realty Link
meta: Pre-approval vs. pre-qualification: learn the real difference, why pre-approval carries more weight, and how each affects your Central Indiana home offer.
hero_sub: Two similar-sounding steps that carry very different weight with sellers.
definition: Pre-qualification is a quick, informal estimate of how much you might borrow based on information you share. Pre-approval is a stronger, verified commitment from a lender after reviewing your documents and credit.
qa_lead: Both terms describe early mortgage steps, but they aren't equal. Pre-qualification is a fast estimate based on numbers you provide. Pre-approval means a lender has verified your income, assets, and credit and put it in writing. In a competitive Central Indiana market, a pre-approval letter tells sellers your offer is real.
qa_facts: Soft or none vs. full review
sections: What Pre-Qualification Really Is

Pre-qualification is the lightest touch. You tell a lender your income, debts, and rough savings, and they estimate a loan amount. Nothing is verified, so it's a helpful starting point but not a promise.
It's useful early on to understand your ballpark budget before you start touring homes.
Why Pre-Approval Carries More Weight

For pre-approval, the lender collects documents — pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements — and pulls your credit. The resulting letter states a specific amount they're prepared to lend, subject to a property and final underwriting.
Because it's backed by verification, sellers and their agents take pre-approved buyers far more seriously, especially when multiple offers are on the table.
Which One You Need in Central Indiana
When homes move quickly, a pre-approval letter is close to essential. Many sellers won't seriously consider an offer without one, and having it ready lets you act fast on the right house.
Start the mortgage conversation early. Getting pre-approved before you shop keeps you from falling for a home outside your range and strengthens every offer you make.
faqs: Does pre-approval guarantee a loan?
No. It's a strong commitment based on verified information, but final approval still depends on the property and underwriting.
Will pre-approval hurt my credit?
It involves a credit check, but the impact is usually minor and temporary, especially if you shop lenders within a short window.
How long is a pre-approval good for?
Letters are typically valid for a couple of months, since income and credit can change; your lender can refresh it if your search runs longer.

title: What Is Amortization? | Your Realty Link
meta: Amortization is how your mortgage is paid off over time, with each payment split between interest and principal. See how it works for Indiana homeowners.
hero_sub: The reason your early mortgage payments feel like they're barely denting the balance.
definition: Amortization is the process of paying off a loan through regular, equal payments over time, with each payment covering both interest and a portion of the principal balance.
qa_lead: On a typical fixed-rate mortgage, your monthly payment stays the same, but what's inside it shifts. Early on, most of each payment goes to interest and only a little to principal. Over the years that flips. An amortization schedule shows this split for every payment.
sections: How Amortization Works

When you take a fixed-rate loan, the lender calculates one steady payment that will pay off the balance by the end of the term. Because you owe the most at the start, the interest portion is largest early and shrinks as the balance falls.
By the final years, nearly all of each payment is reducing principal. This is why building meaningful equity through payments alone takes time.
Reading an Amortization Schedule

An amortization schedule is a table listing every payment, how much goes to interest, how much to principal, and your remaining balance. It's a clear way to see the true cost of a loan over its full life.
A mortgage calculator can generate this for you so you can compare loan terms before you commit.
Paying Down Faster

Any extra money you put toward the loan is applied directly to principal, which shrinks the balance and the interest you'll pay going forward. Even occasional extra payments can shorten the loan and save a meaningful amount over time.
A shorter term, like paying on a 15-year schedule instead of 30, amortizes faster with higher payments but far less total interest.
faqs: Why is so much of my early payment interest?
Interest is charged on your outstanding balance, which is highest at the start, so early payments are interest-heavy by design.
Does making extra payments help?
Yes. Extra payments reduce principal directly, lowering future interest and shortening the life of your loan.
Are all mortgages amortized?
Most traditional fixed-rate mortgages are fully amortized, though some loan types have interest-only periods or balloon payments that work differently.

title: What Is Home Equity? | Your Realty Link
meta: Home equity is the share of your home you truly own — its value minus what you still owe. Learn how equity builds and grows for Central Indiana homeowners.
hero_sub: The part of your home's value that's truly yours, and one of the biggest ways families build wealth.
definition: Home equity is the portion of your home that you actually own — the difference between your home's current market value and the amount you still owe on your mortgage.
qa_lead: Home equity is simply your home's value minus what you owe on it. If your house would sell for more than your remaining loan balance, that gap is your equity. It grows as you pay down your mortgage and as your home's value rises. A quick home valuation is the easiest way to estimate where you stand.
qa_facts: Market value minus what you owe
HELOC, home equity loan, refinance, sale
sections: How Equity Is Built

Equity grows two ways. First, every mortgage payment chips away at your loan balance, so you owe a little less each month. Second, when local home values rise, your property may be worth more even before you've paid anything extra.
Improvements that add real value and a strong Central Indiana market can both move equity in your favor over time.
Equity and Mortgage Insurance

If you bought with a smaller down payment, you may be paying private mortgage insurance. As you build equity and reach a common threshold of about 20 percent, you can often request to have PMI removed, lowering your payment.
Watching your equity grow isn't just satisfying — it can put money back in your pocket.
Putting Equity to Work

Homeowners tap equity in several ways: a home equity line of credit, a home equity loan, or a cash-out refinance for goals like renovations. The largest payoff, though, usually comes when you sell and roll equity into your next home.
If you're weighing a move, knowing your equity helps you plan your next purchase. Reach out anytime to talk it through.
faqs: How do I calculate my home equity?
Estimate your home's current market value and subtract your remaining mortgage balance; the difference is your equity.
Can home equity go down?
Yes. If local home values fall or you borrow against the home, your equity can shrink, though paying down your loan works the other way.
Do I have to sell to use my equity?
No. Options like a HELOC, home equity loan, or cash-out refinance let you access equity without selling, though selling is often the simplest way.

title: What Is a Deed? | Your Realty Link
meta: A deed is the legal document that transfers home ownership from seller to buyer. Learn the common deed types and how a deed differs from title in Indiana.
hero_sub: The signed, recorded document that actually moves a home from seller to buyer.
definition: A deed is the legal document that transfers ownership of real estate from one party to another. Signing and recording the deed is how a home officially changes hands.
qa_lead: A deed is the paperwork that legally transfers a home's ownership at closing. It names the seller and buyer, describes the property, and is signed and then recorded with the county. A deed isn't the same as title — title is your ownership right, while the deed is the document that conveys it. Title insurance helps protect that ownership.
sections: Deed vs. Title

People use these words interchangeably, but they're different. Title is the concept of legal ownership — your right to the property. The deed is the physical, signed document that transfers that right from the seller to you.
At closing you receive a deed; owning valid title is what that deed gives you.
Common Types of Deeds

A general warranty deed offers the strongest protection, with the seller guaranteeing clear ownership going back through the property's history. A special warranty deed guarantees only the seller's own period of ownership.

A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the seller has with no guarantees, so it's typically used between people who trust each other, like family members or in divorce transfers, rather than in a standard sale.
How Deeds Are Handled in Indiana

Indiana closings are usually handled by a title company rather than an attorney. The title company prepares the deed, coordinates escrow, and makes sure the signed deed is recorded with the county recorder so the transfer becomes part of the public record.
Recording matters: it's how the world knows you're the owner and helps protect your claim against later disputes.
faqs: Is a deed the same as a title?
No. Title is your legal ownership, and the deed is the document that transfers that ownership to you.
Who keeps the deed after closing?
You do, as the new owner, and a copy is recorded with the county so there's a permanent public record.
What's a quitclaim deed used for?
It transfers whatever interest someone has without warranties, so it's common between trusted parties like family or in divorce, not typical sales.

h1: What Is a Comparative Market Analysis (CMA)?
title: What Is a Comparative Market Analysis? | Your Realty Link
meta: A comparative market analysis (CMA) uses recent nearby sales to estimate what your home is worth. Learn how an agent builds a CMA in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: How your agent pinpoints a realistic price using what similar homes actually sold for.
definition: A comparative market analysis (CMA) is an agent's estimate of a home's likely market value, based on recent sales of similar nearby properties. It helps set a smart listing or offer price.
qa_lead: A CMA is how a real estate agent estimates what your home is worth right now. Your agent gathers recent sales of comparable homes nearby, adjusts for differences, and factors in current market activity to recommend a price range. It's the foundation for pricing a listing or shaping an offer. Request a free home valuation to get started.
sections: How a CMA Is Built

Your agent starts by pulling comparable homes — recently sold, similar in size, age, style, and location. Active and pending listings help gauge current competition. From there, the agent adjusts for differences like an extra bedroom, an updated kitchen, or a larger lot.
In Central Indiana, this data comes through the MIBOR-powered MLS, so a local agent is working from accurate, up-to-date sales rather than public estimate tools.
CMA vs. Appraisal

A CMA and an appraisal both estimate value, but they serve different roles. A CMA is a pricing tool your agent prepares, usually at no cost. An appraisal is a formal valuation by a licensed appraiser that your lender orders during financing.
A well-built CMA can help you avoid an appraisal gap later by pricing in line with what the market supports.
Why Accurate Pricing Matters

Price too high and a home can sit, pushing up days on market and inviting lowball offers. Price too low and you leave money on the table. A careful CMA aims for the sweet spot that attracts strong buyers.
Whether you're selling or making an offer, a current CMA keeps your decision grounded in real numbers.
faqs: Is a CMA free?
In most cases, yes. Agents typically prepare a CMA at no cost as part of helping you sell or make an offer.
Is a CMA as accurate as an appraisal?
It's a strong, data-based estimate, but an appraisal is a formal, licensed valuation; the two can differ and serve different purposes.
How often should I get a CMA?
Market conditions shift, so if you're actively planning to sell or buy, a CMA from within the last few weeks is most reliable.

title: What Is a Homestead Exemption? | Your Realty Link
meta: Indiana's homestead exemption lowers property taxes on your primary residence. Learn how the standard deduction and property-tax caps work in Indiana.
hero_sub: An Indiana homeowner benefit that can meaningfully lower the property taxes on the home you live in.
definition: In Indiana, a homestead exemption is a set of property-tax benefits for your primary residence that lowers the taxable value of your home and caps how much property tax you can owe.
qa_lead: Indiana's homestead benefits reduce property taxes on the home you own and live in as your main residence. They work by lowering your home's taxable assessed value through deductions and by capping your tax bill. You claim them by filing with your county auditor. If you're buying, ask about this early — it can affect your ongoing housing costs.
sections: How Indiana's Homestead Benefits Work

Indiana offers a homestead standard deduction that reduces the assessed value of your primary home, plus a supplemental homestead deduction that reduces it further. A lower assessed value generally means a lower property-tax bill.
These benefits apply only to a home you own and occupy as your principal residence — not to rentals, vacation homes, or investment property.
The Property-Tax Caps

Indiana's constitution caps property taxes as a share of a home's gross assessed value. For a qualifying homestead, the bill is capped at 1 percent of assessed value, while other residential and commercial property face higher caps of 2 and 3 percent.
This cap, often called the circuit breaker, is a major reason claiming your homestead status matters for keeping housing costs predictable.
How to Claim It

You claim the homestead deduction by filing with your county auditor, and it's commonly handled around the time you close. Once it's on file, it generally stays in place as long as you own and live in the home.
If you've recently bought or aren't sure your homestead is filed, it's worth confirming with your county — a missed filing can quietly raise your tax bill.
faqs: Do I have to reapply every year?
Usually no. Once your homestead deduction is on file in Indiana, it typically remains until your ownership or use of the home changes.
Can I claim a homestead on more than one home?
No. The benefit applies only to your primary residence, so a second home or rental doesn't qualify.
When should I file for the homestead deduction?
Often at or shortly after closing; your title company or county auditor can confirm the deadline and process for your county.

h1: What Are Indiana's Property Tax Caps?
title: What Are Indiana's Property Tax Caps? | Your Realty Link
meta: Indiana's property tax caps limit your annual bill to a share of your home's assessed value. Learn how the 1%, 2%, and 3% circuit breaker caps really work.
hero_sub: Indiana's built-in limit on how much property tax you can owe — and how to keep yours as low as it should be.
definition: Indiana's property tax caps, often called the circuit breaker, limit your annual property tax bill to a set percentage of your home's gross assessed value. Owner-occupied homes are capped at 1%, other residential property and farmland at 2%, and most other property at 3%.
qa_lead: Indiana caps how much property tax you can owe based on your home's gross assessed value. For an owner-occupied home (your homestead), the cap is 1% of assessed value; other residential property and farmland are capped at 2%, and most other property at 3%. It's commonly called the "circuit breaker." See our real estate glossary for related terms.
sections: How Indiana's Property Tax Caps Work

Every property in Indiana gets a "gross assessed value" from the county assessor. The caps limit your total annual bill to a percentage of that value, no matter how high local tax rates climb. Owner-occupied homes fall under the 1% cap, second homes and rentals under 2%, and commercial and most other property under 3%.

Because the cap is tied to assessed value rather than a fixed dollar amount, your ceiling rises and falls as your assessment changes. If your calculated bill would exceed the cap, the circuit breaker credit reduces it back down.
The Homestead Deduction Lowers the Base

To get the 1% homestead cap, you have to file for the homestead deduction on the property you live in as your primary residence. That deduction, along with the supplemental homestead deduction, reduces the assessed value your tax is figured on before the cap is even applied.

You can only claim the homestead on one property, and the paperwork is usually handled at or shortly after closing. If you're buying, ask your title company and county auditor about filing so you don't miss it for the year.
Why Two Similar Homes Can Have Different Bills

Two nearly identical houses on the same street can carry different tax bills. The differences come from whether each owner filed the homestead deduction, when the home last sold, prior assessment history, and any additional deductions (such as those for veterans or seniors) that one owner qualifies for and the other doesn't.

That's why we tell buyers to look at a property's actual assessed value and deductions, not just last year's tax figure — the number can change once the home changes hands. Fold estimated taxes into your monthly payment with our mortgage calculator.
How Taxes Fit Into Your Closing
Property taxes in Indiana are generally paid in arrears, which means at closing they're prorated between buyer and seller. Your title company handles that math as part of escrow.
Understanding your cap helps you budget for the actual bill after you move in, rather than being surprised by it.
faqs: Do property tax caps apply automatically?

The cap itself applies automatically, but the lower 1% homestead cap only kicks in once you've filed the homestead deduction on your primary residence. Filing that paperwork is the step people most often miss.
Will my property taxes go up after I buy?

They can. The prior owner's deductions don't transfer to you, and the assessment may change, so the seller's old tax figure isn't a guaranteed preview of yours. Always confirm the current assessed value and eligible deductions.
Are property tax caps the same in every Indiana county?
The 1%, 2%, and 3% caps are statewide, but local tax rates differ by county, city, and school district, so two homes with the same cap percentage can still owe different amounts.

title: What Is a Conventional Loan? | Your Realty Link
meta: A conventional loan is a mortgage not backed by the government like FHA or VA. Learn how conventional loans work and when they fit Central Indiana buyers.
hero_sub: The most common type of mortgage, explained in plain English.
definition: A conventional loan is a mortgage that isn't insured or guaranteed by a government agency such as the FHA, VA, or USDA. It's offered by private lenders and follows guidelines set by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
qa_lead: A conventional loan is the most common type of mortgage. Unlike FHA, VA, or USDA loans, it isn't backed by the government — it's issued by a private lender following Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines. It often appeals to buyers with steady credit, and if you put down less than 20%, you'll usually pay private mortgage insurance until you build enough equity.
qa_facts: Private lenders, not a government agency
As low as 3% for some qualified buyers
sections: How a Conventional Loan Works

With a conventional loan, a private lender — a bank, credit union, or mortgage company — lends you money to buy a home, and you repay it with interest over a set term, commonly 15 or 30 years. Because there's no government insurance behind the loan, lenders look closely at your credit history, income, debt, and down payment.

Down payments can be lower than many buyers expect, sometimes as little as 3% for qualified borrowers. If you put down less than 20%, you'll typically carry PMI until your equity reaches the point where it can be removed.
Conforming vs. Jumbo Loans

Most conventional loans are "conforming," meaning they fall within the loan limits set each year for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. For higher-priced homes above that limit, you'd need a "jumbo" loan, which is non-conforming and usually comes with stricter requirements.
In most of Central Indiana, home prices keep the majority of buyers comfortably within conforming limits, though luxury purchases in areas like Carmel or Zionsville can push into jumbo territory.
Conventional vs. FHA and VA

FHA loans are government-insured and can be more forgiving on credit and down payment, but they carry their own mortgage insurance for the life of many loans. VA loans, for eligible veterans and service members, often require no down payment. A conventional loan can be attractive when your credit and savings are solid, because PMI can eventually come off and lower your long-term cost.
There's no single "best" loan — the right choice depends on your finances and goals. A local lender can compare options with you side by side.
Is a Conventional Loan Right for You?

If you have reliable income, a reasonable debt load, and some savings for a down payment, a conventional loan is often worth pricing out. Run the numbers with our mortgage calculator, and if you're new to the process, our first-time buyer resources walk through what to expect.
When you're ready, reach out and we'll connect you with trusted Central Indiana lenders who can compare loan types for your situation.
faqs: How much do I need to put down on a conventional loan?
It varies by lender and program, but qualified buyers can sometimes put down as little as 3%. Putting down 20% or more lets you avoid private mortgage insurance.
Can I remove PMI from a conventional loan?
Yes. Unlike some FHA mortgage insurance, conventional PMI can usually be cancelled once you've built enough equity in the home, which can lower your monthly payment over time.
Is a conventional loan better than an FHA loan?
Neither is automatically better. Conventional loans can cost less long term for buyers with strong credit, while FHA loans may be easier to qualify for. Compare both with a lender.

title: What Is an HOA (Homeowners Association)? | Your Realty Link
meta: An HOA (homeowners association) sets neighborhood rules and charges dues for shared spaces. Learn how HOAs work before you buy a home in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: The rules, dues, and fine print behind neighborhood living.
definition: A homeowners association (HOA) is an organization that governs a neighborhood or community, sets rules for the properties in it, and charges owners dues to maintain shared areas and amenities.
qa_lead: An HOA, or homeowners association, manages a planned community or condo development. If you buy in one, you automatically become a member, agree to follow its rules (called covenants, or CC&Rs), and pay regular dues. In return, the HOA maintains common areas and shared amenities. Many newer Central Indiana subdivisions have one.
qa_facts: Automatic when you buy in the community
sections: What an HOA Does

An HOA is a governing body — usually run by a volunteer board of resident homeowners, sometimes with a professional management company — that oversees a neighborhood, condo building, or planned development. Its job is to maintain shared property and enforce a common set of standards so the community stays consistent and well-kept.

Common areas an HOA might maintain include entrance signage, sidewalks, retention ponds, playgrounds, pools, clubhouses, and landscaping in shared spaces. In condos and townhomes, the HOA often handles exterior building maintenance too.
HOA Dues and What They Cover

HOA dues fund the association's budget. How much you pay depends on the community and what it maintains — a subdivision with just a pond and a common entrance costs far less than a condo with a pool, gym, and exterior upkeep. Dues can be billed monthly, quarterly, or annually.

Associations also keep a reserve fund for big-ticket repairs. Occasionally, if reserves fall short, an HOA may levy a "special assessment" — a one-time charge on owners. It's worth asking about a community's reserves and assessment history before you buy.
Rules, Covenants, and Restrictions

When you buy in an HOA community, you agree to its covenants, conditions, and restrictions — the CC&Rs. These can govern things like exterior paint colors, fences, sheds, parking, short-term rentals, and even the type of mailbox you can install. The goal is to protect property values, though the rules aren't for everyone.
Review the CC&Rs carefully. If you plan to rent the home, run a home business, or park an RV, make sure the community allows it before you're committed.
What Indiana Buyers Should Check Before Closing

In Indiana, HOA documents are part of your due diligence. Before closing, request the current dues, the CC&Rs, meeting minutes, and the association's financials. Your agent can help you gather these and read the seller's disclosure.
HOA dues also factor into your monthly budget, so include them when you run the numbers on our mortgage calculator.
faqs: Are HOA dues required?
Yes. If a property is in an HOA, paying dues isn't optional — it's a legal obligation tied to owning the home, and unpaid dues can lead to fines or a lien against the property.
Can an HOA really tell me what I can do with my home?
Within the limits of its recorded covenants, yes. HOAs can enforce rules on exterior changes, landscaping, parking, and rentals. Always read the CC&Rs before buying so there are no surprises.
Do all homes in Central Indiana have an HOA?
No. Many older neighborhoods have none, while most newer subdivisions and condo developments do. Your agent can tell you whether a specific property comes with one.

title: What Happens on Closing Day? | Your Realty Link
meta: Closing day is when a home sale becomes official and ownership transfers. See what happens at an Indiana closing, what to bring, and when you get the keys.
hero_sub: The day the home officially becomes yours — here's what to expect.
definition: Closing day is the final step of a real estate transaction, when ownership of the home officially transfers from the seller to the buyer and the paperwork and funds are completed.
qa_lead: Closing day is when a home sale becomes official. Buyer and seller sign the final documents, funds are exchanged, and ownership legally transfers. In Indiana, closings are typically handled by a title company rather than an attorney, and the signing itself usually takes about an hour. Once it's done and recorded, you get the keys.
qa_facts: Around an hour at the table
Photo ID and any required funds
Deed transfers; you get the keys
sections: Who's at the Closing Table

In a typical Central Indiana closing, you'll meet with a closing agent from the title company who guides both sides through the documents. The buyer, seller, and their real estate agents may attend — sometimes together, sometimes separately. Lenders usually don't attend in person, but their loan documents are part of the package.
Buyers and sellers don't always sit in the same room; it's common for each party to sign at different times or locations, especially when schedules or distance make it easier.
What You'll Sign and Pay

Buyers sign the loan documents, the closing disclosure, and paperwork accepting the deed. Sellers sign the deed transferring ownership and documents confirming payoff of any existing mortgage. You'll also settle the money: buyers bring their down payment and closing costs, usually by wire or cashier's check, and sellers receive their proceeds.
Your earnest money deposit is credited toward what you owe, and prorated items like property taxes are squared up between buyer and seller.
How Indiana Closings Work

Indiana is a "title company" state, which means a licensed title company — not an attorney — usually conducts the closing. The title company also handles the escrow of funds, issues title insurance, and records the deed with the county after signing.
Recording is what makes the transfer official in the public record. In most cases it happens the same day or the next business day, and that's typically when keys change hands.
Before and After You Sign
Before closing day, you'll do your final walk-through to confirm the home's condition. On the day itself, bring a valid photo ID and be ready to sign a lot of pages.
Afterward, keep your closing documents somewhere safe — you'll want them for taxes and future reference. Questions about your closing? Get in touch.
faqs: How long does closing day take?
The signing itself usually takes around an hour, though it can be quicker or longer depending on the loan. The bigger timeline is the weeks of preparation leading up to it.
What do I need to bring to closing?
A valid government-issued photo ID and any funds you owe, usually sent by wire or brought as a cashier's check. Your title company or agent will tell you the exact amount ahead of time.
When do I get the keys?
Usually once the sale is funded and the deed is recorded, which is often the same day or the next business day. Your agent will confirm the exact hand-off with you.

h1: What Is a Buyer's Agency Agreement?
title: What Is a Buyer's Agency Agreement? | Your Realty Link
meta: A buyer's agency agreement is a contract hiring an agent to represent you. Learn what it covers, how agents get paid, and why it's now standard in Indiana.
hero_sub: The contract that puts a real estate agent officially on your side.
definition: A buyer's agency agreement is a written contract between a homebuyer and a real estate agent that defines their working relationship, the agent's duties, and how the agent is compensated.
qa_lead: A buyer's agency agreement is a written contract that hires a real estate agent to represent you as a buyer. It spells out what the agent will do for you, how long the agreement lasts, and how they get paid. In Indiana, having buyers sign an agreement before touring homes has become standard practice, and it makes the agent legally your advocate.
qa_facts: A contract hiring your buyer's agent
A fiduciary duty to you, the buyer
Terms and length can be discussed
sections: What the Agreement Does

A buyer's agency agreement turns a casual relationship into a formal one. Once you sign, your agent owes you fiduciary duties — loyalty, confidentiality, honest advice, and putting your interests first. Without an agreement, an agent you're working with may technically represent the seller or simply be a facilitator, not your advocate.
The document typically names the agent and brokerage, describes the services they'll provide, sets a time period, and often defines the geographic area or type of property you're searching for.
Why Agents Ask Buyers to Sign One

Recent changes in how real estate commissions are handled nationwide have made written buyer agreements the norm. Practically, many agents and MLS systems now expect buyers to have a signed agreement in place before touring homes. It protects you by making the agent's role and duties clear from the start.
Think of it less as a trap and more as a job description — it's the point where an agent officially goes to work for you.
How Buyer's Agents Get Paid

The agreement states how your agent is paid and by whom. Historically, sellers often covered the buyer's agent commission, and in many transactions that's still negotiated. But the agreement makes the arrangement explicit, so you know up front what you might owe if the seller doesn't cover it.
Compensation is negotiable and varies by transaction. Ask your agent to walk you through the numbers and how they fit into your overall closing costs.
What to Look For Before You Sign

Read the term length and whether it's exclusive. Ask what happens if you're not satisfied and how to end the agreement early. Make sure you understand the compensation section and any "protection period" that applies after it ends.
A good agent will happily explain every line. Learn more about buyer representation or reach out with questions before you sign anything.
faqs: Do I have to sign a buyer's agency agreement?

In practice, most agents now ask you to sign one before showing homes, and it's become standard across the industry. The terms, including length, are negotiable, so discuss anything you're unsure about.
How long does a buyer's agency agreement last?
It varies. Some cover a single showing, others run for weeks or months. The length is negotiable, so ask for a term you're comfortable with before signing.
Can I cancel a buyer's agency agreement?
Often yes, depending on the terms. Many agreements include a way to end the relationship, but confirm the cancellation and any protection-period language before you sign.

title: What Is a Final Walk-Through? | Your Realty Link
meta: A final walk-through is your last look at a home before closing. Learn what to check, how it fits the timeline, and what to do if something isn't right.
hero_sub: Your last look before the keys are yours.
definition: A final walk-through is the buyer's last visit to a home shortly before closing, done to confirm the property's condition and that agreed-upon repairs and terms have been met.
qa_lead: A final walk-through is your last look at the home right before closing day. It's not another inspection — it's a chance to confirm the house is in the condition you agreed to, that any negotiated repairs are done, and that nothing has changed since your offer. It usually happens within a day or two of closing.
qa_facts: A buyer's last look before closing
Your agent addresses it before closing
sections: What You're Checking For

During the walk-through, you're confirming the home is in the shape you expect. Check that agreed-upon repairs were completed, that fixtures and appliances included in the sale are still there, and that the seller has removed their belongings and any trash. Test the basics — lights, faucets, toilets, garage door, heating and cooling, and outlets.

Also look for anything new: damage from moving out, a leak that appeared since your last visit, or items that were supposed to convey but are missing. Bring your purchase agreement and inspection notes so you can compare.
How the Walk-Through Fits the Timeline

The final walk-through is usually scheduled within a day or two of closing, once the seller has moved out. It's the last checkpoint after your inspection, appraisal, and any repair negotiations are complete. Skipping it isn't wise — it's your chance to catch problems while you still have leverage, before ownership transfers.
If your purchase was subject to repairs handled through a contingency, the walk-through is where you verify that work actually got done.
What to Do If Something's Wrong

If something isn't right, don't panic and don't feel pressured to sign anyway. Tell your agent right away. Depending on the issue, the closing can be delayed, funds can be held back in escrow to cover a repair, or the seller can be asked to make it right before you close.
Most walk-throughs go smoothly, but the whole point is to protect you. Have questions about your walk-through or closing? Reach out and we'll help.
faqs: Is a final walk-through the same as a home inspection?

No. An inspection is a detailed professional evaluation done earlier in the process. The walk-through is a quick visual check right before closing to confirm the home's condition hasn't changed and repairs were completed.
What if the seller hasn't finished agreed-upon repairs?
Let your agent know immediately. Options include delaying closing, holding money in escrow to cover the work, or requiring the seller to complete it before the sale is finalized.
Can I skip the final walk-through?
You can, but it's rarely a good idea. It's your last chance to spot issues while you still have negotiating power, so most buyers take advantage of it.

title: What Is an As-Is Sale? | Your Realty Link
meta: An as-is sale means the seller won't make repairs, but you can still inspect. Learn how as-is home sales work in Indiana and what buyers and sellers should know.
hero_sub: Sold in current condition — but you still have more rights than you might think.
definition: An as-is sale is a real estate transaction in which the seller offers the property in its current condition and won't make repairs, though the buyer can typically still inspect and back out based on what they find.
qa_lead: An as-is sale means the seller is offering the home in its current condition and doesn't plan to make repairs or give credits for them. It does not mean you give up your right to inspect the property. In Indiana, sellers still generally have to complete a seller's disclosure, and buyers can usually still walk away if an inspection reveals a problem.
qa_facts: The seller can hide known defects
sections: What "As-Is" Really Means

Selling a home "as-is" signals that the seller won't be making repairs or improvements before closing and won't negotiate credits for the property's condition. The price often reflects that. It's a way of saying, "what you see is what you get."

Importantly, as-is refers to condition, not disclosure. In Indiana, sellers of most residential homes are still required to complete a seller's disclosure form and can't knowingly conceal or misrepresent defects they're aware of.
You Can Still Inspect

An as-is sale doesn't take away your right to a home inspection. Most buyers should still hire an inspector to understand exactly what they're buying. Depending on how your offer is written, you may keep an inspection contingency that lets you cancel if the inspection turns up something you can't live with.

The difference is expectation: in an as-is deal, you generally can't ask the seller to fix what the inspection finds. You can, however, use that information to decide whether to move forward or walk away.
Why Sellers Choose As-Is

Sellers choose as-is for many reasons. Estate and probate sales, where heirs are settling a loved one's property, are often as-is because no one has the time or funds to make repairs. Foreclosures and investor flips are commonly as-is too, as are situations where a seller simply wants a faster, simpler sale.
An as-is listing isn't a red flag by itself — it just tells you the seller's starting position on repairs. Plenty of solid homes are sold this way.
Tips for Buyers and Sellers in Indiana

If you're buying as-is, budget for potential repairs, read the disclosure closely, and lean on your inspection. If you're selling as-is, know that pricing and honest disclosure matter more than ever — a fair price and full transparency attract serious buyers.
Thinking about selling? Start with a free home valuation or contact us to talk through your options.
faqs: Can I still get an inspection on an as-is home?
Yes. As-is refers to the seller not making repairs, not to your right to inspect. Most buyers should still hire an inspector so they fully understand the home's condition before closing.
Does "as-is" let the seller hide problems?
No. In Indiana, sellers of most homes must still complete a seller's disclosure and can't knowingly conceal known defects. As-is only means they won't repair those issues.
Why would someone sell a house as-is?
Common reasons include estate or probate sales, foreclosures, investor properties, or a seller who wants a quicker, simpler transaction without negotiating repairs.

title: What Is a Closing Disclosure? | Your Realty Link
meta: A Closing Disclosure spells out your final loan terms and closing costs, delivered at least three business days before your Indiana closing to review.
hero_sub: The paperwork that spells out exactly what you will pay and sign for at the closing table.
definition: A Closing Disclosure is a standardized five-page form that details your final loan terms, monthly payment, and closing costs before you sign at the closing table.
qa_lead: Your lender must send you the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing so you have time to review it against your earlier Loan Estimate. Compare the two side by side and flag any number that jumped.
qa_facts: At least 3 business days before closing
sections: What's Inside the Closing Disclosure

The form breaks out your loan amount, interest rate, monthly payment, and every closing cost line item, from lender fees to title charges and prepaid escrow. It also shows your total cash to close so there are no surprises at the table.
Because Indiana closings are typically run by a title company rather than an attorney, your closing agent or lender coordinates getting this document to you on time.
Why the Three-Day Window Matters

Federal rules require the three-business-day review period so you are not handed surprise numbers minutes before signing. If key terms change significantly after that, the clock can reset and push closing back.
Our agents recommend reviewing the Closing Disclosure line by line as soon as it arrives and asking your lender about any figure that does not match your Loan Estimate.
faqs: What's the difference between a Loan Estimate and a Closing Disclosure?
The Loan Estimate is an early preview of your likely costs; the Closing Disclosure shows your actual, final numbers shortly before closing.
Can numbers still change after I get the Closing Disclosure?
Small changes can happen, but significant increases in certain fees can trigger a new three-day review period.
Who sends the Closing Disclosure?
Your mortgage lender prepares and delivers it, though your agent and title company can help you interpret it.
What should I check first?
Compare the loan amount, interest rate, monthly payment, and total closing costs against your Loan Estimate.

title: What Is Cash to Close? | Your Realty Link
meta: Cash to close is the total amount a buyer brings to closing: down payment plus closing costs and prepaids, minus credits and earnest money already paid.
hero_sub: The single dollar figure that tells you what to actually bring to the closing table.
definition: Cash to close is the total amount a buyer must provide at closing, combining the down payment, closing costs, and prepaid items minus any credits and earnest money already paid.
qa_lead: Your cash to close is the bottom-line number on your Closing Disclosure, not just your down payment. It typically arrives by cashier's check or wire, and your lender or title company will confirm the exact amount a few days before closing.
qa_facts: Down payment, closing costs, and prepaids
Credits and earnest money already paid
Wire or cashier's check, per your title company
sections: How Cash to Close Is Calculated

Start with your down payment, then add closing costs like lender fees, title charges, and prepaid items such as homeowners insurance and property tax reserves. Subtract any seller credits and the earnest money you already put down, and what is left is your cash to close.
Your final number can shift slightly from your Loan Estimate as real invoices and prorations come in, which is why the Closing Disclosure is the figure to trust.
Getting the Funds There Safely

Most title companies require a wire transfer or cashier's check rather than a personal check for cash to close. Always confirm wiring instructions by phone using a number you already have on file, never one from an email alone.
Our agents walk buyers through this step so the funds arrive on time and safely, with no last-minute scrambling.
faqs: Is cash to close the same as my down payment?
No. It includes the down payment plus closing costs and prepaids, minus credits and earnest money already paid.
When do I find out the exact amount?
Your Closing Disclosure, issued at least three business days before closing, shows the final figure.
Can I pay cash to close with a personal check?
Most title companies require a wire or cashier's check above a small threshold, so confirm their preferred method.
What if I don't have enough cash to close?
Talk to your lender early about seller concessions, gift funds, or down payment assistance options.

title: What Are Prorations at Closing? | Your Realty Link
meta: Prorations split ongoing costs like property taxes between buyer and seller based on the closing date. Indiana's arrears billing makes tax prorations tricky.
hero_sub: Splitting the bills fairly between buyer and seller for the exact days each of you owned the home.
definition: Prorations divide ongoing costs like property taxes between buyer and seller based on how many days each owned the home during the billing period, settled on the settlement statement.
qa_lead: Because Indiana property taxes are billed a year in arrears, prorating them accurately takes extra care so neither side over- or underpays. Your title company calculates the split and shows it on your settlement statement.
sections: Why Indiana Property Tax Prorations Take Extra Care

Indiana bills property taxes for the prior year, so the tax bill you are prorating at closing often does not match what either party will actually owe going forward. Title companies typically estimate using the most recent bill and note that figures are approximate.
Ask your title company to walk through the specific tax proration method they are using so you understand what you are being credited or charged for.
Other Items That Can Be Prorated
Beyond property taxes, prorations can cover HOA dues, prepaid utilities transferred to the buyer, and occasionally rents on an investment property. Each is split based on the closing date.
These figures show up as small credits or debits on your Closing Disclosure and settlement statement, so review them alongside the bigger line items.
faqs: Why are Indiana property tax prorations more complicated?
Indiana bills taxes a year behind, so the closing proration is often an estimate rather than the exact final amount.
Who calculates prorations?
Your title company calculates them and shows the results on the settlement statement.
Can HOA dues be prorated too?
Yes, prepaid HOA dues are commonly prorated between buyer and seller at closing.
Will I owe more property tax later because of the proration?
It's possible if the proration was based on an older bill. Ask your title company how they estimated the amount.

title: What Are Recording Fees? | Your Realty Link
meta: Recording fees are charges paid to the county recorder to enter your new deed and mortgage into public record, a small, standard part of closing costs.
hero_sub: A small, standard closing cost that makes your new deed and mortgage official public record.
definition: Recording fees are charges paid to the county recorder's office to officially enter your new deed and mortgage into the public record.
qa_lead: Recording fees are collected at closing and passed through to the county recorder so your deed and mortgage are on file. They are a standard, relatively modest line item compared to bigger costs like lender fees or title insurance.
qa_facts: Your Closing Disclosure and settlement statement
sections: What Gets Recorded and Why

When you buy a home, the county recorder's office needs an official copy of your new deed and, if you financed the purchase, your mortgage document. Recording puts the transaction into the public record, which protects your ownership and establishes the lender's lien.
Each county sets its own per-page recording fee, which your title company collects at closing and forwards to the recorder.
How Recording Fees Fit Into Your Closing Costs

Recording fees are usually a small fraction of your overall closing costs compared to lender fees, title insurance, or prepaid escrow items. They are itemized separately on your Closing Disclosure so you can see exactly what is being charged.
Because they are set by the county rather than negotiable, there is little room to shop around on this particular fee.
faqs: Who pays recording fees, buyer or seller?
This is negotiable, but the buyer typically pays the fee to record the deed and mortgage.
Do recording fees vary by county?
Yes, each Indiana county recorder sets its own fee schedule.
Are recording fees the same as transfer tax?
No. Indiana does not charge a transfer tax; recording fees are a separate administrative charge for filing documents.
Can I negotiate recording fees?
No, they are set by the county recorder and are not negotiable, unlike some lender or title fees.

title: What Is a Transfer Tax? | Your Realty Link
meta: A transfer tax is a fee some states charge when property changes hands, based on sale price. Indiana levies no state or county real estate transfer tax.
hero_sub: One closing cost Indiana sellers and buyers do not have to budget for.
definition: A transfer tax is a fee some states charge when real estate changes ownership, typically based on the sale price; Indiana does not levy a state or county real estate transfer tax.
qa_lead: Good news for Central Indiana buyers and sellers: Indiana does not charge a state or county real estate transfer tax, unlike many other states. You will still see a modest recording fee to file your deed, but not a percentage-of-price transfer tax.
sections: Why Indiana Does Not Have a Transfer Tax

Many states charge a transfer tax calculated as a percentage of the sale price whenever a deed changes hands. Indiana chose not to adopt one, which keeps closing costs somewhat lower here than in states that do.
If you are relocating from a state that does charge transfer tax, this is one line item you can simply cross off your Indiana closing cost worksheet.
What You'll See Instead

Instead of a transfer tax, Indiana closings include a modest county recording fee to file the new deed and mortgage, plus the usual lender, title, and prepaid items detailed on your Closing Disclosure.
Sellers do complete a Sales Disclosure Form with the county, which is a reporting requirement rather than a tax.
faqs: Does Indiana charge a real estate transfer tax?
No. Indiana does not levy a state or county real estate transfer tax.
Will I still pay something to record my deed?
Yes, a separate, smaller recording fee covers filing your deed and mortgage with the county.
Is the Sales Disclosure Form a tax?
No, it is a reporting form filed with the county assessor, not a transfer tax.
Do other states near Indiana charge transfer tax?
Practices vary by state, so check with your agent if you are moving across state lines.

title: What Is a Settlement Statement? | Your Realty Link
meta: A settlement statement itemizes every credit and charge for buyer and seller at closing, often the ALTA statement that accompanies the Closing Disclosure.
hero_sub: The itemized accounting that shows exactly where every closing dollar comes from and goes.
definition: A settlement statement is an itemized accounting of every credit and charge for both buyer and seller at closing, often prepared as an ALTA statement alongside the Closing Disclosure.
qa_lead: Your settlement statement lines up every cost and credit in the transaction side by side, from your earnest money deposit to prorations and agent commissions. It is the document to review closely, since it is the final word on where the money moved.
qa_facts: All buyer and seller credits and charges
sections: What's Included on the Settlement Statement

The settlement statement lists every dollar in the deal: purchase price, loan amount, deposits already paid, prorated taxes and HOA dues, agent commissions, and each closing fee, split into buyer and seller columns.
Because it is comprehensive, it is a useful cross-check against your Closing Disclosure, especially for sellers, who do not otherwise receive a Closing Disclosure of their own.
Why Sellers Rely on This Document

Buyers get a federally mandated Closing Disclosure, but sellers' numbers most often show up on the settlement statement instead, detailing their net proceeds after paying off the mortgage, commissions, and closing costs.
Our agents review the settlement statement with sellers ahead of closing day so the final proceeds figure is never a surprise.
faqs: Is a settlement statement the same as a Closing Disclosure?
They are related but not identical. Buyers get a Closing Disclosure; the settlement statement covers both sides of the transaction in one document.
Who prepares the settlement statement?
Your title company prepares it as part of coordinating the closing.
When do I see it?
You should receive a preliminary version a few days before closing so you can review it in advance.
What if I find an error on it?
Contact your title company or agent right away, before closing, so it can be corrected.

h1: What Does a Title Company Do?
title: What Does a Title Company Do? | Your Realty Link
meta: A title company is the neutral third party that searches the title, issues title insurance, and conducts the closing for Central Indiana buyers and sellers.
hero_sub: The neutral third party that clears the title, holds the money, and runs the closing.
definition: A title company is a neutral third party that searches the property's title history, issues title insurance, and conducts the closing itself.
qa_lead: In Indiana, closings are typically run by a title company rather than an attorney, so this is the office where you will sign your final paperwork. They perform the title search, issue title insurance, and hold funds in escrow until everything is ready to record.
qa_facts: Title search, title insurance, escrow, closing
Often negotiated between buyer and seller
sections: What Happens Behind the Scenes

Before closing, the title company searches public records for liens, judgments, or ownership gaps, then issues a title commitment showing what needs to be cleared. On closing day, they prepare the settlement statement, collect and disburse funds, and record the new deed and mortgage with the county.
Because they hold funds in escrow and coordinate everyone's paperwork, choosing an experienced, responsive title company matters as much as choosing a good lender.
Who Picks the Title Company
In many Central Indiana contracts, the choice of title company is negotiable between buyer and seller, and our agents can recommend companies with a strong track record of closing on time.
Whoever you choose, they remain neutral, working to close the transaction correctly rather than advocating for either party.
faqs: Does Indiana use attorneys or title companies to close?
Most Central Indiana closings are handled by title companies rather than real estate attorneys.
Can I choose my own title company?
Often yes, this is typically negotiable in the purchase agreement.
Is the title company on my side?
They are neutral. Their job is to close the transaction correctly, not to represent buyer or seller.
What if the title search finds a problem?
The title company will require it to be resolved, such as paying off an old lien, before closing can proceed.

title: What Is the Possession Date? | Your Realty Link
meta: The possession date is when a buyer gets the keys and legal right to occupy the home, usually closing day but sometimes negotiated separately in writing.
hero_sub: The day the keys actually change hands, which is not always the same day you close.
definition: The possession date is the day a buyer receives keys and the legal right to occupy the home, most often closing day itself but sometimes negotiated separately.
qa_lead: Most Central Indiana contracts set possession at closing, but buyer and seller can agree to a different date, such as a short post-closing occupancy for the seller. Whatever is agreed goes in writing in the purchase agreement.
qa_facts: Seller stays a few extra days post-closing
Determines who is responsible for the home and utilities
sections: Same-Day vs. Delayed Possession

When possession happens at closing, the buyer typically gets keys once the deed and funds have recorded, sometimes the same afternoon. When a seller needs extra time to move, the parties can negotiate a delayed or post-closing occupancy period, often with a daily fee to compensate the buyer.
Whichever arrangement you choose, put the exact date, time, and any occupancy fee in writing so there is no ambiguity.
Protecting Yourself Around the Possession Date

If the seller will occupy the home after closing, buyers should consider a short-term occupancy agreement outlining daily rent, a security deposit, and what happens if the seller does not vacate on time. A final walk-through right before closing helps confirm the home's condition before keys change hands.
Our agents help negotiate possession terms that work for both sides, especially in a competitive market where sellers may need a little extra time.
faqs: Does possession always happen on closing day?
Most often, yes, but it can be negotiated to happen a few days before or after closing.
What if the seller wants to stay after closing?
Buyer and seller can agree to a post-closing occupancy period, typically with a daily fee in writing.
Should I schedule the final walk-through around possession?
Yes, plan your final walk-through close to closing so the home's condition matches what was agreed.
What happens if the seller won't leave on the possession date?
This should be addressed in the occupancy agreement, which can include penalties for overstaying.

title: What Is Closing Wire Fraud? | Your Realty Link
meta: Closing wire fraud is a scam where criminals impersonate a title company or agent to send fake wiring instructions. Always verify by phone before wiring funds.
hero_sub: A costly scam that targets buyers right when the biggest wire of the transaction is due.
definition: Closing wire fraud is a scam in which criminals impersonate a title company, lender, or agent and send fake wiring instructions to trick buyers into sending their closing funds to a fraudulent account.
qa_lead: Scammers often hack or spoof email accounts involved in a transaction, then send convincing but fake wiring instructions right before closing. Always verify wire details by phone using a number you already have on file, such as from your title company's printed paperwork, never a number from the email itself.
qa_facts: Fake or hacked emails with altered wiring instructions
Verify by phone using a known, independently sourced number
Wire funds based on email instructions alone
Call your bank and the title company immediately
sections: How the Scam Typically Works

Criminals monitor email threads between buyers, agents, lenders, and title companies, then send a spoofed email right before closing with wiring instructions that look legitimate but route to the scammer's account. Once funds are wired, they are often very difficult or impossible to recover.
Because so much money moves right at closing, this is one of the highest-value targets for real estate scammers nationally, not just in Central Indiana.
How to Protect Yourself

Never rely solely on wiring instructions received by email, even if they appear to come from your title company. Call your title company directly using a phone number you sourced independently, such as from their website or earlier paperwork, and verbally confirm the account and routing numbers before you send anything.
If you ever suspect fraud, contact your bank immediately to attempt a wire recall, then notify your title company and agent right away.
faqs: How do I verify wiring instructions are legitimate?
Call your title company using a phone number you already have, not one from the email, and confirm the details verbally.
What should I do if I already sent a wire to the wrong account?
Contact your bank immediately to request a wire recall, then notify your title company and law enforcement.
Can title companies reverse a fraudulent wire?
Sometimes, if caught within hours, but there is no guarantee, which is why prevention matters most.
Are email wiring instructions ever safe to trust alone?
No. Always verify by phone before wiring any closing funds, no matter how legitimate the email looks.

title: What Is a Home Warranty? | Your Realty Link
meta: A home warranty is a service contract that helps cover repair or replacement of major home systems and appliances that break down, usually for one year.
hero_sub: A service contract that helps cushion the cost when a major system or appliance fails after you move in.
definition: A home warranty is a service contract that helps cover the repair or replacement of major home systems and appliances that break down from normal wear, typically for one year.
qa_lead: A home warranty is different from title insurance or a home inspection — it is ongoing coverage for things like your HVAC system, water heater, or major appliances after you move in. Sellers sometimes offer one to reassure buyers, and coverage can usually be renewed afterward.
qa_facts: Major systems and appliances that fail from normal wear
Seller, as a concession, or buyer directly
Homeowners insurance or a home inspection
sections: What a Home Warranty Actually Covers

Home warranty plans typically cover core systems like HVAC, plumbing, and electrical, along with major appliances such as the water heater, oven, or dishwasher, when they fail from normal wear and tear. Coverage tiers and exclusions vary by provider, so it is worth reading the contract before relying on it.
It is not a substitute for a thorough home inspection, which evaluates the current condition of the home rather than insuring against future breakdowns.
Why Sellers Often Offer One

Including a home warranty is a low-cost way for a seller to reassure a buyer who is nervous about an older furnace or water heater, and it can be a useful negotiating tool during offer discussions. Buyers can also purchase a plan directly if the seller does not include one.
Our agents can point you toward reputable providers and help you weigh whether a warranty makes sense for a particular home's age and systems.
faqs: Does a home warranty replace homeowners insurance?
No. Homeowners insurance covers major disasters like fire or storm damage; a home warranty covers mechanical breakdowns of systems and appliances.
Who pays for the home warranty?
Either the seller as a concession or the buyer directly; it is negotiable and often written into the purchase agreement.
Are all repairs automatically covered?
No, coverage depends on the plan's terms, and pre-existing conditions or certain components may be excluded.
Can I renew a home warranty after the first year?
Yes, most plans can be renewed annually for an additional premium.

title: What Is a Condominium? | Your Realty Link
meta: A condominium is a home where you own your unit and share ownership of common areas through an HOA. Here's how condo ownership works for Central Indiana buyers.
hero_sub: Own your space, share the upkeep - condo living trades yard work for shared amenities and a monthly HOA bill.
definition: A condominium is a form of ownership where you hold title to your individual unit while sharing ownership of the building, grounds, and amenities with other owners through a homeowners association.
qa_lead: In a condo, you own everything inside your unit's walls, while the HOA owns and maintains the roof, exterior, and common areas. Monthly dues cover that upkeep along with amenities like pools or fitness rooms, so budgeting for HOA fees is just as important as the mortgage payment.
sections: How Condo Ownership Works

When you buy a condominium, your deed covers the interior space of your unit, not the land or structure around it. The building, roof, landscaping, and shared amenities belong collectively to every owner through the association, which is why condo purchases always come with an HOA and monthly dues.

Those dues fund routine maintenance, insurance on the shared structure, and often a reserve fund for big-ticket repairs down the road. Before writing an offer, ask for the HOA's budget and reserve study so you know the dues are realistic.
Condo vs. Townhouse vs. Single-Family Home

A condo differs from a townhouse mainly in what you own: condo owners typically own only interior air space, while townhouse owners usually own the structure and the ground it sits on. A single-family home owner owns the whole property outright, with no association required.
Central Indiana condos are common in and around downtown Indianapolis and in select suburban developments, appealing to buyers who want low-maintenance living without giving up ownership entirely.
Financing a Condominium

Not every loan works the same way for condos. Conventional, FHA, and VA lenders often require the condo project itself to be approved before they will finance a unit in it, since the lender is also relying on the HOA's financial health.
Your lender or agent can check a project's approval status early, which helps avoid surprises after you are already under contract.
faqs: Are condo fees the same as HOA dues?
Yes - condo fees are simply the HOA dues charged to condo owners, covering shared maintenance, insurance, and amenities.
Can I get a mortgage for a condo the same way as a house?
Often, but the lender typically also needs to approve the condo project itself, which can add an extra step compared to financing a single-family home.
Do condos appreciate in value like houses?
Condos can appreciate, though their value is also tied to how well the HOA is managed and funded, so a healthy association matters to resale.
What happens if I do not pay HOA dues?
The association can place a lien on your unit and pursue collection, so unpaid dues are a serious issue to resolve before closing on a resale.

title: What Is a Townhouse? | Your Realty Link
meta: A townhouse is an attached home where you typically own the structure and land, not just the interior. See how townhouse ownership compares in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: Attached like a condo, owned more like a house - the townhouse sits in between.
definition: A townhouse is an attached home, usually sharing one or two walls with neighboring units, where the owner typically holds title to both the structure and the small lot it sits on.
qa_lead: Townhouses split the difference between a condominium and a single-family home: you get the shared walls and lower price point of attached living, but you usually own your own roof, siding, and yard instead of relying on an association for the whole exterior. Many, though not all, Central Indiana townhouse communities still carry an HOA for shared streets, entrances, or green space.
sections: How Townhouse Ownership Differs From a Condo

The biggest distinction between a townhouse and a condo is what's on your deed. Condo owners generally own only the interior air space of their unit, while townhouse owners usually own the exterior walls, roof, and the ground beneath the home, similar to a detached house.

That means townhouse owners are often responsible for their own exterior maintenance and homeowners insurance on the structure, even when an HOA exists to maintain shared streets, entrances, or a clubhouse.
When a Townhouse Comes With an HOA

Most newer Central Indiana townhouse developments are set up as a planned unit development with an HOA that maintains common areas, enforces community rules, and collects dues. Some older or smaller townhouse rows have no formal association at all.
If an HOA is in place, review its CC and Rs and financials the same way you would for a condo, since dues and rules can vary widely between communities.
faqs: Do I own the land under a townhouse?
Usually yes - most townhouse owners hold title to the structure and a small footprint of land, unlike a condo where ownership is typically limited to the interior.
Is a townhouse cheaper than a single-family home?
Townhouses are often more affordable than comparable single-family homes in the same area, largely because the lot is smaller and some maintenance is shared.
Do all townhouses have HOA dues?
Not all, but most newer communities do, since shared streets, entrances, and amenities need ongoing upkeep.
Can a townhouse appreciate as well as a detached home?
It can, though appreciation is also influenced by the health of the HOA and how well the broader community is maintained.

title: What Is a Single-Family Home? | Your Realty Link
meta: A single-family home is a standalone house on its own lot with no shared walls. See what sets this home type apart for Central Indiana buyers and sellers.
hero_sub: One house, one lot, one owner - the most common home type in Central Indiana.
definition: A single-family home is a standalone residential structure built on its own lot, not attached to any neighboring home, with the owner holding title to both the house and the land.
qa_lead: A single-family home stands alone on its own lot, unlike a condominium or townhouse that shares walls or common ownership with neighbors. It is the most common home type across Marion County and the surrounding suburbs, and it gives owners full control over the property without relying on an association for exterior upkeep.
qa_facts: Possible, but not required by the home type itself
sections: What Makes a Home Single-Family

A single-family home is defined by what it is not attached to: no shared walls, no shared roof, and no collective ownership structure like a condo association. The owner is responsible for the entire structure and yard, and any maintenance, without needing another owner's sign-off.
This is different from a townhouse, which shares walls, or a condominium, where the interior is owned individually but the building and grounds are shared.
Single-Family Homes and HOAs

Standing alone does not mean an HOA is off the table. Many single-family subdivisions across Central Indiana, especially newer construction, are organized as a planned unit development with an association that maintains entrances, common areas, or a neighborhood pool.
Older, established neighborhoods and rural properties are more likely to have no HOA at all, so it's worth confirming either way before you fall in love with a house.
faqs: Is every single-family home in an HOA?
No - plenty of single-family neighborhoods, especially older or rural ones, have no HOA, while many newer subdivisions do.
What is the difference between a single-family home and a duplex?
A single-family home has one owner and one household, while a duplex is a two-unit structure that can be owned as one property or sold as separate units.
Are single-family homes a good investment in Central Indiana?
They are the most widely bought and financed home type in the area, which generally supports steady demand, though every investment depends on the specific property and market.
Do single-family homeowners have to maintain the exterior themselves?
Yes, since there is no association owning the structure, the homeowner is fully responsible for the roof, siding, yard, and everything else.

h1: What Is a Planned Unit Development (PUD)?
title: What Is a Planned Unit Development (PUD)? | Your Realty Link
meta: A planned unit development, or PUD, is a community of homes and shared amenities governed by an HOA. Learn how PUDs work for Central Indiana home buyers.
hero_sub: Your own home and lot, plus shared amenities and rules that come with the neighborhood.
definition: A planned unit development, or PUD, is a residential community where owners hold title to their individual home and lot while a homeowners association governs and maintains shared amenities and common areas.
qa_lead: In a PUD, you own your house and the ground beneath it outright, much like any single-family home, but you also belong to an HOA that maintains shared spaces like entrances, trails, or a pool. Many newer Central Indiana subdivisions, including both single-family and townhouse communities, are structured this way.
qa_facts: HOA oversees common areas and rules
sections: How a PUD Is Structured

Unlike a condo, where the association typically owns the building exterior, a PUD lets each owner hold title to their own home and lot. The HOA's role is narrower: maintaining shared amenities, common green space, and enforcing the community's CC and Rs.
PUDs can include single-family homes, townhouses, or a mix of both, which is why the label describes the community's governance more than a specific building style.
What a PUD Means for Buyers
Buying in a PUD means budgeting for monthly or annual HOA dues on top of your mortgage, and agreeing to follow the community's rules on things like exterior changes, parking, and landscaping.

It also usually means access to amenities the HOA maintains, such as pools, walking trails, or a clubhouse, which is part of why many newer subdivisions across Hamilton, Hendricks, and Johnson counties are built this way.
faqs: Is a PUD the same as an HOA community?
A PUD is a type of HOA community, specifically one where owners hold title to their own home and lot rather than sharing ownership of the building itself.
Do all PUDs have amenities like pools?
Not all, but many newer PUDs include shared amenities, since that is often part of what the HOA dues fund.
Can a PUD include townhouses?
Yes - a PUD describes the governance structure, so it can include single-family homes, townhouses, or a mix, depending on the community.
What should I review before buying in a PUD?
Ask for the HOA's CC and Rs, budget, and any pending special assessments so you understand the rules and costs before you commit.

title: What Are CC and Rs? | Your Realty Link
meta: CC and Rs are the covenants, conditions, and restrictions that govern an HOA community. Learn what they cover and why to review them before buying in Indiana.
hero_sub: The rulebook every HOA community runs on - and one every buyer should read before closing.
