definition: CC and Rs, short for covenants, conditions, and restrictions, are the recorded rules that govern what owners can and cannot do within an HOA community, from exterior paint colors to parking and pets.
qa_lead: CC and Rs are legally binding once you buy in an HOA community, covering everything from fence height to whether you can park a boat in the driveway. They are recorded against the property, so they transfer to every future owner and are worth reading in full before you write an offer, not after.
qa_facts: County land records, tied to the property
The HOA board or management company
sections: What CC and Rs Typically Cover

CC and Rs spell out what owners can and cannot do with their property while it's part of the community. Common provisions address exterior paint and materials, fencing, landscaping, parking, pets, and sometimes whether a home can be rented out.
Because the rules are recorded against the property in county land records, they run with the land and bind every future owner, not just whoever agreed to them originally.
Why Buyers Should Read Them Before Closing
It's easy to focus on price and condition and skip the fine print, but CC and Rs can affect how you actually live in a home, whether you can add a fence, park an RV, or run a home business.
Ask your agent or the seller for a current copy along with the HOA's resale certificate early in the process, so any dealbreaker surfaces before you are under contract, not after.
faqs: Can CC and Rs change after I buy?
Yes, most associations can amend their CC and Rs through a member vote, though the process and required approval percentage vary by community.
What happens if I violate the CC and Rs?
The HOA can typically issue a warning, fine, or in some cases pursue further action, depending on the violation and the association's enforcement policy.
Are CC and Rs the same in every HOA?
No, each community writes and records its own, so rules can vary significantly even between neighboring subdivisions.
Where can I get a copy of the CC and Rs before buying?
Your agent can typically request them from the seller or HOA management company, and they are also recorded with the county.

title: What Is a Special Assessment? | Your Realty Link
meta: A special assessment is a one-time HOA charge to cover a major expense beyond regular dues. Learn how they work and what Central Indiana buyers should ask.
hero_sub: The bill that shows up when an HOA's regular dues are not enough to cover a big repair.
definition: A special assessment is a one-time charge an HOA levies on all owners to pay for a major expense, such as a roof replacement or road repair, that isn't covered by regular monthly dues.
qa_lead: When an HOA faces a large expense its reserve fund cannot fully cover, it can levy a special assessment, a one-time charge on top of normal dues, split among owners. Before buying into any HOA community, ask whether a special assessment is pending or recently passed, since it can mean an unexpected bill soon after closing.
qa_facts: One-time, on top of regular dues
Roof, roads, major repairs, insurance shortfalls
All owners, usually split evenly or by unit size
sections: Why HOAs Levy Special Assessments

Regular HOA dues are meant to cover routine maintenance and build up a reserve fund for future repairs. When a major expense comes up faster than the reserve can absorb, such as storm damage, an aging roof, or an insurance premium spike, the association can vote to levy a special assessment to close the gap.
A community with a healthy reserve fund is generally less likely to need frequent special assessments, which is one reason reviewing HOA financials matters before you buy.
What to Ask Before You Buy

Ask for the HOA's meeting minutes, reserve study, and any notice of a pending or recent special assessment. This information is often included in the community's resale certificate, which sellers typically provide during the sale.
If a special assessment is already approved, find out whether it's a one-time payment or spread over installments, and whether it's the buyer's or seller's responsibility at closing.
faqs: Is a special assessment the same as regular HOA dues?
No, regular dues are ongoing, while a special assessment is a separate, one-time charge for a specific major expense.
Who pays a special assessment, the buyer or the seller?
It depends on the timing and the purchase agreement, so this is worth clarifying and putting in writing before closing.
How much can a special assessment cost?
The amount varies widely depending on the project and how it's split among owners, which is why reviewing HOA documents before buying matters.
Can I refuse to pay a special assessment?
Generally no, once approved by the association it becomes a binding obligation, and unpaid amounts can result in a lien.

h1: What Is an HOA Reserve Fund?
title: What Is an HOA Reserve Fund? | Your Realty Link
meta: A reserve fund is the savings an HOA sets aside for major future repairs. Learn why a healthy reserve matters when buying in a Central Indiana HOA community.
hero_sub: The HOA's savings account for the big repairs that regular dues alone cannot cover.
definition: A reserve fund is the money an HOA sets aside from dues to pay for future major repairs and replacements, such as roofs, roads, or clubhouse renovations, without needing to levy a special assessment.
qa_lead: A portion of every owner's HOA dues typically goes into the reserve fund, building up savings for expenses that are predictable but not annual, like repaving a shared road. A well-funded reserve reduces the odds of a surprise special assessment, so it's one of the first things to check before buying into a community.
qa_facts: A portion of regular HOA dues
Ask for the HOA's reserve study or financials
Higher chance of a special assessment
sections: Why Reserve Funds Matter

Every shared structure and amenity eventually needs major work, whether that's a new roof, repaved streets, or pool equipment. A reserve fund lets an HOA plan and save for those costs gradually instead of hitting owners with a large bill all at once.
Associations that skip or underfund their reserve often end up relying on special assessments when something big finally breaks, which can catch new owners off guard.
Checking a Reserve Fund Before You Buy

Before buying in an HOA community, ask for the association's reserve study, a document that estimates the remaining life and replacement cost of major shared components, and compares that to what's currently saved.
A reserve funded well below the recommended level is a signal to ask more questions, since it may mean higher dues or a special assessment is on the horizon.
faqs: How much should be in an HOA reserve fund?
There is no single number, since it depends on the community's age, amenities, and upcoming repair needs, which is why a reserve study matters more than a dollar figure alone.
Can I see the reserve fund balance before buying?
Yes, this information is typically part of the HOA's financials or resale certificate, which your agent can request during the sale.
What happens if the reserve fund runs low?
The HOA may raise dues, levy a special assessment, or delay needed repairs, none of which are ideal for owners.
Is a reserve fund the same in every HOA?
No, funding levels and how contributions are calculated vary significantly from one association to another.

title: What Is a Common Area? | Your Realty Link
meta: A common area is shared community property, like pools and sidewalks, owned collectively by HOA members. See how common areas work in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: The pool, the clubhouse, the sidewalks - the parts of the community everyone owns together.
definition: A common area is any part of a community that's owned and maintained collectively by all HOA members rather than by an individual owner, such as pools, clubhouses, sidewalks, entrances, and green space.
qa_lead: Common areas belong to the whole HOA, not to any single owner, which is why your monthly dues help pay for their upkeep. In a condo, the common area can even include the building's roof and exterior walls, while in a single-family or townhouse community it's usually limited to shared amenities and grounds.
qa_facts: Shared collectively by all HOA members
What counts as common area differs
sections: What Counts as a Common Area

In a single-family or townhouse HOA, common areas are usually limited to shared spaces like entrances, walking trails, ponds, or a community pool. In a condominium, the definition often extends to the building itself, including hallways, the roof, and exterior walls.
The community's governing documents, including the CC and Rs, define exactly what's considered common area and what falls under an individual owner's responsibility.
How Common Areas Are Maintained

Regular HOA dues fund the day-to-day upkeep of common areas, from mowing to pool maintenance, while a reserve fund typically covers larger, less frequent projects like resurfacing a parking lot or replacing a roof.
Well-maintained common areas are often a good sign of a financially healthy association, which is worth noting when you're comparing communities.
faqs: Do I have to pay for common area maintenance even if I don't use it?
Yes, HOA dues typically cover all common areas regardless of how often an individual owner uses them.
Who is liable if someone is injured in a common area?
The HOA generally carries insurance for common areas, though liability can depend on the specific circumstances.
Can common areas be turned into private property?
Not without a formal process, since common areas are owned collectively and changes usually require association approval.
Does every HOA community have common areas?
Most do, even if it's just a shared entrance or green space, though the scope varies widely between communities.

h1: What Is an HOA Resale Certificate?
title: What Is an HOA Resale Certificate? | Your Realty Link
meta: A resale certificate discloses an HOA's dues, rules, finances, and pending assessments when a home sells. Learn why Central Indiana buyers should review it.
hero_sub: The HOA's full disclosure packet, handed over the moment a home in its community goes up for sale.
definition: A resale certificate is a document package an HOA provides when a member's home is sold, disclosing current dues, rules, financial standing, and any pending or recent special assessments.
qa_lead: Before closing on a home in an HOA community, the seller typically orders a resale certificate from the association, giving the buyer a clear picture of dues, the reserve fund, and whether a special assessment is pending. Reviewing it closely can reveal costs or restrictions that aren't obvious from a showing alone.
qa_facts: Typically the seller, through the HOA
Reveals costs and restrictions before you commit
sections: What's Inside a Resale Certificate

A resale certificate typically lists current HOA dues, any outstanding balance on the seller's account, a summary of the association's finances and reserve fund, and whether any special assessment has been approved or is under discussion.
It often includes a copy of the community's CC and Rs and other governing documents, so buyers can see the rules they will be agreeing to as a new owner.
Why Buyers Should Review It Carefully
A resale certificate can surface issues that never come up during a showing, like a lawsuit involving the HOA, a history of rising dues, or a reserve fund that's underfunded for upcoming repairs.
Your agent can help you read through it and flag anything worth negotiating or walking away from before you're locked into a contract.
faqs: Who pays for the resale certificate?
This is typically negotiated between buyer and seller, though the seller often orders and initially covers the cost since it comes from their HOA account.
How long does it take to get a resale certificate?
Timing varies by HOA management company, so it's worth requesting one early in the transaction to avoid delays before closing.
What if the resale certificate shows a pending special assessment?
This is worth discussing with your agent and possibly negotiating who covers the cost, since it can add a significant expense after closing.
Is a resale certificate required for every HOA sale?
Most HOA communities require one as part of the sale process, though specific requirements can vary by association.

title: What Is Radon Testing? | Your Realty Link
meta: Radon testing checks for a naturally occurring radioactive gas common across Indiana. Learn why Central Indiana buyers test for it and what happens next.
hero_sub: A quick, inexpensive test for an invisible gas that shows up in homes across Central Indiana more often than most buyers expect.
definition: Radon testing measures the level of radon, a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can seep into homes from the soil, using a short-term or long-term monitor placed in the lowest livable level.
qa_lead: Radon is colorless and odorless, so the only way to know a home's level is to test for it. Many Central Indiana buyers add radon testing to their home inspection, since parts of the state are known for elevated readings.
qa_facts: Usually the buyer, during the inspection period
A mitigation system, often vented through the roof
sections: Why Radon Testing Matters in Indiana

Radon comes from uranium breaking down in soil and rock, and levels vary block by block, not just county by county. A neighboring home testing low doesn't guarantee the same result next door, which is why buyers test each individual property rather than relying on general area reputation.

Because it's invisible and odorless, radon is easy to overlook without a dedicated test. It's a separate service from a general home inspection, though the two are commonly scheduled together during the same visit.
How the Test Works and What Happens With a High Reading

A small monitor sits undisturbed in the lowest livable area of the home, usually the basement, for several days while doors and windows stay closed as much as possible. The results come back as a number in picocuries per liter (pCi/L).

If the reading comes back elevated, it doesn't mean the deal falls apart. Buyers often use it as a point of negotiation, asking the seller to install or pay for a mitigation system that vents the gas safely outside. Many Central Indiana homes already have one installed from a prior sale.
faqs: Is radon testing required in Indiana?
No, it's not legally required, but it's a common and inexpensive addition to the inspection period, especially since radon is prevalent in parts of the state.
How much does radon testing cost?
It's typically a modest add-on to a standard home inspection, well below the cost of most other inspection services.
Does every home need a mitigation system?
No. Many homes test well below the action level. A system is only recommended when the reading meets or exceeds the EPA's guidance.
Can I test for radon myself?
Yes, DIY kits exist, but most buyers use a certified inspector during the contingency period so the results carry weight in negotiations.

h1: What Is a Wood-Destroying Insect Inspection?
title: Wood-Destroying Insect Inspection | Your Realty Link
meta: A wood-destroying insect inspection checks for termites and other pests that damage wood. Learn when it's required for Central Indiana buyers and sellers.
hero_sub: Often called a termite report, this inspection can make or break loan approval on certain financing.
definition: A wood-destroying insect inspection, commonly called a termite report, is a licensed inspector's evaluation of a property for termites and other pests that damage structural wood.
qa_lead: This inspection looks specifically for termites, carpenter ants, and other wood-destroying pests, along with visible damage they've caused. It's a separate report from a general home inspection, and some loan types require it before closing.
qa_facts: VA loans in most cases; often FHA
Termites, carpenter ants, and existing wood damage
sections: Why This Inspection Exists

Wood-destroying insects can cause serious structural damage long before it's visible from a walkthrough. A licensed inspector examines the foundation, crawl space, exterior wood, and other vulnerable areas for active infestation or past damage.
Central Indiana's humid summers and older housing stock in some neighborhoods make this a routine check rather than a rare one, even on well-maintained homes.
VA Loans and Other Requirements

VA-backed loans generally require a clear wood-destroying insect report before closing, and in Indiana the seller is typically expected to cover this cost on VA transactions. FHA and other loan types don't always require it outright, but a lender may call for one if the appraiser flags a concern.
If the report finds active infestation or damage, the seller usually needs to treat the issue and, in some cases, repair the damage before the loan can move forward.
faqs: Do I need this inspection with a conventional loan?
It's not automatically required the way it is on VA loans, but many buyers order one anyway as part of their due diligence, especially in older homes.
What happens if termites are found?
The home typically needs to be treated by a licensed pest control company, and any structural damage may need repair before closing on certain loan types.
Who pays for the inspection?
It's negotiable and spelled out in the purchase agreement, though sellers often cover it on VA transactions.
Is this the same as a general pest inspection?
It's narrower. A wood-destroying insect report focuses on termites and similar pests and their damage, not general pest concerns like rodents.

h1: What Is a Reconsideration of Value?
title: What Is a Reconsideration of Value? | Your Realty Link
meta: A reconsideration of value is a formal request to revisit a low home appraisal using added comparable sales. See how the process works in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: A structured way to challenge a low appraisal instead of simply accepting it and renegotiating from scratch.
definition: A reconsideration of value is a formal request asking the appraiser to revisit a completed appraisal, typically supported by additional comparable sales or corrected property facts.
qa_lead: When a home appraisal comes in below the contract price, a reconsideration of value gives the buyer's agent a chance to submit stronger comparable sales or point out factual errors for the appraiser to review. It doesn't guarantee a higher number, but it's one of the standard options when facing an appraisal gap.
qa_facts: Usually the buyer's agent, through the lender
Recent comparable sales or factual corrections
Not guaranteed; the appraiser may adjust or hold the value
Shortly after the appraisal report is received
sections: When a Reconsideration Makes Sense

This request works best when there's a clear, documentable reason the appraisal may be off, such as recent comparable sales the appraiser didn't use, an incorrect square footage figure, or upgrades that weren't accounted for. A reconsideration based purely on frustration with the number rarely succeeds.
It's typically pursued quickly after the report comes back, since financing timelines don't pause for the review.
What Happens Next

The buyer's agent compiles supporting comparable sales, often with help from the listing agent, and submits the package through the lender back to the appraiser. The appraiser isn't obligated to change the value, and in many cases the original number stands.

If the reconsideration doesn't move the needle, buyers and sellers still have other paths forward, including renegotiating price, the buyer covering the gap in cash, or invoking an appraisal contingency to exit the contract.
faqs: How long does a reconsideration of value take?
It varies, but it's usually resolved within several days to about a week, since most contracts are on a financing deadline.
Does a reconsideration always raise the value?
No. Appraisers review the new information, but they aren't required to change their opinion of value.
Who pays for a reconsideration of value?
There's typically no separate fee. It's a review of the existing appraisal, not a new inspection.
What if the value still comes in low?
Buyers and sellers can renegotiate the price, the buyer can cover the difference in cash, or the buyer may be able to exit through an appraisal contingency.

title: What Is Gross Living Area (GLA)? | Your Realty Link
meta: Gross living area (GLA) is the finished above-grade square footage appraisers use for value. See why it can differ from a home's listed square footage.
hero_sub: The square footage number your appraiser actually cares about, and it's not always the one on the listing.
definition: Gross living area, or GLA, is the finished, above-grade square footage of a home that an appraiser uses when comparing it to similar sold properties.
qa_lead: GLA only counts finished space above grade, meaning a finished basement generally isn't included the same way. That's a common reason a home appraisal and a listing description can cite different square footage for the same house.
qa_facts: Drives the comparable sales the appraiser selects
The appraiser, using standardized measurement methods
sections: Why GLA and Listed Square Footage Can Differ

Listings sometimes include finished basement space in the total square footage shown to buyers, while an appraiser's GLA calculation typically keeps that space separate and values it differently. Neither number is wrong; they're just measuring different things for different purposes.
This distinction matters most in Central Indiana homes with finished basements or converted spaces, where the gap between listed square footage and GLA can be a few hundred square feet.
How GLA Affects Comparable Sales

Appraisers select comparable sales based partly on similar GLA, so a home with an unusually large or small GLA relative to its neighborhood can be harder to value precisely. This is one reason two homes that look similar from the street can appraise differently.
If a reconsideration of value is needed after a low appraisal, GLA accuracy is often one of the first things a buyer's agent double-checks.
faqs: Does a finished basement add to GLA?
Usually not in the same category as above-grade space. It's typically valued separately, though it can still add to a home's overall worth.
Why does my appraisal show different square footage than my listing?
The appraiser measures using standardized above-grade guidelines, while listing square footage sometimes includes finished basement or other space.
Can I dispute an appraiser's GLA measurement?
Yes, if you believe it's inaccurate, this is one of the details commonly raised in a reconsideration of value.
Does GLA affect my home's market value?
It's one factor among several appraisers weigh, alongside condition, lot, upgrades, and recent comparable sales.

h1: What Is a Well and Septic Inspection?
title: What Is a Well and Septic Inspection? | Your Realty Link
meta: A well and septic inspection checks water quality and septic system condition for homes outside city utilities. See why it matters in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: Essential due diligence for the many Central Indiana properties that sit outside municipal water and sewer lines.
definition: A well and septic inspection evaluates the water quality of a private well and the condition of a private septic system, typically used together on rural or unincorporated properties.
qa_lead: Well and septic systems are common on homes near the edges of Central Indiana counties, where city utilities don't reach. Because these systems aren't covered by a standard home inspection, buyers typically order a separate well and septic inspection during the inspection period.
qa_facts: Water quality, flow rate, pump function
Tank condition, drain field function, capacity
sections: Why These Systems Need Their Own Inspection

A general home inspector typically doesn't test well water quality or evaluate a septic system's function, since both require specialized equipment and training. A separate inspector tests the well for water quality and flow, and evaluates the septic tank and drain field for signs of failure.
Repairs to either system can be significant, so catching problems before closing matters more here than with most other inspection items.
What to Expect During the Inspection

The well inspection usually involves a water sample sent to a lab for quality testing, along with a check of flow rate and pump condition. The septic inspection typically includes pumping or opening the tank to check its condition, along with an evaluation of how well the drain field is handling wastewater.
If issues turn up, buyers commonly negotiate repairs or a credit, similar to how they'd handle findings from a standard home inspection.
faqs: Is a well and septic inspection required in Indiana?
It's not legally required for most sales, but lenders and buyers commonly require or strongly recommend it for properties using private systems.
How much does it cost?
It varies by provider and property, and is typically ordered alongside or shortly after the general home inspection.
What if the septic system fails inspection?
Buyers and sellers usually negotiate repairs, replacement, or a price adjustment, similar to other inspection findings.
Do all rural Central Indiana homes have well and septic systems?
Many do, especially near county edges, but always confirm rather than assume, since some rural areas are served by rural water utilities.

h1: What Is a Lead-Based Paint Disclosure?
title: What Is a Lead-Based Paint Disclosure? | Your Realty Link
meta: A lead-based paint disclosure is a federally required notice for homes built before 1978. See what it covers and what it means for Indianapolis buyers.
hero_sub: A federal requirement for older homes that gives buyers a chance to test before they're locked into the purchase.
definition: A lead-based paint disclosure is a federally required notice, used for homes built before 1978, informing buyers of any known lead-based paint hazards and their right to test for lead.
qa_lead: Federal law requires sellers of homes built before 1978 to disclose any known lead-based paint hazards and give buyers a set window to test for lead before finalizing the purchase. This is separate from Indiana's standard seller's disclosure form.
qa_facts: A window to inspect or test for lead
sections: Why This Disclosure Is Required

Lead-based paint was commonly used in homes until it was banned for residential use in 1978, so many older neighborhoods in and around Indianapolis include homes that fall under this requirement. Sellers must disclose any known lead paint or lead hazards, along with any related reports they have, even if they believe the home is safe.

This rule applies regardless of the home's condition or whether the seller has ever tested for lead. The point of the disclosure is to give buyers information and options, not to declare the home hazardous.
What Buyers Should Know Before Signing

Buyers of pre-1978 homes typically receive an EPA pamphlet on lead hazards along with the disclosure, and federal law gives them a standard window, usually up to 10 days, to conduct a lead paint inspection or risk assessment before becoming bound to the purchase, unless that right is waived in writing.

This right can be waived to speed up a transaction, but buyers of older homes, especially those with young children, often choose to use it, particularly on properties with visible peeling or chipping paint.
faqs: Does every home need this disclosure?
No, only homes built before 1978 fall under this federal requirement.
Can I skip the lead inspection window?
Yes, buyers can waive this right in writing, though it's worth considering carefully on older homes.
Does the disclosure mean the home definitely has lead paint?
No. It discloses what the seller knows and gives buyers the option to test, but it doesn't confirm lead paint is present.
Is this the same as Indiana's seller's disclosure form?
No, they're separate documents. The lead-based paint disclosure is a federal requirement specific to pre-1978 homes.

title: What Is Assessed Value? | Your Realty Link
meta: Assessed value is the value your county assigns to your home for property tax purposes. Learn how it differs from market value for Central Indiana homeowners.
hero_sub: The number your county uses to calculate your property tax bill, and it's often not the same as what your home would actually sell for.
definition: Assessed value is the value a county assessor assigns to a property for property tax purposes, calculated using standardized methods rather than a live sale.
qa_lead: Every county in Indiana assesses property annually or periodically to determine each home's value for tax purposes. This figure is separate from market value, which reflects what a buyer would actually pay in today's market, so don't be surprised if the two numbers don't match.
qa_facts: Calculating property tax, alongside the tax rate
Your county assessor or auditor's website
Yes, through your county assessor's office
sections: How Assessed Value Is Determined

County assessors use standardized valuation methods, comparable sales data, and periodic reassessments to arrive at each property's assessed value. Indiana law requires assessments to reflect market value-in-use, but the timing and methodology mean the figure can lag behind actual market conditions, especially in fast-moving neighborhoods.

Assessed value gets combined with your local tax rate and applicable deductions to calculate your property tax bill. For specific dollar figures on deductions or exemptions, your county auditor's office or the Indiana Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF) is the accurate source, since these amounts can change.
Why the Gap Between Assessed and Market Value Matters
In a rising market, assessed value often trails behind what homes are actually selling for, which is common and doesn't mean anything is wrong. In a cooling market, the opposite can happen.

If a homeowner believes their assessed value is inaccurate, most Indiana counties offer a formal appeal process. Indiana's constitutional property tax caps also limit how much of a homeowner's assessed value can go toward tax, which is worth understanding alongside your specific assessment; see property tax caps for how that protection works.
faqs: How often is assessed value updated in Indiana?
Counties reassess periodically and may adjust values annually through trending; check with your county assessor for the current schedule.
Can I appeal my assessed value?
Yes, Indiana counties have a formal appeal process if you believe your assessment doesn't reflect your property accurately.
Does a higher assessed value mean my home is worth more on the market?
Not necessarily. Assessed value and market value are calculated differently and can diverge, especially in a shifting market.
Where can I find my current assessed value?
Your county assessor's or auditor's website typically has a property search tool with your current assessment on file.

title: What Is Market Value? | Your Realty Link
meta: Market value is what a home would likely sell for in an open sale today. See how it differs from assessed value for Central Indiana buyers and sellers.
hero_sub: What your home would actually fetch on the open market today, as opposed to the figure your county uses for taxes.
definition: Market value is the price a property would likely sell for in an open, competitive sale between a willing buyer and a willing seller, with neither under unusual pressure.
qa_lead: Market value reflects current buyer demand, recent comparable sales, and a home's condition and location. It's distinct from assessed value, the figure your county uses for property taxes, which can lag behind or diverge from what buyers are actually paying.
qa_facts: A real estate agent's CMA or a licensed appraiser
Assessed value, list price, and asking price
sections: How Market Value Is Estimated

Real estate agents estimate market value using a comparative market analysis (CMA), which looks at recently sold homes similar in size, condition, and location. Lenders instead rely on a licensed appraiser's independent opinion, which follows a more formal process but the same basic logic of comparable sales.
Because it's tied to current conditions, market value shifts with supply, demand, interest rates, and the season, unlike assessed value, which updates less frequently.
Market Value vs. Assessed Value vs. List Price

These three numbers often get confused, but they serve different purposes. Assessed value is set by the county for tax purposes and can trail actual market conditions. List price is what a seller chooses to ask, influenced by their agent's market value estimate but ultimately a strategic decision. Market value is the estimate of what a willing buyer would actually pay.

A knowledgeable local agent can walk a Central Indiana seller through where their home likely falls, and where the list price should sit relative to that estimate, before the home ever hits the market.
faqs: Is market value the same as my home's list price?
Not exactly. List price is a strategic choice a seller makes, often informed by market value but not required to match it exactly.
How is market value different from assessed value?
Assessed value is set by the county for tax purposes and can lag behind current conditions; market value reflects what a buyer would pay today.
Who determines market value?
Real estate agents estimate it through a CMA, and licensed appraisers provide a formal opinion of value for lenders.
How can I find my home's current market value?
A local agent can prepare a free comparative market analysis based on recent, comparable sales in your area.

title: What Is a Mill Rate? | Your Realty Link
meta: The mill rate is the local tax rate used to help calculate your property taxes. See how it works alongside assessed value for Central Indiana homeowners.
hero_sub: One piece of the property tax formula, expressed in dollars per thousand of taxable value.
definition: A mill rate is a tax rate expressed as dollars owed per thousand dollars of taxable property value, used along with assessed value and deductions to calculate a property tax bill.
qa_lead: Your property tax bill is generally driven by your assessed value, applicable deductions, and the local tax rate, sometimes referenced as a mill rate, set by the taxing units in your area. Rates vary by county, city, school district, and other local taxing bodies, so two similarly valued homes in different parts of Central Indiana can have different bills.
qa_facts: Local taxing units (county, city, schools, etc.)
Your assessed value and any deductions
Your county auditor or treasurer's office
sections: How the Mill Rate Fits Into Your Tax Bill

Property tax bills are built from several taxing units layered together, such as the county, city or town, school corporation, and library district, each with its own rate. These combine into the total rate applied to your property's taxable assessed value after deductions.
Because so many local units contribute to the total, rates can differ noticeably between neighboring Central Indiana communities, even when home values are similar.
Indiana's Property Tax Caps Provide a Ceiling

Regardless of how local rates add up, Indiana's constitutional property tax caps limit how much of a home's gross assessed value can actually go toward property tax, generally 1 percent for a homestead, 2 percent for other residential and agricultural property, and 3 percent for most other property. See property tax caps for a full explanation.

For the specific rate and deduction figures that apply to a particular property, Your Realty Link always points clients to their county auditor or the Indiana Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF), since these figures are set locally and can change.
faqs: Is the mill rate the same everywhere in Central Indiana?
No, it varies by taxing district, since it's built from county, city, school, and other local unit rates layered together.
Where can I find my property's exact tax rate?
Your county auditor or treasurer's office publishes current rates and can explain how they apply to your property.
Does a higher mill rate always mean a higher tax bill?
Not necessarily on its own; your assessed value and any deductions also factor into the final bill.
Do Indiana's tax caps protect me from a high mill rate?
Yes, the constitutional caps limit the total percentage of assessed value that can go to tax, regardless of how local rates combine.

h1: What Is Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale?
title: Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale | Your Realty Link
meta: Capital gains tax applies to profit from selling a home for more than you paid. See how special federal rules can reduce it for Central Indiana sellers.
hero_sub: A tax on profit, not on the full sale price, and one that many primary-residence sellers end up owing little or nothing on.
definition: Capital gains tax is a federal tax on the profit realized when a property is sold for more than its purchase price and eligible costs, calculated as the difference between the sale proceeds and the seller's basis.
qa_lead: If you sell a home for more than you paid, the profit can be subject to capital gains tax. Many primary-residence sellers reduce or eliminate this through the capital gains exclusion, so it's worth understanding both together before assuming a large tax bill.
qa_facts: Profit (sale price minus basis and costs)
The capital gains exclusion, for many owner-occupied sales
sections: How the Tax Is Calculated

Capital gains tax is based on your gain, generally the sale price minus your original purchase price, eligible closing costs, and the cost of qualifying improvements over the years you owned the home. This total is called your basis, and a higher basis means a smaller taxable gain.

Keeping records of major improvements, like a new roof, an addition, or a kitchen remodel, can meaningfully reduce taxable gain when it's time to sell, so many Central Indiana homeowners hold onto receipts for larger projects.
Why Many Home Sellers Owe Little or Nothing

For owners who've lived in the home as their primary residence for at least two of the past five years, the capital gains exclusion can shelter a substantial portion of the profit from tax entirely. This is a major reason most everyday home sales in Central Indiana don't trigger a capital gains bill.

Investment properties and second homes don't qualify for this exclusion the same way, which is one reason 1031 exchange strategies come up often for investors. Because tax rules are personal and change over time, Your Realty Link recommends sellers confirm their specific situation with a CPA or tax advisor rather than relying on general guidance.
faqs: Will I owe capital gains tax when I sell my primary home?
Many owner-occupants owe little or nothing thanks to the capital gains exclusion, but every situation is different, so check with a tax professional.
Does capital gains tax apply to investment properties the same way?
Investment and rental properties generally don't get the primary-residence exclusion, which is why strategies like a 1031 exchange are common among investors.
What records should I keep to reduce my taxable gain?
Save receipts and documentation for major capital improvements, such as additions, roof replacements, and significant renovations.
Is capital gains tax a local Indiana tax?
No, it's primarily a federal tax on profit, separate from Indiana's property tax system and the sales disclosure filed at closing.

h1: What Is the Capital Gains Exclusion?
title: What Is the Capital Gains Exclusion? | Your Realty Link
meta: The capital gains exclusion lets many homeowners exclude a large share of profit when selling a primary residence. See how it works for Indiana sellers.
hero_sub: The federal break that keeps most everyday home sales from triggering a big tax bill.
definition: The capital gains exclusion is a federal tax provision allowing eligible homeowners to exclude a significant portion of the profit from selling a primary residence they've owned and lived in for at least two of the past five years.
qa_lead: This exclusion is the main reason most primary-residence sellers don't owe capital gains tax on a typical home sale. Eligibility generally depends on ownership and residency timelines, so it's worth confirming your specific situation with a tax professional before you list.
qa_facts: Primary residences, not most investment property
Owned the home for at least 2 of the last 5 years
Lived in it as a primary residence for at least 2 of the last 5 years
sections: Who Typically Qualifies

To qualify, a seller generally needs to have owned and used the home as a primary residence for at least two of the five years before the sale, and the two years don't need to be consecutive. Life events like a job relocation, health issue, or other unforeseen circumstance can sometimes allow for a partial exclusion even if the full timeline isn't met.

Because eligibility rules and specific dollar thresholds can be nuanced and change over time, Your Realty Link always recommends confirming details with a CPA rather than assuming eligibility based on general information.
Why This Matters for Central Indiana Sellers

For many long-term Central Indiana homeowners, appreciation over years of ownership can add up to a meaningful gain, and this exclusion is often the difference between owing tax on that gain and owing nothing at all. It's one reason sellers shouldn't assume a large tax bill just because their home has gained significant value.
This exclusion doesn't apply the same way to second homes or investment properties, which is where strategies like a 1031 exchange become relevant for investors looking to defer tax on a sale.
faqs: Do I qualify for the capital gains exclusion if I've only owned my home for a year?
Generally you'd need at least two years of ownership and use as a primary residence, though certain exceptions may apply, so check with a tax professional about your situation.
Does this exclusion apply to rental properties?
No, it's generally limited to primary residences. Rental and investment properties don't qualify the same way.
Can I use this exclusion more than once?
It's typically available again after meeting the ownership and use requirements for a new primary residence, but confirm timing rules with a tax advisor.
Where can I get a definitive answer for my sale?
A CPA or tax professional can review your specific ownership history and give you an accurate answer before you sell.

h1: What Is a Sales Disclosure Form?
title: What Is a Sales Disclosure Form? | Your Realty Link
meta: A sales disclosure form is an Indiana filing that reports a property's sale price and details used for county tax assessment. See how it fits into closing.
hero_sub: A routine Indiana filing that reports your sale to the county, usually handled quietly as part of closing.
definition: A sales disclosure form is an Indiana document filed with the county when real property is sold, reporting the sale price and transaction details used for property tax assessment.
qa_lead: Indiana requires most property sales to be reported to the county through a sales disclosure form, which helps the county assessor keep assessed value data current. This is typically prepared and filed as part of closing, so most buyers and sellers barely notice it happening.
qa_facts: Usually the title company or closing agent
Helps counties keep assessed values current
sections: Why Indiana Requires This Filing

Counties rely on actual sale prices to keep their assessment records reasonably aligned with real market activity. Without a steady flow of reported sales, assessed values could drift further from reality over time, which is part of why this form exists.

It's required for most property transfers, though certain transaction types have exemptions. Your title company or closing agent typically handles the filing as a routine part of the closing process, not something buyers or sellers need to track down separately.
What It Means for Buyers and Sellers

For most transactions, there's little for buyers or sellers to actively do beyond providing accurate information; the form is prepared and filed alongside other closing paperwork. It's one of several documents that quietly keep the county's property records accurate after a sale.

Because it feeds directly into assessed value calculations, an accurately filed sales disclosure form is part of what keeps future property tax assessments grounded in real transaction data, rather than outdated estimates.
faqs: Do I need to personally file the sales disclosure form?
No, this is typically handled by the title company or closing agent as part of the standard closing process.
Is the sales disclosure form public record?
Generally yes, since it's filed with the county auditor along with other property transfer information.
Does every property sale require this form?
Most standard sales require it, though certain transfer types have exemptions; your title company can confirm for your specific transaction.
How does this form affect my property taxes?
It reports your sale price to the county, which helps inform future assessed value updates for the property.

title: What Is a Cap Rate? | Your Realty Link
meta: Cap rate measures a rental property's yearly income against its price, helping Central Indiana investors compare potential returns before they buy a property.
hero_sub: A quick way to size up how much income a rental property might generate relative to its price.
definition: Capitalization rate, or cap rate, is a rental property's yearly net operating income divided by its purchase price, expressed as a percentage.
qa_lead: Cap rate is a simple ratio investors use to compare income potential across properties: net operating income divided by price. A higher cap rate generally means more income relative to price, but it often comes with more risk or a less desirable location, so it's one data point among several.
sections: How Cap Rate Is Calculated

To find a property's cap rate, divide its net operating income by its purchase price or current market value. NOI is the property's income after operating expenses like taxes, insurance, and maintenance, but before the mortgage payment. Because it excludes financing, cap rate lets investors compare properties on a level playing field regardless of how each buyer plans to pay.

The result is expressed as a percentage. Two properties with the same price but different NOI will land at different cap rates, and that number becomes a shorthand for how the market is pricing risk and return in a given neighborhood or property type.
Using Cap Rate to Compare Properties

Cap rates vary by neighborhood, property condition, and tenant type, so they're most useful for comparing similar properties rather than as a universal target. A property with a higher cap rate may offer stronger income, but it can also signal more deferred maintenance, a tougher rental market, or added risk that the price already reflects.

Cap rate is only one piece of the picture. Serious investors also weigh cash flow, financing costs, and appreciation potential before deciding whether a property fits their goals. Our agents at Your Realty Link can help you pull comparable rental data across Central Indiana submarkets as part of that analysis.
faqs: Is a higher cap rate always better?

Not necessarily. A higher cap rate can reflect stronger income, but it can also point to more risk, older systems, or a less stable rental area, so it's worth digging into why the number is where it is.
What counts as a good cap rate?

There's no single target. It depends on property type, location, and how much risk you're comfortable taking, so compare similar properties in the same submarket rather than chasing a universal number.
Does cap rate include my mortgage payment?
No. Cap rate is calculated before financing costs, so it measures the property's own performance rather than your specific loan terms.
How is cap rate different from cash-on-cash return?
Cap rate looks at income relative to the full property price. Cash-on-cash return looks only at the cash you actually invested, which makes it more personal to your financing.

h1: What Is Cash Flow in Real Estate?
title: What Is Cash Flow? | Your Realty Link
meta: Cash flow is the money left over each month after collecting rent and paying expenses on a rental property. See how Central Indiana investors judge a deal.
hero_sub: The number that tells you whether a rental property is putting money in your pocket each month.
definition: Cash flow is the money left over each month after collecting rent and paying all operating expenses and the mortgage payment on an investment property.
qa_lead: Cash flow is what remains after rent comes in and every bill goes out, including the mortgage. Positive cash flow means the property pays for itself and puts money in your pocket; negative cash flow means you're covering the shortfall yourself. It's a core number alongside net operating income when evaluating a rental.
sections: What Counts as an Expense

Calculating cash flow starts with total rental income, then subtracts operating expenses such as property taxes, insurance, maintenance, property management, and an allowance for vacancy, plus the full mortgage payment. What's left is cash flow.
This differs from net operating income, which stops before the mortgage. Two properties can have identical NOI and very different cash flow depending on how each one is financed.
Why Cash Flow Matters to Investors

Cash flow is what actually shows up in an owner's bank account each month, which makes it a practical measure of whether a rental is sustainable. A property can look attractive on paper but still run negative cash flow if the purchase price, interest rate, or rent level don't line up.

Investors weigh cash flow alongside appreciation potential and tax benefits, since a buy-and-hold strategy often accepts thinner early cash flow in exchange for long-term equity growth. Our agents can help you evaluate rental potential on properties across Central Indiana as part of our investment property services.
faqs: Is positive cash flow guaranteed on every rental?
No. Cash flow depends on purchase price, financing terms, rent levels, and ongoing expenses, so it has to be run for each specific property rather than assumed.
Does cash flow include vacancy?
A realistic cash flow estimate should build in an allowance for vacancy and turnover, since no rental stays occupied one hundred percent of the time.
Can a property have good NOI but poor cash flow?
Yes. NOI is calculated before the mortgage, so a property with strong NOI can still show weak or negative cash flow once financing costs are included.
How often should I review a rental's cash flow?
Most investors review it at least annually, and whenever rents, taxes, insurance, or financing terms change.

h1: What Is a Gross Rent Multiplier (GRM)?
title: What Is a Gross Rent Multiplier? | Your Realty Link
meta: Gross rent multiplier is a quick way to screen rentals by comparing price to yearly rent. Learn how Central Indiana investors use GRM to compare a deal.
hero_sub: A fast first screen for comparing rental properties before you dig into the deeper numbers.
definition: Gross rent multiplier, or GRM, is a property's purchase price divided by its yearly gross rental income, used as a quick way to compare rentals.
qa_lead: GRM is a shortcut: take a property's price and divide it by the total rent it collects in a year. It's a fast way to screen and rank multiple listings before running deeper numbers like net operating income or cash flow. A lower GRM can point to better relative value, but it ignores expenses, so it's a starting point, not a final answer.
qa_facts: Price divided by yearly gross rent
Cap rate and cash flow for a full picture
sections: How to Calculate GRM
To find GRM, divide a property's price by the total rent it brings in over a year. Because the math is simple, it's often the first filter investors apply to a list of potential rental properties.

GRM works in reverse too: multiplying a target GRM by a property's expected annual rent gives a rough sense of what it should be priced at, which is useful when screening a batch of properties quickly.
Where GRM Falls Short

GRM doesn't account for operating expenses, vacancy, or financing, so two properties with the same GRM can perform very differently once real costs are factored in. An older property may need far more in maintenance and management than a newer one, even at the same rent-to-price ratio.

Because of that, investors use GRM to narrow a list of candidates, then move to cap rate and cash flow for a fuller picture before making an offer. Our agents can help pull comparable rent data for properties you're considering across Central Indiana.
faqs: Is a lower GRM always better?
A lower GRM often suggests better relative value, but it should be checked against expenses, condition, and location before drawing conclusions.
How is GRM different from cap rate?
GRM uses gross rent and ignores expenses, while cap rate uses net operating income after expenses, so cap rate gives a more complete picture of return.
What's considered a typical GRM?
Typical ranges vary widely by market, property type, and rent level, so GRM is most useful for comparing similar properties to each other rather than against a fixed target.
Can GRM be used for single-family rentals?
Yes, GRM can be applied to any rental property, though it's especially popular as a fast screening tool for multi-family properties with several rent rolls to compare.

title: What Is After Repair Value (ARV)? | Your Realty Link
meta: After repair value estimates what a property will be worth once renovations are complete. See how ARV guides fix-and-flip decisions in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: An estimate of what a property will be worth once the renovation work is finished.
definition: After repair value, or ARV, is the estimated market value of a property once planned renovations and repairs are complete.
qa_lead: ARV answers the question: what will this property be worth once the work is done? Investors compare recently sold, renovated properties similar in size and finish to the planned result, then use that estimate to work backward into a purchase price and renovation budget for a fix-and-flip project. Getting ARV right is one of the most important steps in the process, since overestimating it can turn a promising deal into a loss.
qa_facts: Comparable sales of similarly renovated homes
Setting purchase price and repair budget
sections: How Investors Estimate ARV

To estimate ARV, investors and their agents look at recently sold properties nearby that are similar in size, layout, and finish level to what the subject property will look like after renovation, similar to how a comparative market analysis works for a standard sale. The goal is to find comparables that reflect the finished product, not the property's current condition.

Because ARV depends heavily on which comparables are chosen and how the finished renovation is scoped, it's easy to be too optimistic. Working with an agent who knows recent renovated sales in the target neighborhood helps keep the estimate grounded in what buyers are actually paying.
Using ARV to Plan a Project

Many investors work backward from ARV, subtracting estimated repair costs, holding costs, selling costs, and a target profit margin, to arrive at the most they can pay for the property. The exact formula and target margin vary by investor and market conditions.

Because ARV is an estimate, not a guarantee, experienced investors build in a cushion for surprises, since renovation costs and timelines often run over budget. Our agents can help pull recent comparable sales across Central Indiana neighborhoods to support an ARV estimate before you make an offer.
faqs: Who determines ARV?
There's no single official source. Investors typically work with a real estate agent or appraiser to review comparable sales and arrive at a realistic estimate.
Is ARV the same as an appraisal?
No. ARV is a forward-looking estimate based on a planned renovation, while a formal appraisal values the property as it exists at a specific point in time.
What happens if ARV is overestimated?
An inflated ARV can lead an investor to overpay for the property or overspend on renovations, leaving little or no profit once the property actually sells.
Does ARV apply outside of fix-and-flip projects?
It's also used when investors renovate a rental to refinance based on the improved value, sometimes called a BRRRR-style strategy.

h1: What Is a Buy-and-Hold Real Estate Strategy?
title: What Is Buy-and-Hold Investing? | Your Realty Link
meta: Buy-and-hold means purchasing a property to rent out long term rather than reselling it quickly. Learn how the strategy works for Central Indiana investors.
hero_sub: Buying a property to keep and rent long term, rather than flipping it for a quick profit.
definition: Buy-and-hold is an investing strategy of purchasing a property and keeping it long term to earn rental income and build equity through appreciation and loan paydown, rather than reselling it quickly.
qa_lead: With a buy-and-hold strategy, an investor purchases a property and holds onto it for years, collecting rent along the way while the mortgage balance shrinks and the property potentially appreciates. It's the opposite approach from a fix-and-flip, which aims to sell quickly. Buy-and-hold investors focus on steady cash flow and long-term wealth building rather than a fast payout.
qa_facts: Appreciation and loan paydown over time
sections: How Buy-and-Hold Investors Build Wealth

Buy-and-hold investing combines several ways of building wealth at once: monthly rental income, gradual paydown of the mortgage balance by tenants' rent payments, and potential appreciation in the property's value over time. Because these gains compound over years, buy-and-hold tends to reward patience over quick turnaround.
Some buy-and-hold investors start with house hacking, living in part of a property while renting the rest, then move into acquiring dedicated rental properties as they build experience and capital.
What to Evaluate Before Buying

Before committing to a buy-and-hold purchase, investors typically look at the property's net operating income, expected cash flow, and financing terms, along with location factors like schools, job growth, and access to major employers that tend to support tenant demand over time.

Because the property is held for years, neighborhood trends and local employment growth matter as much as the initial purchase price. Our agents can help you evaluate rental potential and identify Central Indiana submarkets that fit a long-term hold strategy.
faqs: How long do buy-and-hold investors typically keep a property?
There's no fixed timeline, but many buy-and-hold investors plan to hold for at least several years to let appreciation and loan paydown build meaningful equity.
Is buy-and-hold the same as being a landlord?
In practice, yes. Buy-and-hold investors are usually responsible for landlord duties, either directly or through a property manager.
Does buy-and-hold require positive cash flow from day one?
Not always. Some investors accept thin or even negative early cash flow in exchange for long-term appreciation, though a sustainable plan usually needs positive cash flow eventually.
Can buy-and-hold work with single-family homes?
Yes. Buy-and-hold applies to single-family rentals, multi-family properties, condos, and other property types, depending on the investor's goals and market.

title: What Is House Hacking? | Your Realty Link
meta: House hacking means living in part of a property while renting out the rest to help cover the mortgage. See how it works for first-time Indiana buyers.
hero_sub: Living in one part of your property while tenants help cover the mortgage on the rest.
definition: House hacking is living in one unit or portion of a property, such as one unit of a duplex or a room in a single-family home, while renting out the rest to help cover the mortgage.
qa_lead: House hacking is a common way first-time investors get started: buy a small multi-family property, such as a duplex, triplex, or fourplex, live in one unit, and rent out the others. The rental income can cover some or all of the mortgage, letting the owner live for less while building equity and landlord experience. It's also possible with a single-family home by renting out extra bedrooms.
qa_facts: Duplex, triplex, fourplex, or single-family with spare rooms
sections: How House Hacking Works

A typical house hack involves buying a small multi-family property, moving into one unit, and renting out the remaining units to tenants. The rent collected can cover a meaningful share of the mortgage payment, sometimes most or all of it, which lowers the owner's personal housing cost while they build equity in the property.

Because the owner occupies the property, some house hackers can qualify for owner-occupant financing terms, which often come with lower down payment requirements than a straight investment property loan. Loan program rules vary, so it's worth talking to a lender early about what's available.
What to Consider Before House Hacking

House hacking means becoming a landlord to your neighbors, which takes some comfort with the day-to-day of managing tenants, handling repairs, and enforcing lease terms. It also means giving up some privacy compared to a typical single-family purchase.

Location and property condition matter just as much as with any rental purchase. Our agents can help first-time investors evaluate small multi-family properties across Central Indiana and connect them with lenders familiar with house hacking, alongside our broader investment property services.
faqs: Do I need to live in the property to house hack?
Yes, house hacking specifically means occupying part of the property, which is also what can make owner-occupant financing available.
What property types work best for house hacking?
Small multi-family properties like duplexes, triplexes, and fourplexes are popular, but renting spare bedrooms in a single-family home is also a form of house hacking.
How long do I need to live in the property?
Financing requirements vary by loan program, so check with your lender about any minimum owner-occupancy period tied to your specific loan.
Is house hacking good for someone with no landlord experience?
It's often recommended as a low-risk way to learn landlording, since you're on-site and can address issues quickly, though it still requires real preparation and reliable systems.

title: What Is a 1031 Exchange? | Your Realty Link
meta: A 1031 exchange lets investors defer capital gains tax by reinvesting proceeds into a like-kind property. Learn the basics for Central Indiana investors.
hero_sub: A tax strategy that lets investors roll proceeds from one investment property into another, deferring the tax bill.
definition: A 1031 exchange is a tax strategy, named for Section 1031 of the tax code, that lets an investor defer capital gains tax by reinvesting the proceeds from selling one investment property into another like-kind property within strict deadlines.
qa_lead: A 1031 exchange allows an investor to sell a property and reinvest the proceeds into another investment property without immediately paying capital gains tax on the sale. The rules are strict, including tight replacement-property deadlines and a requirement to use a qualified intermediary, so it's always done with an intermediary and a tax professional rather than attempted alone.
qa_facts: Defer capital gains tax on investment property sales
Must be like-kind investment or business property
sections: How a 1031 Exchange Works

In a typical 1031 exchange, an investor sells a property, and instead of taking the proceeds directly, a qualified intermediary holds the funds. The investor then has a limited window to identify potential replacement properties and a further window to close on one, reinvesting the proceeds to defer the tax that would otherwise be due on the sale.

Because the replacement property must be like-kind, meaning another investment or business-use real property, and because the deadlines and paperwork are strict, working with a qualified intermediary and a tax advisor experienced in 1031 exchanges is essential from the very start of the process, ideally before the original property even goes under contract.
Why Investors Use a 1031 Exchange

A 1031 exchange lets investors move equity from one property into another, for example trading up to a larger property or consolidating several properties into one, without losing a portion of their proceeds to capital gains tax along the way. Over multiple exchanges, this can meaningfully accelerate portfolio growth.

Because timing matters so much, investors considering a 1031 exchange should line up their intermediary and start researching replacement properties before listing the property they're selling. Our agents can help identify like-kind replacement properties across Central Indiana on the timeline a 1031 exchange requires.
faqs: Do I have to buy an identical property type?
No. Like-kind is interpreted broadly for real estate. It generally just needs to be investment or business-use property, not a personal residence, rather than an identical property type.
What is a qualified intermediary?
A qualified intermediary is a neutral third party required by IRS rules to hold the sale proceeds during a 1031 exchange, since the investor can't take possession of the funds directly.
Can I use a 1031 exchange on my personal home?
No, 1031 exchanges apply to investment and business-use property, not primary residences. A different capital gains exclusion applies to personal homes.
What happens if I miss a 1031 exchange deadline?
Missing a deadline typically disqualifies the exchange, which means the sale is treated as a normal taxable sale, so investors need a tax professional tracking the timeline closely.

title: What Is Cash-on-Cash Return? | Your Realty Link
meta: Cash-on-cash return measures the yearly cash flow against the actual cash you invested in a property. Learn how Central Indiana investors use this metric.
hero_sub: A return measure based on the actual cash you put into a deal, not the full price of the property.
definition: Cash-on-cash return is a rental property's yearly pre-tax cash flow divided by the actual cash the investor put into the deal, expressed as a percentage.
qa_lead: Cash-on-cash return measures performance based on your actual out-of-pocket investment, such as your down payment, closing costs, and any renovation costs, rather than the full purchase price. It's calculated by dividing annual cash flow by that invested cash amount. Because financing changes how much cash an investor puts in, cash-on-cash return can vary a lot between an all-cash purchase and a leveraged one, even for the same property.
qa_facts: Yearly cash flow divided by cash invested
Down payment, closing costs, and rehab costs
sections: How Cash-on-Cash Return Is Calculated

To calculate cash-on-cash return, start with the property's annual cash flow, meaning income after all expenses and the mortgage payment, then divide it by the total cash the investor actually put in. That figure typically includes the down payment, closing costs, and any upfront repair spending, but not the full loan amount.
This makes cash-on-cash return a measure of how hard your actual dollars are working, which is different from cap rate, a metric that looks at the full property value regardless of financing.
Why Financing Changes the Number

Because cash-on-cash return only counts the cash actually invested, using more leverage, meaning a smaller down payment, can increase the calculated return, since less of the investor's own money is tied up, even though the dollar amount of cash flow may be similar or lower. This is why an all-cash buyer and a financed buyer can see very different cash-on-cash figures for the identical property.

Investors typically use cash-on-cash return alongside cap rate and total return projections to get a complete picture, since focusing on cash-on-cash return alone can encourage over-leveraging. Our agents can help connect you with lenders and run realistic numbers on properties across Central Indiana.
faqs: How is cash-on-cash return different from cap rate?

Cap rate looks at income relative to the full property value regardless of financing, while cash-on-cash return looks at income relative to the actual cash you invested, so financing has a big effect on it.
Does a bigger down payment mean a better cash-on-cash return?
Not necessarily. A larger down payment ties up more cash, which can lower the calculated cash-on-cash return even if the property's cash flow stays the same.
Is cash-on-cash return the same as total return?
No. Cash-on-cash return only reflects cash flow, not appreciation, loan paydown, or tax benefits, so it understates total return over the long run.
What counts as cash invested?
Typically the down payment, closing costs, and any upfront repair or renovation costs, though investors should define this consistently when comparing deals.

title: What Is Net Operating Income (NOI)? | Your Realty Link
meta: Net operating income is a rental property's income after operating expenses but before the mortgage. Learn how NOI works for Central Indiana investors.
hero_sub: The building-block number behind cap rate and most other rental property math.
definition: Net operating income, or NOI, is a rental property's total income minus its operating expenses, calculated before the mortgage payment is factored in.
qa_lead: NOI takes a property's total rental income and subtracts operating expenses like property taxes, insurance, maintenance, property management, and a vacancy allowance, but stops before the mortgage payment. It's the building block behind cap rate and a key input for figuring cash flow, which does include financing costs.
qa_facts: Cap rate, and feeds into cash flow
sections: What Counts as an Operating Expense

Operating expenses used to calculate NOI typically include property taxes, insurance, routine maintenance and repairs, property management fees, and an allowance for vacancy and credit loss. Capital improvements, like a full roof replacement, are usually treated separately rather than as a routine operating expense.

Because NOI excludes the mortgage payment, it reflects how the property itself performs, independent of how any particular buyer chooses to finance it. That's what makes it useful for comparing properties across different buyers and loan structures.
How NOI Connects to Other Metrics

NOI is the numerator in the cap rate formula, calculated by dividing NOI by the property's price. Subtracting the mortgage payment from NOI produces cash flow, the number that reflects what actually lands in an owner's pocket each month.

Because so many investment calculations start with NOI, getting an accurate, honest estimate of income and expenses matters more than almost any other number in the analysis. Our agents can help you evaluate realistic income and expense figures on rental properties across Central Indiana.
faqs: Does NOI include the mortgage payment?
No. NOI is calculated before the mortgage. Once the mortgage payment is subtracted from NOI, the result is cash flow.
What expenses are excluded from NOI?
Mortgage payments, income taxes, and capital improvements are generally excluded, along with depreciation, which is a non-cash accounting item.
Why do investors care about NOI specifically?
NOI isolates the property's own performance from financing decisions, which makes it the standard input for cap rate and for comparing properties regardless of how each is financed.
Is NOI the same for every investor on the same property?

It should be close, since NOI is based on the property's actual income and operating costs rather than the buyer's financing, though estimates can vary based on assumptions about vacancy and management costs.

h1: What Is a Fix and Flip?
title: What Is a Fix and Flip? | Your Realty Link
meta: A fix and flip means buying, renovating, and reselling a property for profit. Learn how the strategy works for real estate investors in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: Buying, renovating, and reselling a property fairly quickly to capture a profit.
definition: A fix and flip is an investment strategy of buying a property, renovating it, and reselling it relatively quickly for a profit.
qa_lead: In a fix and flip, an investor buys a property, often one priced below market due to its condition, completes renovations, then lists it for sale. Success depends on accurately estimating repair costs and projecting a realistic after repair value, since the margin between purchase price plus repairs and the final sale price is where the profit, or loss, comes from.
qa_facts: Profit from resale, not rental income
Purchase price, repair budget, after repair value
Cost overruns and market shifts during the hold
sections: How a Fix and Flip Works

A fix and flip starts with finding a property priced to reflect its condition, then carefully budgeting the renovation and estimating the after repair value, meaning what the property will sell for once the work is complete. The gap between total costs, including purchase price, repairs, holding costs, and selling costs, and the projected sale price is the investor's target profit margin.

Because the project happens on a compressed timeline compared to buy-and-hold investing, accurate budgeting and a reliable contractor matter enormously. Cost overruns or delays eat directly into the profit margin.
Risks and Considerations

Fix and flip projects carry real risk: renovation costs can run over budget, permitting and inspections can take longer than planned, and the resale market can shift during the hold period. Financing costs also add up the longer a property sits before selling.

Because timing and accuracy matter so much, many investors work closely with an agent who knows recent renovated comparable sales in the target neighborhood, to keep the after repair value estimate grounded in reality before finalizing the purchase price. Our agents support fix-and-flip investors across Central Indiana as part of our broader investment property services.
faqs: How long does a typical fix and flip take?
Timelines vary widely based on the scope of renovation and local permitting, but flips are generally measured in months rather than years.
What's the biggest risk in a fix and flip?
Underestimating repair costs or overestimating after repair value are the most common ways a flip's profit margin disappears.
Do I need cash to fix and flip?
Some investors use cash, while others use short-term renovation or hard money financing; either way, financing costs need to be factored into the overall budget.
Is fix and flip riskier than buy-and-hold?
It carries different risks. Fix and flip is more exposed to short-term cost and timeline swings, while buy-and-hold is more exposed to long-term market and tenant risk.

title: What Is an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage (ARM)? | Your Realty Link
meta: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) starts with a lower fixed rate, then adjusts periodically after that. See how ARMs compare for Central Indiana homebuyers.
hero_sub: A lower introductory rate today in exchange for payments that can change down the road.
definition: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) is a home loan with an interest rate that stays fixed for an initial period, then adjusts periodically based on market conditions.
qa_lead: An ARM usually offers a lower rate for the first 3, 5, 7, or 10 years, then adjusts on a set schedule tied to a market index. Weigh it against a fixed-rate mortgage based on how long you plan to keep the loan.
qa_facts: Fixed for a set period, then adjusts
Buyers who expect to move or refinance before the adjustment
Rate caps limit how much and how often it can rise
sections: How the Fixed Period Works

During the initial fixed period, an ARM's rate and monthly principal-and-interest payment don't change, and in many cases that starting rate is lower than what a comparable fixed-rate mortgage offers. The length of the fixed period is built into the loan's name; a 7/1 ARM, for example, holds its rate steady for seven years before the first adjustment.
That lower starting rate is the main appeal. It can mean a lower monthly payment or more buying power in the early years, which is why ARMs sometimes get a second look in higher-rate environments.
What Happens After the Rate Adjusts

Once the fixed period ends, the rate adjusts on a set schedule, commonly once a year, based on a market index plus a margin set by the lender. Federal rules require rate caps that limit how much the rate can move at each adjustment and over the life of the loan, so payments can't spike without limit.

Because of that uncertainty, our agents encourage ARM shoppers to plan around their actual timeline in the home, not just the introductory rate, and to talk through the loan's specific cap structure with their lender before signing.
faqs: Is an ARM riskier than a fixed-rate mortgage?
It carries more uncertainty since the rate can rise after the fixed period, but built-in rate caps limit how much it can increase at once.
Can I refinance out of an ARM before it adjusts?
Yes, many buyers plan to refinance into a fixed-rate loan or sell the home before the first adjustment, though refinancing depends on qualifying again at that time.
Are ARMs common in Central Indiana?
They're less common than fixed-rate loans here, but some buyers use them intentionally for shorter-term ownership plans or new construction timelines.
What index do ARMs typically use?
Most ARMs are tied to a published market index such as the SOFR, plus a set margin added by the lender.

title: What Is a Fixed-Rate Mortgage? | Your Realty Link
meta: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate and monthly payment for the entire loan term, making budgeting simple for Central Indiana homebuyers.
hero_sub: The same rate and payment from your first mortgage bill to your last.
definition: A fixed-rate mortgage is a home loan whose interest rate, and therefore its principal-and-interest payment, never changes for the life of the loan.
qa_lead: With a fixed-rate mortgage, your rate is locked in at closing and stays the same whether market rates rise or fall later. It's the most predictable option, and the natural alternative to an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM).
qa_facts: Never changes for the loan term
Buyers who value predictability or plan to stay long-term
Principal and interest stay level; taxes and insurance can still shift
sections: Why Predictability Is the Main Advantage

Because the rate never moves, your principal-and-interest payment is the same in year one as it is in year thirty. That predictability makes it easier to budget and is one reason fixed-rate loans remain the most common choice among Central Indiana buyers.
Your total monthly housing payment can still shift over time if your property taxes or homeowners insurance change, since those are usually collected through escrow alongside principal and interest.
30-Year vs. 15-Year Terms
