A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage spreads payments out for lower monthly costs, while a 15-year term pays off faster and usually carries a lower rate, but with a noticeably higher monthly payment. The right choice depends on your monthly budget and long-term plans.
Some buyers start with a 30-year loan for flexibility, then make extra principal payments when they can, without committing to the higher required payment of a 15-year term.
faqs: Is a fixed-rate mortgage more expensive than an ARM?
It often starts with a slightly higher rate than an ARM's introductory rate, but it never adjusts, so there's no risk of a future increase.
Can I pay off a fixed-rate mortgage early?
Most conventional fixed-rate loans allow extra principal payments without penalty, though it's worth confirming with your specific lender.
What loan terms are available?
30-year and 15-year terms are most common, though some lenders offer other lengths like 20-year or 10-year options.
Do taxes and insurance change even with a fixed rate?
Yes. The interest rate is fixed, but property taxes and homeowners insurance can change over time and adjust your total escrow payment.

title: What Is a Loan Estimate? | Your Realty Link
meta: A loan estimate is a standardized form lenders provide after you apply, showing projected rate, payment, and closing costs. Use it to compare Indiana lenders.
hero_sub: A standardized snapshot of your loan terms, delivered within days of applying.
definition: A loan estimate is a three-page federal disclosure that lenders must provide within three business days of a mortgage application, outlining projected rate, payment, and closing costs.
qa_lead: Every lender is required to use the same loan estimate format, which makes it possible to compare offers side by side using the exact same categories. Line it up against the closing disclosure you'll receive later to make sure nothing changed unexpectedly.
qa_facts: Rate, monthly payment, closing costs, and cash to close
Lets you compare lenders using identical categories
sections: What's Included on the Form

The loan estimate lays out your projected interest rate, monthly principal-and-interest payment, estimated taxes and insurance, and an itemized breakdown of closing costs. It also shows whether your rate is locked and for how long, and flags any prepayment penalty or balloon payment.

Because every lender must use the identical three-page format, you can set two loan estimates side by side and compare the same line items, rather than trying to decode different paperwork from each company.
Using It to Compare Lenders

Shopping multiple lenders within a short window and comparing their loan estimates is one of the most effective ways to find a competitive rate and reasonable fees on a Central Indiana purchase. Pay particular attention to the interest rate, any discount points, and total closing costs, not just the monthly payment.
A loan estimate is not a final commitment from the lender. Your actual terms can still change if your financial picture, the property, or market rates shift before closing.
faqs: Is a loan estimate a guarantee of my final rate?
No. It's a good-faith estimate based on the information you provided; your final terms are confirmed later in the closing disclosure.
Does getting a loan estimate cost anything?
Lenders can't charge more than a credit report fee before you receive the loan estimate and indicate you want to proceed.
How is a loan estimate different from pre-approval?
A loan estimate details projected costs for a specific loan you've applied for, while a pre-approval is a lender's broader assessment of how much you can borrow.
Can I ask for a new loan estimate if my situation changes?
Yes, lenders issue a revised loan estimate when certain circumstances change, such as your credit, the loan amount, or the property.

title: What Is Mortgage Principal? | Your Realty Link
meta: Principal is the amount you originally borrowed on a mortgage, separate from interest. Learn how it's paid down over time on Central Indiana home loans.
hero_sub: The core amount you borrowed, and the number that shrinks with every on-time payment.
definition: Principal is the original amount you borrow on a mortgage, not counting interest, and it's the balance you're paying down with each mortgage payment.
qa_lead: Every mortgage payment splits between principal, which reduces what you owe, and interest, which is the lender's charge for the loan. Early in the loan, more of each payment goes toward interest; see amortization for how that mix shifts over time.
qa_facts: The amount borrowed, not including interest
Loan estimate, closing disclosure, monthly statement
Mostly interest, with a smaller principal share
Applied directly to principal, reducing total interest paid
sections: How Principal Fits Into Your Payment

Your monthly mortgage payment is usually a blend of principal, interest, taxes, and insurance, often summarized as PITI. The principal and interest portion stays level on a fixed-rate loan, but the split between the two shifts every month as your balance goes down.

In the early years of a 30-year loan, the majority of each payment covers interest rather than principal. Over time, as the balance shrinks, a larger share of each payment chips away at principal instead.
Paying Down Principal Faster

Making extra payments earmarked for principal, even modest ones, reduces the balance you're paying interest on and can shorten the life of the loan. Many Indiana lenders allow this without a prepayment penalty, but it's worth confirming before you commit to a plan.
Our agents often walk buyers through how extra principal payments affect long-term interest costs, especially for those planning to stay in a home for many years.
faqs: Does my down payment reduce my principal?
Yes. A larger down payment lowers the amount you finance, which is your starting principal balance.
Why does so little of my early payments go to principal?
Interest is calculated on your outstanding balance, which is highest at the start of the loan, so more of each early payment covers interest.
Can I make extra principal payments anytime?
Most conventional loans allow it, but confirm with your lender whether payments must be specifically designated as principal-only.
Is principal the same as my loan balance?
Yes, your remaining principal is your current loan balance, which decreases with every payment that includes a principal portion.

title: What Is Mortgage Underwriting? | Your Realty Link
meta: Mortgage underwriting is the lender's in-depth review of your finances and the property before final loan approval. Here's what Indiana buyers can expect.
hero_sub: The final, closest look a lender takes before saying yes to your loan.
definition: Underwriting is the process where a lender's underwriter verifies your income, assets, credit, and the property's value before issuing final loan approval.
qa_lead: Once you've submitted your documents, an underwriter checks everything against the lender's guidelines, including your debt-to-income ratio, credit history, and the appraisal. Underwriting is often the step that decides whether your loan moves toward closing on schedule.
qa_facts: Income, assets, credit, debt, and the appraisal
Days to a few weeks, depending on the lender
Clear to close, conditional approval, or denial
Additional documents or a letter explaining an item on file
sections: What an Underwriter Actually Checks

An underwriter verifies the documents you've provided, income, bank statements, tax returns, and credit history, and confirms they match the loan program's requirements. They also review the appraisal to make sure the property supports the loan amount, and check your loan-to-value ratio against program limits.
It's common for an underwriter to come back with conditions, a request for a specific document, an updated pay stub, or an explanation letter for a large deposit, before issuing final approval.
Staying On Track During Underwriting

Because underwriters are re-checking your financial picture right up to closing, lenders generally advise against opening new credit, changing jobs, or making large purchases while a loan is in underwriting. Even small changes can trigger extra scrutiny or delay your closing date.
Responding quickly to any underwriter requests is one of the best ways to keep your transaction moving toward its scheduled closing day.
faqs: How long does underwriting take?
It varies by lender and loan complexity, but often takes anywhere from a few days to a couple of weeks.
What does 'clear to close' mean?
It means the underwriter has approved your loan with no outstanding conditions, and you're ready to schedule closing.
Can I still be denied after pre-approval?
Yes, pre-approval is preliminary. Underwriting is the deeper verification, and a loan can still be denied if something doesn't check out.
Should I avoid big purchases during underwriting?
Yes. Large purchases or new credit can change your debt-to-income ratio and jeopardize your approval.

h1: What Is a Mortgage Interest Rate?
title: What Is a Mortgage Interest Rate? | Your Realty Link
meta: Your mortgage interest rate is the yearly percentage a lender charges to borrow the loan amount. See what shapes rates for Central Indiana homebuyers.
hero_sub: The single number that drives your monthly payment more than almost anything else.
definition: An interest rate is the yearly percentage a lender charges to borrow money, applied to your outstanding loan balance to determine your principal-and-interest payment.
qa_lead: Your interest rate is set based on factors like your credit score, down payment, loan type, and market conditions the day you lock. Even a small difference in rate can move your monthly payment meaningfully, which is why comparing offers and understanding APR matters.
qa_facts: Credit score, down payment, loan type, and market conditions
Your loan estimate and rate lock agreement
Determines whether the rate can change later
Discount points can buy the rate down
sections: What Influences Your Rate

Lenders price your interest rate based on a mix of factors: your credit score and history, your down payment size, the loan program, the property type, and broader market conditions on the day you apply or lock. A stronger credit profile and larger down payment generally lead to a more competitive rate.
The rate you're quoted early in shopping isn't guaranteed until it's locked. See rate lock for how that window works.
Interest Rate vs. APR

Your interest rate determines your base principal-and-interest payment, while the APR wraps in certain lender fees to show a fuller yearly cost of the loan. Comparing both figures, not just the rate, gives a more complete picture when weighing offers from different Central Indiana lenders.
Even a modest rate difference compounds meaningfully over a 30-year term, which is why our agents encourage buyers to shop more than one lender before choosing.
faqs: Why did two lenders quote me different rates?
Rates vary by lender based on their own pricing, overhead, and the loan programs they offer, so shopping multiple lenders is worth the effort.
Does my credit score really affect my rate?
Yes, credit score is one of the biggest factors in rate pricing; a higher score typically unlocks a lower rate.
Can I negotiate my interest rate?
You can sometimes buy down your rate with discount points, and comparing competing offers can also give you leverage.
Is a lower rate always the best deal?
Not necessarily. A lower rate paired with high fees or points can cost more overall than a slightly higher rate with fewer costs, so compare the full loan estimate.

title: What Is APR (Annual Percentage Rate)? | Your Realty Link
meta: APR combines your mortgage interest rate with certain lender fees into one yearly cost figure. Use it to compare loan offers accurately in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: A fuller yearly cost figure that helps you compare loans beyond the rate alone.
definition: The annual percentage rate (APR) is a yearly cost figure that combines your interest rate with certain lender fees, giving a fuller picture than the rate alone.
qa_lead: Because APR bundles in costs like some lender fees along with the interest rate, it usually runs a bit higher than the rate itself. Comparing APR across lenders on your loan estimate is one of the more reliable ways to spot the better overall deal.
qa_facts: Interest rate plus certain lender fees
Slightly higher than your quoted interest rate
Comparing total loan cost across lenders
sections: Why APR Runs Higher Than Your Rate

Your interest rate reflects only the cost of borrowing the principal, while APR folds in certain finance charges, like some lender fees, required by the loan, then spreads that added cost across the loan term to produce a single yearly figure. That's why the APR on your loan estimate is typically a bit higher than the interest rate itself.
A wider gap between the two numbers often signals more upfront fees baked into the loan, which is worth asking your lender to explain.
Using APR to Compare Lenders

Because federal disclosure rules require the same APR calculation method across lenders, it gives Central Indiana buyers a more apples-to-apples way to compare offers than the interest rate alone. Still, it's smart to look at both the rate and the APR, along with total cash to close, before choosing a lender.
APR assumes you keep the loan for its full term, so it can be less useful if you expect to sell or refinance within just a few years.
faqs: Is APR always higher than the interest rate?
Almost always, since it adds certain fees on top of the interest rate, though the gap size varies by lender and loan.
Does a lower APR always mean a better loan?
Generally yes, but also review the interest rate itself and how long you plan to keep the loan, since APR assumes the full term.
Where do I find my APR?
It's disclosed on your loan estimate and again on your closing disclosure before you sign.
Do discount points affect APR?
Yes, paying points to lower your rate is factored into the APR calculation.

title: What Are Discount Points? | Your Realty Link
meta: Discount points are an optional upfront fee, roughly 1% of your loan per point, paid to lower your mortgage rate. Here's when they make sense in Indiana.
hero_sub: Pay a bit more upfront in exchange for a lower rate over the life of the loan.
definition: Discount points are an optional, upfront fee paid at closing, with each point generally costing about 1% of the loan amount, in exchange for a lower interest rate.
qa_lead: Buying discount points trades cash at closing for a lower interest rate and, in turn, a lower monthly payment. Whether it's worth it comes down to how long you plan to keep the loan, since the upfront cost needs time to pay for itself.
qa_facts: About 1% of the loan amount per point
A modest reduction in your interest rate per point
Months to years, depending on the rate reduction
Buyers planning to keep the loan long-term
sections: How Points Lower Your Rate

Each discount point you purchase generally costs about 1% of your loan amount and buys down your interest rate by a modest amount, though the exact reduction varies by lender and market conditions. Points are itemized on your loan estimate so you can see the cost and rate side by side.
You can typically buy a fraction of a point, a full point, or several points, depending on how much upfront cost you're willing to trade for a lower rate.
Calculating Your Break-Even Point

The key question with discount points is how long it takes the monthly savings to recover the upfront cost, known as the break-even point. If you plan to keep the loan well past that point, paying points can save real money over the life of the loan.
If you expect to sell or refinance within just a few years, the upfront cost of points often doesn't have enough time to pay off, so a lender-provided comparison is worth reviewing carefully.
faqs: Are discount points tax-deductible?
They may be deductible as mortgage interest in the year paid, but tax treatment depends on your situation, so check with a tax professional.
Is buying points the same as an origination fee?
No, origination fees cover the lender's cost of processing your loan, while discount points are optional and specifically buy down your rate.
How many points can I buy?
It varies by lender and loan program, but many allow you to buy a fraction of a point up to several points.
Do points make sense for every buyer?
No, they generally benefit buyers who plan to keep the loan long enough to pass the break-even point; shorter-term owners often skip them.

h1: What Is a Mortgage Rate Lock?
title: What Is a Mortgage Rate Lock? | Your Realty Link
meta: A rate lock is your lender's commitment to hold a quoted interest rate for a set window while your loan is processed. Here's how it protects Indiana buyers.
hero_sub: Your rate, held in place while the rest of your loan comes together.
definition: A rate lock is a lender's guarantee to hold your quoted interest rate for a specific window of time, typically 30 to 60 days, while your loan moves through processing and underwriting.
qa_lead: Locking your rate protects you from market increases while your loan is processed, though it also means you generally won't benefit if rates drop after you lock. Ask your lender about the exact length of your lock and what happens if closing day gets pushed back.
qa_facts: You usually won't get the benefit if rates fall after locking
Often available for a fee if closing is delayed
sections: When and Why to Lock Your Rate

Many buyers lock their rate once they're under contract and have a reliable closing timeline, since locking earlier protects against rate increases while your loan is in underwriting. Locking too early, before you have a firm contract, can mean paying extension fees if the purchase takes longer to close than expected.
Some lenders offer a float-down option, letting you capture a lower rate if the market improves after you lock, though this typically comes with its own cost.
What Happens If Your Closing Is Delayed

If your closing date moves past your lock expiration, most lenders will extend the lock for an additional fee, or in some cases re-lock at current market rates. This is one reason it's worth building in a reasonable buffer when your loan officer sets the original lock period.
Staying responsive to underwriting requests helps keep your transaction on schedule and reduces the chance you'll need a costly extension.
faqs: How long does a typical rate lock last?
Most locks run 30 to 60 days, though some lenders offer shorter or longer windows depending on the loan program.
What if rates drop after I lock?
In most cases you keep your locked rate even if the market improves, unless your lender offers a float-down option.
Does locking my rate cost money?
Many standard locks are included at no extra charge, but longer locks or extensions can carry a fee, so ask your lender directly.
What happens if my lock expires before closing?
Your lender will typically offer an extension for a fee, or you may need to re-lock at the current market rate.

title: What Is Debt-to-Income Ratio (DTI)? | Your Realty Link
meta: Debt-to-income ratio (DTI) compares your monthly debt payments to your gross income, and lenders use it to gauge how much you can safely borrow in Indiana.
hero_sub: A quick math check lenders use to see how much loan you can comfortably carry.
definition: Debt-to-income ratio (DTI) is the percentage of your gross monthly income that goes toward debt payments, including your proposed mortgage payment, used by lenders to evaluate borrowing capacity.
qa_lead: Lenders add up your monthly debts, including credit cards, car loans, and your future mortgage payment, then divide by your gross monthly income to get your DTI. A lower ratio generally makes it easier to qualify and can affect your rate during underwriting.
qa_facts: Monthly debt payments divided by gross income
Proposed mortgage payment plus other recurring debts
Lower ratios generally qualify more easily
Vary by loan type, so check with your lender
sections: How DTI Is Calculated

Lenders total your recurring monthly debt payments, credit cards, auto loans, student loans, and the proposed housing payment, then divide that figure by your gross monthly income before taxes. The result is expressed as a percentage and often broken into a front-end ratio, housing costs only, and a back-end ratio that combines all debts.
Your DTI is one of several factors lenders weigh alongside credit score, down payment, and cash reserves when they evaluate your loan-to-value ratio and overall application.
Ways to Improve Your DTI

Paying down revolving debt, avoiding new loans before applying, and, where possible, increasing documented income can all help lower your DTI before you apply. Some buyers also choose a lower purchase price specifically to keep their ratio comfortably within their loan program's limits.
Our agents often coordinate with a buyer's lender early in the process so pricing expectations line up with what a comfortable DTI actually supports.
faqs: What DTI do I need to qualify for a mortgage?
Limits vary by loan program and lender, so it's best to confirm your specific threshold with a lender during pre-approval.
Does DTI include my proposed mortgage payment?
Yes, lenders calculate DTI using your total debts including the new mortgage payment you're applying for, not just your existing debts.
Can I lower my DTI before applying?
Yes, paying down credit cards or other loans, and avoiding new debt, are common ways to bring your ratio down before you apply.
Is DTI the same as my credit score?
No, they're separate measures. DTI looks at your income versus debt payments, while your credit score reflects your borrowing and repayment history.

title: What Is a Loan-to-Value Ratio (LTV)? | Your Realty Link
meta: Your loan-to-value ratio (LTV) compares your loan amount to your home's appraised value. See how LTV affects your rate, PMI, and buying power locally.
hero_sub: The single number that tells a lender how much cushion stands between your loan and your home's value.
definition: The loan-to-value ratio (LTV) is the percentage of a home's appraised value covered by the mortgage, found by dividing the loan amount by the appraised value.
qa_lead: Your loan-to-value ratio (LTV) is your loan amount divided by your home's appraised value, shown as a percentage. A lower LTV generally means a stronger position with a lender and can help you avoid PMI on a conventional loan.
qa_facts: Loan amount vs. home's appraised value
Above roughly 80% LTV on conventional loans
Bigger down payment or added equity over time
sections: How Lenders Use Your LTV

Because a mortgage is secured by the home itself, lenders watch how much equity cushion exists in case they ever had to resell the property. A lower LTV, built with a larger down payment, generally supports better loan terms and more flexibility on interest rate and program options.
LTV works alongside your debt-to-income ratio as one of the core numbers underwriters review, but it focuses on the property rather than your income.
LTV and Mortgage Insurance

On most conventional loans, an LTV above roughly 80 percent means the lender requires private mortgage insurance to offset the added risk. Government-backed loans like FHA and USDA have their own insurance or guarantee fee structures regardless of LTV.
As you pay down principal or your home's value rises, your LTV improves over time, which is one reason many owners eventually ask their lender to drop mortgage insurance.
faqs: What is a good LTV?
A lower LTV is generally viewed favorably by lenders, though acceptable ranges vary by loan program and lender.
Does LTV affect my interest rate?
It can. Lenders often price loans more favorably when LTV is lower because their risk is reduced.
Can I lower my LTV without a bigger down payment?
Yes. Paying down principal over time or a rise in appraised value both improve your LTV.
Is LTV calculated the same way for a refinance?
The concept is the same, but a refinance LTV compares your new loan amount to your home's current appraised value, not your original purchase price.

title: What Is PITI in a Mortgage Payment? | Your Realty Link
meta: PITI stands for principal, interest, taxes, and insurance, the four parts that make up a typical monthly mortgage payment for Central Indiana homeowners.
hero_sub: The full picture of what you'll actually pay each month, not just principal and interest.
definition: PITI is shorthand for the four components of a standard mortgage payment: principal, interest, taxes, and insurance.
qa_lead: PITI adds up the four pieces of your monthly mortgage payment: principal, interest, property taxes, and insurance. Lenders qualify you based on your full PITI, not just the loan payment, so it directly affects how much home you can afford alongside your debt-to-income ratio.
qa_facts: Portion that reduces your loan balance
The lender's charge for the loan
Property taxes, often collected through escrow
Homeowners insurance, plus PMI if required
sections: The Four Parts of PITI

Principal and interest make up your base loan payment, gradually paying down what you borrowed while covering the lender's cost of the money. See amortization for how that balance shifts over the loan term.

Taxes and insurance are usually collected monthly and held in escrow, then paid on your behalf when the county tax bill or insurance premium comes due, so you rarely have to write a separate large check.
Why PITI Matters for Qualifying

When a lender calculates how much you can borrow, they weigh your full PITI against your income, not just principal and interest. A home with higher property taxes or HOA dues can lower the loan amount you qualify for even at the same purchase price.
Comparing homes by PITI, rather than list price alone, gives a more accurate sense of what a property will actually cost you each month.
faqs: Does PITI include HOA dues?
No. HOA dues are a separate cost lenders often factor in when qualifying you, but they aren't part of the PITI acronym itself.
Why are my taxes and insurance included in my mortgage payment?
Many lenders escrow taxes and insurance so they're paid automatically and on time, protecting their collateral and helping you avoid one large annual bill.
Can I pay my own taxes and insurance instead of escrowing?
Sometimes, depending on your loan program and down payment size. Ask your lender whether a waiver is available.
Does PMI count as part of PITI?
PMI is typically folded into the insurance portion of the payment when it applies.

h1: What Is a Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC)?
title: What Is a Home Equity Line of Credit? | Your Realty Link
meta: A home equity line of credit (HELOC) lets you borrow against your home's equity as needed, with a variable rate and revolving balance, much like a credit card.
hero_sub: A flexible credit line secured by your home, ready to draw on when you need it.
definition: A home equity line of credit (HELOC) is a revolving credit line secured by the equity in your home, letting you borrow, repay, and borrow again up to a set limit.
qa_lead: A HELOC lets you tap the equity in your home as a revolving credit line, similar to a credit card, rather than receiving one lump sum. Most HELOCs carry a variable rate, so your payment can change as rates move.
qa_facts: Revolving credit line, not a lump sum
A set number of years to borrow, then a repayment period
sections: How a HELOC Works

A HELOC typically has two phases: a draw period, when you can borrow against the line as needed and often make interest-only payments, followed by a repayment period, when you pay down both principal and interest. Your available credit is based on your equity and the lender's maximum combined loan-to-value limit.
Because the rate is usually variable, your monthly payment can rise or fall over time, which differs from a fixed-rate home equity loan that hands you one lump sum at a set rate.
Common Uses for a HELOC

Homeowners often use a HELOC for renovations, debt consolidation, or as a flexible financial cushion, since you only pay interest on what you actually draw. Some Central Indiana buyers and investors also use one to help fund a down payment on another property.
Because your home secures the line, missed payments put your property at risk, so it's worth borrowing only what fits comfortably in your budget.
faqs: What's the difference between a HELOC and a home equity loan?
A HELOC is a revolving line you draw from as needed at a variable rate, while a home equity loan gives you one lump sum at a fixed rate.
Can I get a HELOC on a rental property, not just my primary home?
Many lenders offer HELOCs on primary residences, and some extend them to investment properties, though terms and requirements vary.
Does a HELOC affect my ability to qualify for other loans?
Yes. Lenders factor your HELOC balance and payment into your debt-to-income ratio when you apply for other financing.
Is the interest on a HELOC tax-deductible?
It may be in certain cases, such as when funds are used to improve the home securing the loan. Confirm your specific situation with a tax professional.

title: What Is a Jumbo Loan? | Your Realty Link
meta: A jumbo loan is a mortgage above the conforming loan limit for the county, so it can't be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. See how jumbo loans work locally.
hero_sub: The financing buyers need when a home's price climbs past the conforming loan limit.
definition: A jumbo loan is a mortgage that exceeds the conforming loan limit set for the county, meaning it cannot be purchased by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac and typically requires stricter underwriting.
qa_lead: A jumbo loan finances a home priced above the conforming loan limit for the county, so it falls outside standard conventional loan guidelines backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Because lenders can't offload these loans as easily, they often require stronger credit, a bigger down payment, and more cash reserves.
qa_facts: Loan amount above the county's conforming limit
No — jumbo loans fall outside those limits
Stronger credit and a larger down payment
Higher-priced homes in markets like Carmel and Zionsville
sections: What Makes a Loan Jumbo

Each county has a conforming loan limit set annually, and any mortgage above that amount is classified as jumbo. In Central Indiana, jumbo financing shows up most often on higher-priced homes in markets like Carmel and Zionsville, though the exact limit can vary by county and loan type.
Because jumbo loans aren't backed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, the lender carries more of the risk directly, which shapes how they underwrite the loan.
Qualifying for a Jumbo Loan

Lenders typically look for stronger debt-to-income ratios, higher credit scores, and larger cash reserves on a jumbo loan than on a conventional one. A larger down payment is common too, since it lowers the lender's exposure.
Rates and terms on jumbo loans vary more by lender than conventional loans do, so it's worth comparing a few options before choosing one.
faqs: How is the conforming loan limit determined?
Loan limits are set annually and can vary by county based on local home prices; any loan above that amount is considered jumbo.
Do jumbo loans require a bigger down payment?
Often, yes. Many jumbo programs ask for a larger down payment than a typical conventional loan, though requirements vary by lender.
Is the interest rate on a jumbo loan higher?
It depends on the lender and market conditions. Jumbo rates aren't automatically higher, but underwriting is generally stricter.
Can a jumbo loan be an ARM or a fixed rate?
Both are available. Jumbo borrowers can typically choose between a fixed-rate mortgage and an adjustable-rate mortgage depending on the lender.

title: What Is a Mortgage Broker? | Your Realty Link
meta: A mortgage broker is a licensed professional who shops your loan application across multiple lenders to find the right fit, rather than lending money directly.
hero_sub: A go-between who shops your loan across multiple lenders instead of lending the money themselves.
definition: A mortgage broker is a licensed professional who works with multiple lenders to find and arrange a mortgage on a borrower's behalf, rather than funding the loan directly.
qa_lead: A mortgage broker doesn't lend money directly; instead, they submit your application to several mortgage lenders to compare rates and programs on your behalf. This can help when your situation, such as self-employment or a lower credit score, calls for more than one option.
qa_facts: Shops your loan to multiple lenders
Typically a fee paid by the lender or borrower
Buyers wanting to compare several loan programs
sections: Broker vs. Direct Lender

Working with a mortgage lender directly means you're applying with one institution's own programs and pricing. A broker instead gathers your information once and shops it across a network of lenders, which can widen your options, especially for less common loan scenarios.
Because a broker isn't funding the loan, they don't carry the final underwriting decision. That authority stays with whichever lender ultimately approves and closes your loan.
When a Broker Can Help

Buyers with more complex income, credit challenges, or a need for a specialized loan program sometimes benefit most from a broker's wider access to lenders. First-time buyers who want to compare several offers side by side may also find a broker helpful.
Whichever route you choose, our agents regularly work with both brokers and direct lenders and can point you toward responsive local options in Central Indiana.
faqs: Does a mortgage broker cost more than going direct to a lender?
Not necessarily. Broker compensation varies and is disclosed upfront, so it's worth comparing total costs, not just the interest rate.
Can a mortgage broker guarantee loan approval?
No broker or lender can guarantee approval before underwriting reviews your full file.
Is a mortgage broker the same as a loan officer?
No. A loan officer typically works for one lender, while a broker works with multiple lenders on your behalf.
Should I use a broker or go straight to a bank?
Both can work well. It often comes down to your specific situation and how many options you want to compare.

title: What Is a Mortgage Lender? | Your Realty Link
meta: A mortgage lender is the bank, credit union, or company that underwrites and funds your home loan directly. See how a lender differs from a mortgage broker.
hero_sub: The institution that actually puts up the money and makes the final call on your loan.
definition: A mortgage lender is the financial institution, such as a bank, credit union, or direct mortgage company, that underwrites and funds a home loan.
qa_lead: A mortgage lender reviews your application, underwrites the loan, and provides the actual funds at closing. Unlike a mortgage broker, who shops your loan to others, the lender makes the final approval decision and services or sells the loan afterward.
qa_facts: Banks, credit unions, direct mortgage companies
A lender funds the loan; a broker shops it
sections: What a Lender Actually Does

From application to closing, your lender verifies your income, assets, and credit, orders the appraisal, and moves your file through underwriting. Once approved, the lender funds the loan at closing and either services it going forward or sells it to another company that will.
Different lenders specialize in different programs, from conventional and jumbo loans to FHA, VA, and USDA financing, so it's worth confirming a lender offers the program that fits your situation.
Choosing a Lender in Central Indiana

Local and regional lenders often bring faster communication and familiarity with Indiana closing customs, while larger national lenders may offer a wider menu of programs. Getting a pre-approval from your chosen lender early gives you a clear budget before you start touring homes.
Our agents work with local lenders regularly and can point you toward responsive options as part of your home search.
faqs: What's the difference between a lender and a broker?
A lender funds your loan directly and makes the final approval decision; a broker shops your application to multiple lenders on your behalf.
Can I switch lenders after getting pre-approved?
Yes, though it may mean restarting parts of the application and documentation process with the new lender.
Does my real estate agent choose my lender?
No. You choose your own lender, though your agent can share names of local lenders other clients have had good experiences with.
How long does it take a lender to close a loan?
Timelines vary by lender and loan type, but most conventional purchases close within a few weeks of a clean application.

title: What Is a Prepayment Penalty? | Your Realty Link
meta: A prepayment penalty is a fee some loans charge for paying off the mortgage early through a sale or refinance. Learn when they apply and how to check yours.
hero_sub: A fee a small number of loans charge if you pay them off faster than planned.
definition: A prepayment penalty is a fee charged by certain mortgage loans when the borrower pays off all or a large part of the balance earlier than scheduled, such as through a sale or refinance.
qa_lead: A prepayment penalty charges you a fee for paying your mortgage off early, whether through a home sale or a refinance. Most conventional mortgages issued today don't include one, but it's still worth checking your loan estimate and closing documents to be sure.
qa_facts: A fee for paying off a loan early
Your loan estimate and closing disclosure
Selling, refinancing, or large extra payments
sections: Why Prepayment Penalties Exist

Lenders earn money over the life of a loan through interest, so paying it off early reduces that expected income. A prepayment penalty offsets some of that loss on the small share of loans that still include one.
Modern lending rules have made prepayment penalties far less common than they once were, and many loan programs prohibit them outright.
How to Check Your Loan

Your loan estimate and closing disclosure will both disclose whether your loan includes a prepayment penalty, so review those documents closely before signing. If you plan to sell or refinance within the first few years, this is worth confirming upfront.
If you're unsure whether your current mortgage has one, your loan servicer or the original closing paperwork can confirm it.
faqs: Are prepayment penalties legal in Indiana?
Prepayment penalty rules depend on the loan type and federal regulations; many modern mortgage programs prohibit them, though it's still worth verifying your specific loan.
Do FHA or VA loans have prepayment penalties?
Government-backed loans like FHA and VA generally do not allow prepayment penalties.
How do I know if my loan has one?
Check your loan estimate and closing disclosure, or ask your lender or servicer directly.
Does selling my home early trigger a prepayment penalty?
It can, if your loan includes one and you sell within the penalty period. Most current loans do not have this feature.

title: What Is Mortgage Forbearance? | Your Realty Link
meta: Mortgage forbearance is a temporary pause or reduction in payments a lender may grant during a hardship. Learn how it works and what happens once it ends.
hero_sub: Temporary breathing room from your lender when a hardship makes payments hard to keep up with.
definition: Forbearance is a temporary agreement with a mortgage lender to pause or reduce payments during a financial hardship, with the skipped amount repaid later rather than forgiven.
qa_lead: Forbearance lets you pause or reduce mortgage payments for a set period during a hardship, such as job loss or a medical event. The amount you don't pay isn't forgiven — you and your lender work out a repayment plan once the forbearance period ends.
qa_facts: Job loss, illness, or other hardship
sections: How Forbearance Works

To request forbearance, you contact your loan servicer and explain your hardship. If approved, your servicer sets a temporary plan, often for a period of months, during which your required payment is paused or reduced.

Once the forbearance period ends, you'll typically repay the missed amount through a repayment plan, a loan modification, or by adding it to the end of the loan, depending on what your servicer offers.
Forbearance vs. Other Options

Forbearance is meant to be temporary relief, not a long-term solution, and interest generally continues to accrue during the pause. It's different from a loan modification, which permanently changes your loan terms.
If you're facing a hardship and considering selling instead, our agents can walk you through selling quickly or other options alongside a conversation with your lender.
faqs: Does forbearance hurt my credit?
It can, depending on how your servicer reports it and your loan program's specific rules. Ask your servicer directly before entering forbearance.
How long does forbearance typically last?
Terms vary by lender and hardship type and can sometimes be extended, so ask your servicer about the specific timeline they're offering.
Do I have to repay everything at once when forbearance ends?
Not usually. Most servicers offer a repayment plan, modification, or other option rather than requiring a lump sum.
Is forbearance the same as a loan modification?
No. Forbearance is temporary payment relief, while a modification permanently changes your loan's terms.

h1: What Is a Rate Cap on an ARM?
title: What Is a Rate Cap on an ARM? | Your Realty Link
meta: A rate cap limits how much an adjustable-rate mortgage can increase at each adjustment and over the life of the loan. See how rate caps protect ARM borrowers.
hero_sub: The built-in ceiling that keeps an adjustable-rate mortgage from climbing without limit.
definition: A rate cap is a limit built into an adjustable-rate mortgage that restricts how much the interest rate can increase at each adjustment period and over the life of the loan.
qa_lead: On an adjustable-rate mortgage, a rate cap limits how far your interest rate can rise at each adjustment and across the full loan term. Caps are commonly expressed as three numbers, such as 2/2/5, covering the first adjustment, each later adjustment, and the lifetime maximum.
qa_facts: How much the rate can rise per adjustment and over the loan's life
Keeps payment increases within a predictable range
sections: How Rate Caps Are Structured

A typical cap structure has three parts: the initial adjustment cap, the periodic adjustment cap, and the lifetime cap. Together, they set boundaries on how much your rate, and therefore your payment, can move at each step and over the full term of the ARM.
Cap structures vary by lender and loan program, so it's worth reviewing your specific loan's caps rather than assuming a standard structure applies.
Why Rate Caps Matter to Borrowers

Without a cap, an ARM's rate could theoretically rise sharply at each adjustment. Caps give borrowers a predictable ceiling, which makes it easier to budget for a worst-case scenario before choosing an ARM over a fixed-rate mortgage.
Understanding your loan's specific caps, along with how often adjustments occur, is an important part of deciding whether an ARM fits your plans.
faqs: What does a 2/2/5 cap mean?

It commonly means the rate can rise up to 2 percent at the first adjustment, up to 2 percent at each later adjustment, and up to 5 percent over the life of the loan, though exact structures vary by lender.
Do all ARMs have rate caps?
Most ARMs sold today include caps, but the specific limits vary by lender and loan program, so always confirm your loan's terms.
Can my rate ever go down with an ARM?
Yes. ARM rates adjust based on an index and can move down as well as up, within the loan's cap structure.
Is a rate cap the same as a fixed rate?
No. A rate cap limits how much a variable rate can change; a fixed-rate mortgage doesn't change at all over the loan term.

title: What Is MIBOR? | Your Realty Link
meta: MIBOR is the Metropolitan Indianapolis Board of Realtors, the association that operates the Central Indiana MLS agents use to list, market, and sell homes.
hero_sub: The Realtor association that runs the MLS Central Indiana agents rely on every day.
definition: MIBOR REALTOR Association is the regional trade association for real estate professionals in Central Indiana, and it operates the area's Multiple Listing Service.
qa_lead: MIBOR is the Metropolitan Indianapolis Board of Realtors, the professional association that licenses agents to use the region's MLS and enforces its rules. When you hear an agent mention MIBOR, they mean the organization behind the listing data your search results come from. Your Realty Link agents are MIBOR members in good standing.
qa_facts: Licensed real estate agents and brokers
sections: What MIBOR Does

MIBOR is a regional trade association, not a government body. It sets professional standards, offers continuing education, and maintains the Multiple Listing Service that member agents use to enter and search listings across Central Indiana.

Membership means an agent has agreed to a code of ethics and has access to the same shared listing data as every other MIBOR member, which is part of what makes local searches consistent from one agent to the next.
MIBOR and the MLS

The MLS is the actual database of active, pending, and sold listings. MIBOR is the organization that owns and operates it for this market, similar to how other regions have their own local Realtor association running their own MLS.
Because listings are entered by member agents under MIBOR's rules, buyers get accurate, up-to-date information rather than stale data scraped from elsewhere.
Why It Matters to You

You won't deal with MIBOR directly, but its rules shape how your transaction works, from how quickly a listing has to be entered to what disclosures are required. Working with a Realtor means working with someone who has agreed to MIBOR's standards.
Your Realty Link agents pull directly from the MIBOR MLS, so the listings you see through our property search reflect the same real-time data every other member agent sees.
faqs: Is MIBOR the same as the MLS?
No. MIBOR is the association; the MLS is the database it operates. People often use the names interchangeably.
Do I need to be a MIBOR member to buy or sell a home?
No. Only licensed agents and brokers join MIBOR. As a buyer or seller, you simply work with a member agent.
Does MIBOR cover all of Indiana?
No, MIBOR's MLS covers Indianapolis and a number of surrounding Central Indiana counties, not the whole state.

title: What Is the MLS? | Your Realty Link
meta: The MLS is the shared database Central Indiana agents use to list and track homes for sale, giving buyers and sellers access to the same real-time data.
hero_sub: The shared database that makes almost every home search in Central Indiana possible.
definition: The Multiple Listing Service (MLS) is a shared database where member brokers and agents list properties for sale, giving buyers and sellers access to the same real-time information.
qa_lead: The MLS is the database Central Indiana agents use to enter active listings, track pending sales, and record closed sale prices. It's operated locally by MIBOR, and it's the original source behind most home search sites, including ours.
qa_facts: Limited; data flows out through agent and consumer search sites
sections: Why the MLS Exists

Before shared databases, a buyer had to check with dozens of individual brokerages to see what was for sale. The MLS solves that by requiring member agents to enter their listings in one place, so every other member agent, and through syndication the public, can see the same information.
This cooperative system is also what allows a buyer's agent from one brokerage to show a home listed by a completely different brokerage.
What's Actually in an MLS Listing

A full MLS listing includes far more than the photos and price you see on a public site: square footage, lot details, school district, HOA information, showing instructions, and the listing agreement terms the agent entered.
Because it's maintained by professionals under MIBOR's rules, the data is generally more accurate and current than listings pulled from other sources.
How Buyers and Sellers Use It

As a seller, getting your home into the MLS through a listing agreement is what exposes it to the full pool of active buyers and their agents. As a buyer, MLS data, often through your agent or an IDX search, is the most reliable way to see what's genuinely available.
Your Realty Link's property search pulls directly from the MIBOR MLS feed.
faqs: Can I search the MLS myself?
The MLS itself is for members only, but licensed agents make that data available to the public through IDX-powered search tools like ours.
Is Zillow the same as the MLS?
No. Sites like Zillow license and display MLS data, but they don't operate the database, and their listing details can lag behind the source.
Does every home for sale end up in the MLS?
Most agent-listed homes do. For sale by owner and some off-market listings do not, which is one reason working with an agent widens your search.

title: What Is a Listing Agreement? | Your Realty Link
meta: A listing agreement is the contract that authorizes a brokerage to market and sell your home, sets the commission, and gets it entered into the MIBOR MLS.
hero_sub: The contract that authorizes your agent to market your home and puts it into the MLS.
definition: A listing agreement is the contract between a seller and a brokerage that authorizes the brokerage to market and sell the home, and that sets the commission.
qa_lead: A listing agreement is what turns your home into an official MLS listing. It spells out the listing price, the length of the agreement, the commission, and what marketing the brokerage will provide. Most Central Indiana listings use an exclusive right to sell agreement.
qa_facts: The seller and the listing brokerage
sections: What's Actually in the Agreement
Beyond price and commission, a listing agreement spells out the start and end date, how showings are handled, what's included or excluded from the sale, and the brokerage's marketing commitments.
It also authorizes the brokerage to enter your home into the MLS, which is what exposes it to other agents and their buyers.
Choosing the Right Term and Type

Sellers can negotiate the length of the agreement and, in some cases, the type. An exclusive right to sell is standard because it gives the brokerage full incentive to invest time and marketing dollars, but the details are always negotiable before signing.
Your Realty Link walks every seller through the agreement line by line before anything is signed, as part of our pricing and listing process.
faqs: Can I cancel a listing agreement early?
Many brokerages will release you if the relationship isn't working, but the agreement itself usually runs for its stated term unless both sides agree to end it.
Does signing a listing agreement cost anything upfront?
No. Commission is typically paid out of proceeds at closing, not upfront.
What happens if my home doesn't sell during the term?
The agreement simply expires and you're free to relist, renew, or take the home off the market.

h1: What Is an Exclusive Right to Sell Agreement?
title: Exclusive Right to Sell | Your Realty Link
meta: An exclusive right to sell agreement is the standard listing contract: your brokerage earns commission on any sale in the term, no matter who finds the buyer.
hero_sub: The standard listing agreement that gives your brokerage full incentive to market and sell your home.
definition: An exclusive right to sell agreement is a listing agreement under which the brokerage earns its commission if the home sells during the term, regardless of who finds the buyer.
qa_lead: Under an exclusive right to sell agreement, your brokerage is paid its commission if the home sells while the listing agreement is active, even if you find the buyer yourself. It's the most common type of listing agreement because it gives the brokerage full incentive to invest in marketing.
qa_facts: The listing brokerage, regardless of who finds the buyer
sections: How It Differs From Other Listing Types

In an exclusive agency agreement, a seller who finds their own buyer can avoid paying a commission. Under exclusive right to sell, the brokerage is paid either way, which is why brokerages are generally willing to spend more on photography, marketing, and staging advice.
Most agents in Central Indiana, including Your Realty Link, use this agreement because it aligns everyone's incentives toward the same outcome: a successful sale.
What You Get in Return
In exchange for the guaranteed commission, sellers should expect real marketing: professional photos, MLS entry, showings coordination, and a pricing strategy backed by a comparative market analysis.
This is also the agreement type that gets your home into the MLS, syndicated search sites, and in front of every buyer's agent working in the market.
faqs: Can I still sell to a friend or family member myself?
Under an exclusive right to sell agreement, the brokerage is typically still owed its commission even if you find the buyer, so ask your agent how that scenario is handled before signing.
Is this the only type of listing agreement?
No, but it's by far the most common because it gives the brokerage the strongest incentive to market the home well.
How long does an exclusive right to sell agreement last?
The term is negotiated between the seller and brokerage and commonly runs a few months, though it varies.

title: What Is an Open House? | Your Realty Link
meta: An open house is a scheduled window when a listed home is open for any buyer to tour without an appointment, one tool among several in a home's marketing plan.
hero_sub: A scheduled window when anyone can walk through a listed home without an appointment.
definition: An open house is a scheduled period when a listed home is available for any interested buyer to tour without a private, scheduled showing.
qa_lead: An open house lets buyers tour a home without scheduling an individual tour through the listing agent. It's one marketing tool among several, and it tends to work better for some homes and price points than others. Ask your agent whether an open house fits your specific home's marketing plan.
qa_facts: A few hours on a weekend
Move-in ready homes in active buyer areas
sections: What Happens at an Open House

A listing agent typically staffs the home for a set window, greets visitors, answers questions, and collects contact information from interested buyers. Some visitors are represented by their own agent; others are browsing on their own.

It's common practice to sign in, and in many Central Indiana transactions a buyer without their own agent may be offered the listing agent's assistance, though that raises dual agency considerations worth understanding.
Is an Open House Worth It for Sellers

Open houses generate foot traffic and buzz, but relatively few homes actually sell to someone who walked in during the event itself. Their real value is often exposure, neighbor word-of-mouth, and giving buyer's agents a low-pressure way to preview the home for their clients.
Your Realty Link builds each listing's marketing plan around what actually reaches buyers for that specific home, which may or may not include a public open house.
faqs: Do I need an agent to attend an open house?
No. Open houses are open to the public, though it's a good idea to have your own buyer's agent looking out for your interests before you make an offer.
Are virtual open houses common now?
Some agents offer live virtual walkthroughs as a supplement, but they work best alongside, not instead of, an in-person visit before you buy.
Do sellers have to allow an open house?
No, it's optional and can be discussed as part of the home's overall marketing plan.

title: What Is Home Staging? | Your Realty Link
meta: Staging means arranging furniture and clearing clutter so a home shows well in photos, helping Central Indiana buyers picture themselves living there.
hero_sub: Arranging a home so buyers can picture themselves living there before it ever hits the market.
definition: Staging is the practice of arranging furniture, decor, and clutter in a home so it photographs well and shows at its best to potential buyers.
qa_lead: Staging means preparing a home, room by room, so it presents well in photos and in person. It ranges from a light decluttering pass to full furniture rental, and even modest staging can help buyers picture themselves living there. Ask your agent what level of staging makes sense for your home before listing.
qa_facts: Light decluttering to full furniture rental
Help buyers picture themselves living there
Your listing agent, sometimes a staging professional
sections: Why Staging Helps

Buyers spend most of their decision-making time looking at photos online before ever stepping inside, so a well-staged home tends to photograph better and stand out in search results. In person, staging also helps rooms feel like they serve a clear purpose, which is harder for buyers to picture in a cluttered or empty space.
It's not required, but it's one of the more cost-effective ways to make a strong first impression.
Light Staging vs. Full Staging

Light staging is usually just decluttering, depersonalizing, and rearranging what's already in the home, which most sellers can do with guidance from their agent at little to no cost. Full staging brings in rented furniture and decor, typically for vacant homes or higher price points where the investment is easier to justify.
Your Realty Link agents walk every seller through practical, budget-conscious staging recommendations as part of our pre-listing prep.
faqs: Do I have to hire a professional stager?
No. Many homes benefit from simple decluttering and rearranging that a seller can do with their agent's guidance, without hiring a professional.
Is staging worth the cost?
For many sellers, yes, especially for vacant homes or higher-end listings, but the right level of staging depends on the home and the market.
Does staging affect the appraisal?
No, staging is a marketing tool. An appraisal is based on comparable sales and property characteristics, not decor.

title: What Is an iBuyer? | Your Realty Link
meta: An iBuyer is a company that uses automated pricing to make fast cash offers on homes, trading convenience and speed for fees and a below-market purchase price.
hero_sub: A company that makes fast, algorithm-driven cash offers on homes, convenience with tradeoffs.
definition: An iBuyer is a company that uses automated pricing models to make quick, largely automated cash offers on homes, buying directly from sellers outside the traditional market process.
qa_lead: An iBuyer relies on an algorithm and public data to generate a fast cash offer on your home, often within a day or two. The tradeoff for that speed and convenience is usually a service fee and a price that lands below what a well-marketed listing could bring on the open market.
qa_facts: A service fee plus a below-market price
Sellers who prioritize certainty and speed over top dollar
sections: How iBuyers Price a Home

iBuyers generate an initial offer using an automated valuation model built on public records, recent sales, and the details you provide online, then often adjust after an inspection. Because there's no bidding from real buyers, the price is generally more conservative than what full market exposure could produce.
This is very different from a comparative market analysis, where an agent prices your home based on how buyers are actually competing for similar properties nearby.
Weighing Speed Against Price

An iBuyer sale can make sense for a seller who needs certainty on a closing date, wants to skip showings, or is managing a relocation or estate timeline. The cost of that convenience is typically a service fee plus a purchase price below what a traditional, fully marketed listing would likely bring.
Before accepting an iBuyer offer, it's worth getting a free home valuation from a local agent to see what the traditional route could realistically net you.
faqs: Do iBuyers pay full market value?
Generally not. iBuyers typically price in a discount plus service fees to account for the risk and cost of an automated, no-showings sale.
Are iBuyer offers negotiable?
Some room exists, especially after inspection adjustments, but there's usually less negotiating flexibility than with a traditional buyer.
Is an iBuyer the same as a house-flipping investor?
No. iBuyers use automated pricing at scale, while individual investors typically evaluate homes case by case, often for a fix and flip purchase.

title: What Is a Cash Offer? | Your Realty Link
meta: A cash offer is a purchase offer made without a mortgage, backed by proof of funds instead of loan approval, often leading to a faster, more certain closing.
hero_sub: An offer backed by funds on hand instead of a mortgage, and a strong signal to sellers.
definition: A cash offer is an offer to purchase a home without financing, backed by proof of funds rather than a lender's loan approval.
qa_lead: A cash offer skips the mortgage step entirely, which means no underwriting and no appraisal requirement tied to a lender. That usually translates into a faster, more certain closing, which is a big part of why sellers often favor cash offers even when they aren't the highest price on the table.
qa_facts: Bank or investment statement showing funds
sections: Why Sellers Like Cash Offers

Without a lender involved, there's no risk of financing falling through late in the process, which is one of the more common reasons a deal collapses. Cash deals also often skip a mandatory lender-ordered appraisal, removing another point where a deal can stall.
For a seller weighing multiple offers, a cash offer with clean terms can be more attractive than a higher-priced financed offer with more contingencies.
What Buyers Should Know

Making a cash offer typically requires providing proof of funds upfront, such as a recent bank or brokerage statement, so the seller can verify the money is really available. Buyers should still consider an inspection, even without a lender requiring one.
Cash buyers still benefit from working with an agent to negotiate terms and coordinate closing through a local title company.
faqs: Does a cash offer mean no inspection?
Not necessarily. Cash buyers can still choose to include an inspection contingency; it's simply not required by a lender.
Is a cash offer always the highest offer?
No. Cash offers are often chosen for speed and certainty rather than price, and can sometimes be lower than a financed offer.
Can I make a cash offer using home equity or a line of credit?
Yes, as long as the funds are accessible and verifiable, it still counts as a cash offer since there's no purchase-financing contingency.

h1: What Is Price Per Square Foot?
title: What Is Price Per Square Foot? | Your Realty Link
meta: Price per square foot divides a home's price by its finished square footage, a quick comparison tool that works best alongside a full market analysis.
hero_sub: A quick way to compare homes on paper, useful as a starting point but not the whole story.
definition: Price per square foot is a home's price divided by its finished square footage, used as a rough way to compare properties against each other.
qa_lead: Price per square foot is calculated by dividing the sale or list price by the home's finished square footage. It's a useful starting point for comparing similar homes, but it can be misleading across different home styles, lot sizes, or condition, which is why agents rely on a full comparative market analysis instead.
qa_facts: Price divided by finished square footage
Ignores lot, condition, upgrades, and location
sections: Where It's Useful

Price per square foot works reasonably well when you're comparing similar homes in the same neighborhood, built around the same era, with similar finishes. It gives you a quick, apples-to-apples starting number without digging into a full analysis.
It's also a common shorthand agents and appraisers use in casual conversation about a market, even though it's rarely the final word on value.
Where It Falls Short

A renovated ranch and a dated two-story can carry very similar price-per-square-foot numbers while being worth very different amounts to an actual buyer. Lot size, garage, basement finish, school district, and condition all affect value in ways this single number doesn't capture.
For that reason, Your Realty Link agents use price per square foot only as one input alongside a full comparative market analysis when estimating a home's true market value.
faqs: Does price per square foot include unfinished basement space?
Usually not. Most agents and appraisers count only finished, livable square footage.
Can I use price per square foot to price my own home?
It can be a helpful sanity check, but it shouldn't replace a full comparative market analysis from a local agent.
Why do price-per-square-foot numbers vary so much between neighborhoods?
Location, school district, lot size, and home age all shift what buyers are willing to pay, even for similar square footage.

title: What Is List-to-Sale Ratio? | Your Realty Link
meta: List-to-sale ratio compares a home's final sale price with its last list price as a percentage, showing how much negotiating room a local market allows buyers.
hero_sub: A simple percentage that hints at how much negotiating room a market typically allows.
definition: List-to-sale ratio compares a home's final sale price with its last list price, expressed as a percentage, to show how close sales are landing to asking price.
qa_lead: List-to-sale ratio is the final sale price divided by the last list price, shown as a percentage. A ratio near or above 100 percent suggests a competitive seller's market with little room to negotiate, while a lower ratio suggests buyers have more leverage.
qa_facts: Sale price divided by last list price
sections: How to Read the Number

A 98 percent list-to-sale ratio means homes are typically selling for about 2 percent under their final asking price, on average, across the homes measured. It's a market-level indicator, not a guarantee for any single home, since individual results vary with pricing strategy and condition.
Ratios also shift by price point and neighborhood within the same metro area, so a citywide number can look different from what's happening on a specific street.
Why It Matters for Pricing Strategy

A rising list-to-sale ratio over time often signals growing buyer demand relative to inventory, while a falling ratio can be an early sign that a market is cooling. Sellers and their agents use this trend, alongside days on market and absorption rate, to set realistic pricing expectations.
Your Realty Link tracks these trends across Central Indiana to help sellers price strategically rather than guess.
faqs: Is a list-to-sale ratio over 100 percent common?
It can happen in competitive markets when multiple offers push the final price above the original asking price.
Does list-to-sale ratio include price reductions during the listing?
It compares the final sale price to the most recent list price, so earlier price changes are already reflected in that final list price.
Where can I see current list-to-sale ratios for my area?
Ask a local agent, or check our market updates page for current Central Indiana trends.

title: What Is Absorption Rate? | Your Realty Link
meta: Absorption rate measures how fast homes are selling in an area, shown as months of inventory, helping Central Indiana buyers and sellers read market conditions.
hero_sub: The number that tells you whether a market currently favors buyers or sellers.
definition: Absorption rate measures how quickly homes are selling in a given area, usually expressed as the months of inventory available at the current pace of sales.
qa_lead: Absorption rate estimates how many months it would take to sell off all the current homes for sale at the recent pace of sales. Roughly under four to five months of inventory tends to favor sellers, while more than six tends to favor buyers, though the exact thresholds shift by area and price range.
qa_facts: Active listings divided by average monthly sales
Months of supply, months of inventory
sections: How Absorption Rate Is Calculated

To find absorption rate, divide the number of active listings in an area by the average number of homes selling per month. The result is expressed in months, representing how long the current inventory would last if no new listings came on the market.
This is one of the core numbers MIBOR and other local market reports track to describe overall market conditions across Central Indiana.
Why It Shapes Strategy for Buyers and Sellers

A low absorption rate signals a tight, competitive market where homes move quickly and sellers often have room to hold firm on price. A high absorption rate signals more buyer choice, longer days on market, and more room to negotiate.

Absorption rate can vary sharply by city, price tier, and property type even within the same county, so it's worth asking your agent for numbers specific to your target area rather than a broad metro average.
faqs: Is absorption rate the same everywhere in Central Indiana?
No. It varies by county, city, and even price range, so a metro-wide number can differ from what's happening in a specific area.
What absorption rate counts as a balanced market?
A roughly five to six month supply is commonly considered balanced, though local norms vary.
How often does absorption rate change?
It shifts month to month as new listings, pending sales, and closings are reported, so it's best viewed as a trend rather than a fixed number.

title: What Is a Seller's Market? | Your Realty Link
meta: A seller's market has more buyers than homes for sale, pushing prices up and shortening time on market, and typically giving Central Indiana sellers leverage.
hero_sub: When buyers outnumber available homes, and sellers tend to hold more of the leverage.
definition: A seller's market is a market condition where there are more buyers than available homes for sale, which tends to push prices up and shorten time on market.
qa_lead: In a seller's market, demand outpaces the number of homes for sale, so listings often move fast and sellers face less pressure to negotiate. You'll typically see a low absorption rate and less room for buyers to negotiate terms.
sections: What Drives a Seller's Market

A seller's market usually results from low housing inventory meeting steady or rising buyer demand, whether from population growth, low interest rates, or simply not enough new listings coming onto the market. Conditions can vary by price point even within the same city.
In these conditions, homes often receive multiple offers, and buyers sometimes use an escalation clause to stay competitive without overpaying upfront.
What It Means for Buyers and Sellers

Sellers in this environment often have room to hold firm on price and terms, and homes priced well can move quickly. Buyers need to be prepared to act fast, get fully pre-approved before house hunting, and understand which contingencies they're comfortable adjusting.
Your Realty Link helps sellers price strategically to capture this demand and helps buyers build competitive, protected offers even in a fast-moving market.
faqs: Does a seller's market mean I'll get my full asking price?
Not automatically, but it does generally improve your odds of a faster sale near or above asking, especially if the home is priced and marketed well.
Is all of Central Indiana in the same type of market?
No, conditions can differ significantly by county, city, and price range, so it's worth asking your agent about your specific area.
Should buyers still get an inspection in a seller's market?
Yes. Waiving an inspection is a real risk, and buyers should understand what they're giving up before doing so.

title: What Is a Buyer's Market? | Your Realty Link
meta: A buyer's market has more homes for sale than active buyers, giving Central Indiana buyers more choice, more time, and stronger negotiating power on terms.
hero_sub: When homes for sale outnumber active buyers, and shoppers tend to gain the upper hand.
definition: A buyer's market is a market condition where there are more homes for sale than active buyers, giving buyers more choice and negotiating power.
qa_lead: In a buyer's market, inventory outpaces demand, so homes tend to sit longer and sellers face more pressure to negotiate on price or terms. You'll typically see a higher absorption rate and more room for buyers to negotiate concessions.
sections: What Drives a Buyer's Market

A buyer's market can develop when new listings outpace demand, when interest rates rise and sideline some buyers, or when a local area sees a wave of new construction. Conditions vary by price point, and a buyer's market at one price tier can coexist with tighter conditions at another.
In these conditions, sellers who price realistically from the start tend to do better than those who chase the market down with repeated reductions.
What It Means for Buyers and Sellers

Buyers in this environment often have time to be selective, negotiate price, and ask for concessions like closing cost help or repairs after an inspection. Sellers need sharper pricing, stronger staging and marketing, and realistic expectations about time on market.
Your Realty Link helps sellers stand out through accurate pricing and strong pre-listing prep, and helps buyers use their added leverage wisely.
faqs: Is a buyer's market a good time to sell?
It's more challenging, but homes still sell in a buyer's market when priced accurately and presented well.
Do buyer's markets happen in every part of Central Indiana at once?
Not necessarily. Conditions can vary by county, city, and price range, so check current data for your specific area.
Can a market shift from a buyer's market to a seller's market quickly?
Yes, changes in inventory, interest rates, or demand can shift conditions over just a few months.

title: What Is a Builder Allowance? | Your Realty Link
meta: A builder allowance is the dollar budget a builder sets for flooring, lighting, or fixtures in a new build. Learn how allowances work for Indianapolis buyers.
hero_sub: A spending budget built into your new-home price, and one of the easiest places for costs to creep upward.
definition: A builder allowance is a dollar budget a builder sets aside for a category such as flooring, lighting, or countertops, which the buyer applies toward their selections at the design center.
qa_lead: A builder allowance is a set dollar amount included in your new-home price for a specific finish category, like flooring or light fixtures. Choose selections under the allowance and you stay on budget; go over and the difference gets added to your price, similar to upgrades and options elsewhere in the home.
qa_facts: One finish category, like flooring or lighting
The overage is added to your purchase price
Rarely refunded, so check your contract
sections: How Builder Allowances Work

When you sign a purchase agreement for a new build, certain finish categories, such as flooring, countertops, or light fixtures, come with a set dollar allowance rather than a specific product. You visit the builder's design center, pick your selections, and the cost is measured against that allowance.

If your choices cost more than the allowance, the difference is added to your purchase price as an upgrade. Builders typically require these selections early in construction, often at the very start of the build, so decisions can lock in fast.
Why Allowances Matter for Your Budget

It is easy to assume an allowance covers a full remodel-quality selection, but builder-grade allowances are often set at a baseline level. Walking through a model home can be misleading here, since model homes frequently display upgraded finishes well beyond what the base allowance provides.

Ask your builder for the allowance amount in writing for every category before you sign, and get a sense of what it actually buys, such as a per-square-foot flooring rate or a fixture budget per room.
faqs: Can I get cash back if I spend less than my allowance?
Usually not. Most builders treat allowances as use-it-or-lose-it, so staying under simply avoids extra cost rather than returning money to you.
Are builder allowances negotiable?
Sometimes, especially during slower sales periods or in larger communities. It does not hurt to ask, particularly when you are also negotiating other costs added to the base price.
What if I do not like any of the standard allowance options?
You can typically upgrade beyond the allowance for an additional cost. Ask to see the full options catalog before you tour any models so you know what is realistic for your budget.
Does the allowance apply to structural changes too?
No. Allowances generally cover finish selections, not structural options like moving a wall or adding a room, which are priced separately.

title: What Is a Spec Home? | Your Realty Link
meta: A spec home is a new house a builder constructs speculatively, with finishes usually already chosen so it can close faster. See how it works in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: A new build already underway, with finishes largely decided and often ready to close sooner than a custom home.
definition: A spec home is a home a builder constructs on speculation, without a specific buyer under contract, usually with most or all finish selections already made.
qa_lead: A spec home is built by a developer or builder ahead of finding a buyer, with the floor plan and most finishes already chosen. Because fewer decisions remain, a spec home can often close faster than a fully custom-built home, which makes it a popular option for buyers on a tighter timeline.
qa_facts: Usually already made by the builder
Often a faster close than a custom build
Builder show homes or move-in-ready listings
sections: How a Spec Home Differs From a Custom Build

With a custom build, the buyer works with the builder from the start on the floor plan, lot, and finishes. A spec home skips much of that process. The builder makes the design and finish decisions in advance, often based on what tends to sell well in that community, then lists the home for sale during or after construction.
This can be a good fit if you want a new home without months of selection meetings, though it also means less control over the final look.
What to Check Before You Buy a Spec Home

Ask where the home is in the construction timeline and whether a certificate of occupancy has been issued yet, since that affects your realistic move-in date. Also ask what is still adjustable, some builders allow late-stage buyers to swap minor finishes if construction has not reached that stage yet.
Review the builder warranty just as you would on any new-construction purchase, and have the home inspected even though it has never been lived in.
faqs: Is a spec home the same as a model home?
No. A model home is used to showcase a floor plan to shoppers and is not usually for sale. A spec home is built to be sold, sometimes to a buyer who never saw it under construction.
Can I still make changes to a spec home?
