It depends on the construction stage. Early in the process, some builders allow limited finish changes. Once drywall or flooring is in, most selections are locked.
Are spec homes move-in ready?
Many are complete or nearly complete by the time they are listed, which is one of their main appeals for buyers who need to move quickly.
Do spec homes cost more or less than custom homes?
It varies by builder and community. Since the builder absorbs some of the selection process, pricing is generally comparable to a similarly finished custom home in the same neighborhood.

title: What Is a Model Home? | Your Realty Link
meta: A model home is a finished, upgraded home a builder uses to showcase a floor plan and community. Learn what to watch for on model home tours in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: A builder's best foot forward, and a home worth touring with a clear eye on what is actually included.
definition: A model home is a finished, often upgraded home that a builder maintains to showcase a floor plan and community to prospective buyers.
qa_lead: A model home lets you walk through a builder's floor plan in person before committing, but it is usually decked out with options and finishes beyond the base price. Compare what you see against the builder's included features list, and use a builder allowance sheet to separate what is standard from what costs extra.
qa_facts: Showcase a floor plan and community
No, usually reserved during active sales
Often upgraded beyond the base price
Layout and flow, not final pricing
sections: What a Model Home Is For

Builders furnish and decorate a model home to help buyers picture themselves in the floor plan, and to demonstrate available layouts, room sizes, and popular options in a given community. It is a sales tool as much as a preview.
Because the model is designed to impress, it typically includes premium flooring, lighting, cabinetry, and staging furniture that go well beyond the community's standard, included finishes.
How to Tour a Model Home Wisely

Ask your sales representative for a features sheet that spells out exactly what is standard versus what is an upgrade in the model you are touring. This is the single best way to avoid sticker shock later at the design center when pricing out upgrades and options.
Pay attention to room sizes and traffic flow rather than paint colors or furniture, since staging can make spaces feel larger or cozier than they will once you move in.
faqs: Can I buy the actual model home?
Sometimes, once the builder is ready to release it, often near the end of a community's build-out. These sales usually include furniture or upgrade allowances as part of the deal.
Why does the model home look nicer than what I am quoted?
Model homes are typically loaded with upgrades to show the floor plan at its best. Ask for an itemized list of what is standard versus optional before comparing prices.
Should I bring my own agent to a model home visit?
Yes. The builder's on-site representative works for the builder, so having your own agent represent your interests is a smart step before you sign anything.

title: What Is a Punch List? | Your Realty Link
meta: A punch list is the written record of small fixes a builder still owes you on a new home before or after closing. See how punch lists work in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: The builder's to-do list for finishing what closing day left undone.
definition: A punch list is a record of small, unfinished, or incorrect items a buyer and builder identify on a new home, which the builder agrees to complete.
qa_lead: A punch list is created during your final walk-through of a new build and lists the small items the builder still needs to fix, like touch-up paint, a sticking door, or a missing fixture. Most builders complete punch list items within a set window after closing day.
qa_facts: The final walk-through, before or at closing
Get it in writing and keep a signed copy
sections: How a Punch List Comes Together

Before closing, you and your agent walk the finished home with the builder's representative, noting anything incomplete, damaged, or not built as specified. This becomes the punch list, a written record both sides sign off on.

Common items include paint touch-ups, caulking gaps, sticking doors or windows, missing outlet covers, and minor drywall marks. It is not meant to catch major defects; that is what a home inspection is for.
Getting Punch List Items Completed
Builders typically schedule a follow-up visit or two to knock out the list after you have moved in. Keep a copy of the signed punch list and note the date each item is resolved.
If items linger, put your follow-up requests in writing and reference your builder warranty, since most workmanship items are also covered under its terms.
faqs: Should I get a home inspection even with a punch list?
Yes. A punch list catches cosmetic and minor items you notice on a walk-through; an independent inspection can catch issues in systems and construction that are not visible at a glance.
Can I withhold funds until punch list items are done?
Some purchase agreements allow a small holdback for unfinished items, but this varies by builder and contract. Ask your agent to review your agreement before closing.
How long does a builder have to complete punch list work?
There is no universal timeline; it depends on the builder and market conditions. Get an estimated completion window in writing during your walk-through.
What if I find something after I move in that was not on the list?
Report it promptly. Many items are also covered by your builder warranty even if they were missed during the walk-through.

h1: What Is a Certificate of Occupancy?
title: What Is a Certificate of Occupancy? | Your Realty Link
meta: A certificate of occupancy is the local government sign-off confirming a new home is safe to live in. Learn how it affects closing in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: The official green light that says a new build is safe to move into.
definition: A certificate of occupancy is a document issued by the local building or code enforcement department confirming that a new or renovated home meets code and is safe to occupy.
qa_lead: A certificate of occupancy, often shortened to CO, is issued by the local government after final inspections confirm a new home meets building and safety codes. Closing on new construction, and your possession date, usually cannot happen until it is issued.
qa_facts: The local building or code enforcement department
The home meets code and is safe to occupy
Closing and move-in on most new builds
Delays here can push back your closing date
sections: Why a Certificate of Occupancy Matters

Before a jurisdiction issues a certificate of occupancy, inspectors confirm the electrical, plumbing, mechanical, and structural work all meet local code. This protects buyers from moving into a home that has not been fully signed off as safe.

Because closing and possession are usually tied to this document, construction delays, inspection scheduling, or paperwork backlogs at the local building department can push back your move-in date even after the home looks finished.
What Buyers Should Ask About Timing

Ask your builder where the home stands in the inspection process and get a realistic estimate for when the certificate of occupancy will be issued relative to your target closing date. Building department turnaround times vary by county and by how busy the office is.
Your purchase agreement should spell out what happens if the certificate is delayed, including any adjustments to your rate lock or moving timeline.
faqs: Can I move in before a certificate of occupancy is issued?
No, this is not advisable and is often not legally permitted. Occupying a home without a valid certificate of occupancy can create insurance and liability problems.
Is a certificate of occupancy the same as a final inspection?
They are related but not identical. The final inspection is one of the steps required before the local department will issue the certificate of occupancy.
Who requests the certificate of occupancy?
The builder typically requests it from the local building department once construction and required inspections are complete.
Does an existing home need a certificate of occupancy to sell?
Generally no, unless there has been a major renovation, addition, or change of use that triggered new permits. Rules vary by city and county.

title: What Is a Builder Warranty? | Your Realty Link
meta: A builder warranty covers workmanship and certain systems on a new home for a set period after closing. See how new-home warranties work in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: The builder's promise to stand behind their work after you get the keys.
definition: A builder warranty is coverage a new-home builder provides for workmanship and certain building systems for a defined period after closing, separate from any home warranty service contract.
qa_lead: A builder warranty covers defects in workmanship and materials on a new home, typically with shorter coverage on general items and longer coverage on major structural components. It is different from a home warranty service contract, which is a separately purchased plan covering appliances and systems.
qa_facts: Shorter general coverage, longer structural coverage
The builder, as part of your purchase
A purchased home warranty service contract
sections: How Builder Warranty Coverage Is Typically Structured

Most builder warranties are tiered, with a shorter period, often around a year, covering general workmanship and minor systems, and a much longer period covering major structural components. This tiered approach is common across the industry and is sometimes referred to informally as a 1-2-10 style warranty, though exact terms vary by builder.

Items caught during your punch list walk-through are usually addressed quickly under this warranty, while issues that surface later, like a settling foundation, fall under the longer structural coverage.
Builder Warranty vs. Home Warranty

A builder warranty comes from the company that built your home and is included in the purchase. A home warranty is a separate, optional service contract, often purchased annually, that covers repair or replacement of appliances and systems regardless of who built the home.

New-construction buyers sometimes carry both: the builder warranty for construction defects, and a home warranty for ongoing appliance and system coverage once the builder's coverage narrows over time.
faqs: What does a builder warranty typically exclude?
Normal wear and tear, damage from buyer neglect, and cosmetic issues not noted at your walk-through are commonly excluded. Read your specific warranty document for exact terms.
Is the builder warranty transferable if I sell my home?
Many are transferable to a subsequent buyer for the remainder of the term, which can be a selling point, but this depends on the individual builder's warranty terms.
Do I need a home inspection if I have a builder warranty?
Yes. An inspection can catch issues early, before they grow, and having documentation helps if you need to file a warranty claim later.
What should I do if the builder is slow to respond to a warranty claim?
Put your request in writing with dates and details, and keep copies of all correspondence. If a builder is unresponsive, your agent can often help you determine next steps.

title: What Is a Lot Premium? | Your Realty Link
meta: A lot premium is an added cost a builder charges for a more desirable homesite. Learn what drives lot premiums in Central Indiana new-home communities.
hero_sub: The extra you pay for a better piece of ground beneath your new home.
definition: A lot premium is an additional charge a builder adds to the base home price for a more desirable homesite, such as a larger, wooded, cul-de-sac, or water-view lot.
qa_lead: A lot premium is added on top of a new home's base price when the specific homesite offers something in demand, like extra size, privacy, or a water view, similar to how upgrades and options add cost inside the home itself. Premiums vary widely by community and by how desirable that particular lot is within the plat.
qa_facts: The base price of the home
Size, shape, view, privacy, cul-de-sac location
The builder, per lot or lot type
Sometimes, depending on demand for that lot
sections: What Drives a Lot Premium

Builders price lots within a community differently based on features buyers tend to value: a larger lot, a wooded or walkout-basement grade, a cul-de-sac position, or a water or greenspace view. The more in-demand the lot, the higher the premium tends to be.
Premiums are set at the community level and can change as a neighborhood sells out, since the most desirable lots are often reserved or sold first.
Weighing a Lot Premium Against the Cost

Before paying a premium, ask what specifically it buys you, extra square footage, a certain view, or simply position within the community, and compare it to what similar premiums cost at other new home communities nearby.
A premium lot can also affect resale value down the road, so it is worth thinking about the long-term appeal of that specific homesite, not just how it looks on move-in day.
faqs: Is a lot premium included in the advertised base price?
No, base prices typically reflect the builder's standard lot. A lot premium is added separately once a specific homesite is selected.
Can lot premiums be negotiated?
Sometimes, particularly if the community has been on the market a while or the builder is motivated to sell a specific lot. It does not hurt to ask, especially alongside other pricing questions.
Do all lots in a community have a premium?
No. Many builders designate a standard lot type with no added premium, then charge extra only for specific homesites with in-demand features.
Does a lot premium affect my loan amount?
Yes, since it is part of the total purchase price, it is factored into your financing and appraisal, the same as any other cost included in the contract.

title: What Are Upgrades and Options? | Your Realty Link
meta: Upgrades and options are choices beyond a new home's standard finishes, from better cabinets to added rooms. See how they affect price in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: Everything beyond the standard build sheet, and where a new-home budget most often grows.
definition: Upgrades and options are choices beyond a new home's standard, included finishes, such as premium cabinets, added rooms, or higher-grade flooring, that increase the purchase price.
qa_lead: Upgrades and options let you customize a new build beyond its standard finishes, whether that means better countertops, a finished basement, or an extra bedroom. Most selections happen at the builder's design center, and costs can add up quickly if you are not tracking them against your builder allowance.
qa_facts: Structural options often must be chosen earliest
Added to the base price of the home
sections: Finish Upgrades vs. Structural Options

Finish-level upgrades change the look and feel of a home, think upgraded flooring, cabinetry, or lighting fixtures, and are generally selected against a category's builder allowance. Structural options change the footprint or framing of the home itself, like adding a bay window, a bedroom, or a finished basement.

Structural options usually need to be locked in earliest in the build process, sometimes before the foundation is poured, while some finish selections can be adjusted later depending on the construction stage.
Budgeting for Upgrades and Options

It is easy for a base price to grow substantially once popular upgrades are added, so ask for an itemized options list before you tour a model home, since models are often built to showcase upgraded finishes rather than the standard package.

Prioritize the options that matter most to how you will live in the home or that hold value at resale, structural changes and kitchen upgrades tend to matter more long-term than cosmetic swaps that are easy to change later.
faqs: Which upgrades tend to be worth it at resale?

Kitchen and primary bathroom upgrades, finished basements, and structural additions like extra bedrooms tend to hold value well. Highly personal cosmetic choices are less likely to matter to a future buyer.
Can I add my own contractor for upgrades instead of the builder's design center?

Most builders require upgrades to go through their own process during construction, both for warranty and scheduling reasons. Some buyers add cosmetic work after closing through their own contractor instead.
Do upgrades affect my mortgage approval?
Yes. Upgrades raise the purchase price, which affects your loan amount, so it is worth discussing planned upgrades with your lender early in the process.
Are options the same in every community from the same builder?
Not necessarily. Available options and their costs can vary by community, floor plan, and even by which phase of the neighborhood is being built.

title: What Is a Purchase Agreement? | Your Realty Link
meta: A purchase agreement is the signed contract that sets a home's price, terms, and closing date. See how they work for Central Indiana buyers and sellers.
hero_sub: The document that turns an accepted offer into a binding deal, and spells out exactly what happens next.
definition: A purchase agreement is the written, signed contract between a buyer and seller that sets the price, terms, contingencies, and closing date for a home sale.
qa_lead: Once a seller accepts your offer, that offer becomes the purchase agreement, the master contract everyone follows through closing. In Central Indiana it's usually a MIBOR-standard form your agent prepares, covering price, contingencies, and deadlines. Every later document, from the earnest money receipt to the closing paperwork, traces back to what this contract says.
qa_facts: Your agent, on a MIBOR-standard form
Yes, through a written amendment or counteroffer
sections: What a Purchase Agreement Covers

A purchase agreement lays out far more than price. It sets the earnest money amount, the financing and inspection timelines, what personal property stays with the home, the target closing date, and every contingency either side is relying on.

Because it's a legally binding contract once signed, any change after that point, a repair credit, a moved closing date, an added contingency, has to go through a written amendment or counteroffer, not a verbal agreement.
How It Comes Together

The process typically starts with a buyer's written offer. If the seller doesn't accept it outright, they can counter one or more terms, and the two sides negotiate until everyone signs the same version. That signed document is the purchase agreement.
From there, the clock starts on contingency deadlines like the inspection period and loan approval, all tracked against the closing date named in the contract.
faqs: Is a purchase agreement the same as an offer?
An offer becomes the purchase agreement once the seller accepts it and both parties sign; before that, it's just a proposal.
Can a purchase agreement be canceled?
Yes, but usually only through a contingency that lets a buyer exit, or by mutual written agreement between both parties.
Do I need a lawyer to review it?
Indiana doesn't require one, and your agent handles the standard MIBOR contract, but you're always free to have an attorney review it.
What happens if someone breaks the agreement?
Remedies vary by what the contract allows, from keeping or returning earnest money to, in some cases, legal action; your agent can walk you through your options.

title: What Is a Counteroffer? | Your Realty Link
meta: A counteroffer changes the price or terms of an offer, sending it back to the other side to accept, reject, or counter. Here's how negotiation works in Indiana.
hero_sub: Negotiation rarely ends with the first offer; the counteroffer is how buyers and sellers meet in the middle.
definition: A counteroffer is a response that changes one or more terms of a real estate offer, such as price, closing date, or contingencies, and sends the deal back to the other party to accept, reject, or counter again.
qa_lead: When a seller doesn't love your opening offer but wants to keep negotiating, they'll send back a counteroffer, maybe a higher price, an earlier closing, or fewer contingencies. You can accept it, reject it, or counter it yourself, and deals often go through two or three rounds before landing on a purchase agreement both sides sign.
qa_facts: Any term: price, dates, contingencies, concessions
Often two to three before agreement
Only once both sides sign the same version
sections: How Counteroffers Work
A counteroffer voids the original offer and puts a new proposal on the table. The other side then has the same three choices you did: accept, reject, or counter back.
Nothing is locked in until both parties have signed off on identical terms; verbal agreements or texted changes don't replace the written document.
What Typically Gets Countered
Price is the obvious one, but counters also cover closing dates, what's included in the sale, repair credits, and seller concessions toward closing costs.
In a competitive market, a seller might counter several buyers at once to see who improves their offer, sometimes alongside an escalation clause from one of the buyers.
faqs: Can I counter a counteroffer?
Yes, there's no limit on how many rounds you can go, though most negotiations settle within a few.
Does a counteroffer cancel the original offer?
Yes; once a counter is sent, the original offer is off the table and only the newest terms are live.
Can a seller counter multiple buyers at the same time?
Yes, Indiana sellers can send counters to more than one interested buyer simultaneously until one is signed.
Is there a deadline to respond to a counteroffer?
Counteroffers usually include an expiration time or date; if you don't respond by then, it typically expires.

title: What Is an Escalation Clause? | Your Realty Link
meta: An escalation clause automatically raises your offer above competing bids up to a set limit. Learn how Central Indiana buyers use them to win bidding wars.
hero_sub: A way to stay competitive in a bidding war without guessing how high is too high.
definition: An escalation clause is a provision added to an offer that automatically increases your bid by a set increment above any competing offer, up to a maximum price you choose.
qa_lead: Instead of guessing what a competing buyer might offer, an escalation clause lets your bid rise automatically, by a set increment above the next-highest offer, up to a ceiling you set in advance. It only kicks in if the seller actually has a competing offer to beat, and most versions require the listing agent to show proof.
qa_facts: Auto-raises your offer above competing bids
An increment amount and a maximum price
Only in a genuine multiple-offer situation
A seller's market with several active buyers
sections: How an Escalation Clause Works

You set a starting offer, an increment (how much to increase by), and a ceiling (the most you're willing to pay). If the seller receives a higher competing offer, your price rises by the increment above it, automatically, without a new round of negotiating.
Because it reveals your ceiling to the seller, an escalation clause is a trade-off: it can win a bidding war, but it also shows your hand more than a flat offer would.
When It Makes Sense
Escalation clauses work best when you know you're in real competition and want to avoid losing the home over a small gap, while still protecting yourself from paying far more than you planned.

They're less useful in a slower market with only one offer on the table, since there's nothing to escalate above. Your agent can help you weigh whether one fits your situation, and how it interacts with an appraisal contingency if the winning price ends up above value.
faqs: Does the seller have to prove a competing offer exists?
Most escalation clauses require the listing agent to provide documentation of the competing offer before it triggers.
What if my escalated price is higher than the home appraises for?
You'd still need a plan for the gap, often through an appraisal contingency or by bringing extra cash to closing.
Is an escalation clause the same as bidding blind?
No, you set the maximum yourself in advance, so your price never rises past a number you've already approved.
Do sellers always accept the highest escalated offer?
Not necessarily; sellers can also weigh contingencies, closing timeline, and financing strength, not just price.

title: What Is a Contingency Period? | Your Realty Link
meta: A contingency period is the window to complete a condition, like an inspection or loan approval, before it becomes binding in your Central Indiana contract.
hero_sub: The clock every contingency runs on, and the deadline that decides whether you can still walk away.
definition: A contingency period is the specific window of time set in a purchase agreement during which a buyer must complete a condition, such as an inspection or loan approval, before that condition becomes locked in.
qa_lead: Every contingency in your contract runs on its own clock, and the contingency period is that clock. Miss the deadline for the inspection contingency, for example, and you may lose the right to negotiate repairs or walk away for that reason, even if you never finished the inspection.
qa_facts: The deadline attached to a contract contingency
Set per contingency; negotiated case by case
The related right to cancel or negotiate can end
Yes, with written agreement from both sides
sections: Why the Deadline Matters
A contingency only protects you while its period is open. Once it passes without action, in most contracts that contingency is treated as satisfied or waived, and you lose the leverage it gave you.
This is why your agent tracks these dates closely from the moment the purchase agreement is signed; a missed inspection deadline can mean forfeiting your right to ask for repairs at all.
Extending a Contingency Period
If you need more time, for example your lender needs an extra week for underwriting, both parties can agree in writing to extend the period. Neither side can unilaterally extend it on their own.
Sellers aren't obligated to grant an extension, so requesting one early, before the original deadline passes, gives you the best chance of a yes.
faqs: What happens if I miss my inspection contingency deadline?
In most cases you lose the right to cancel or negotiate based on inspection findings for that contingency once the period closes.
Can a contingency period be shortened to make an offer more attractive?
Yes, buyers sometimes shorten contingency periods to compete in a multiple-offer situation, though it means less time to act.
Who tracks these deadlines?
Your agent and the transaction coordinator typically track every contingency deadline, but it's worth keeping your own calendar too.
Does every contingency have the same period?
No, each contingency, like financing or inspection, is usually given its own separate deadline in the contract.

title: What Is a Financing Contingency? | Your Realty Link
meta: A financing contingency lets a buyer cancel and recover earnest money if their mortgage falls through. See how this protection works for Indiana home buyers.
hero_sub: The safety net that protects your earnest money if your mortgage doesn't come through.
definition: A financing contingency is a clause in a purchase agreement that lets a buyer cancel the contract and recover their earnest money if they're unable to secure mortgage approval by a set date.
qa_lead: Most buyers aren't paying cash, so the financing contingency protects you if your loan falls through for reasons outside your control, like a rate change or an underwriting issue. As long as you cancel within the contingency period and acted in good faith on your loan application, your earnest money is typically returned.
qa_facts: Your earnest money, if financing fails
Buyers using a mortgage, not all-cash buyers
Applying and working with a lender in good faith
sections: Why Buyers Use One

A mortgage isn't guaranteed until underwriting fully approves it, and things can change between your pre-approval and closing, from a job change to a lower appraisal. A financing contingency means those surprises don't automatically cost you your deposit.
Without it, a buyer whose loan falls apart could be in breach of contract and risk losing earnest money, or worse.
What Can Trigger It
Common triggers include a denied loan application, an interest rate that pushes you outside your approved terms, or a lender's underwriting conditions you can't meet in time.
Sellers sometimes see financing contingencies as adding uncertainty, which is one reason all-cash and strongly pre-approved offers can be more attractive in competitive markets.
faqs: Does a financing contingency guarantee I'll get my earnest money back?
If you cancel within the deadline and pursued financing in good faith, yes, though the exact terms are set by your specific contract.
Do cash buyers need a financing contingency?
No, cash buyers typically skip it since there's no loan to fall through, though they may use a proof-of-funds requirement instead.
What if my rate lock expires before closing?
Talk to your lender and agent right away, since this can affect your financing timeline and whether the contingency still applies.
Can I waive a financing contingency to compete for a home?
You can, but it's a real risk since you could lose your earnest money if the loan doesn't close; most agents advise caution before waiving it.

title: What Is an Inspection Contingency? | Your Realty Link
meta: An inspection contingency gives buyers time to inspect a home and negotiate repairs, credits, or walk away. Here's how it protects Central Indiana buyers.
hero_sub: Your chance to look under the hood before you're fully committed to the home.
definition: An inspection contingency is a clause giving the buyer a set period to have the home professionally inspected, then negotiate repairs, request credits, or cancel the contract based on what's found.
qa_lead: Once your offer is accepted, the inspection contingency gives you a window, often about a week to ten days, to hire an inspector and review the home's condition. If issues turn up, you can ask the seller for repairs or a credit, or in most cases walk away and get your earnest money back, all before the contingency period closes.
qa_facts: Roughly one to two weeks, negotiated per contract
Negotiate repairs or credits, or cancel
The contingency right may no longer apply
sections: What the Inspection Covers

A general home inspection looks at the roof, foundation, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and other major systems, and flags visible defects or safety issues. Buyers in Indiana sometimes add specialty inspections too, like radon testing or a well and septic inspection for rural properties.
The inspector's report becomes the basis for any repair request, so it's worth attending the inspection if your schedule allows.
Negotiating After the Inspection
Finding issues doesn't mean the deal is dead. Buyers often request the seller fix specific items, offer a closing credit, or reduce the price, and sellers can agree, counter, or decline.
If negotiations stall, the inspection contingency generally lets the buyer cancel and recover earnest money, though the exact terms depend on the language in your purchase agreement.
faqs: Can I cancel for any reason during the inspection period?
Typically only for issues found during the inspection, not for unrelated reasons; check your contract's exact wording.
Do I have to share the inspection report with the seller?
No, but you'll usually need to reference specific findings if you're requesting repairs or credits.
What if the seller won't fix anything?
You can accept the home as-is, negotiate further, or use the contingency to cancel, depending on your contract's terms.
Should I still get an inspection on new construction?
Yes, most buyers get an independent inspection even on new homes, separate from any municipal or builder inspection.

title: What Is an Appraisal Contingency? | Your Realty Link
meta: An appraisal contingency lets a buyer renegotiate or exit if a home appraises below the offer price. Learn how it works in Central Indiana's real estate market.
hero_sub: Your backup plan if the lender's appraiser values the home for less than you agreed to pay.
definition: An appraisal contingency is a clause allowing a buyer to renegotiate the price, request the seller cover the gap, or cancel the contract if the home's appraisal comes in below the agreed purchase price.
qa_lead: Your lender only lends against what the home is actually worth, so if the appraisal comes back lower than your offer, you're facing an appraisal gap. An appraisal contingency gives you options at that point: ask the seller to lower the price, cover part of the gap in cash yourself, or cancel and get your earnest money back.
qa_facts: Buying above appraised value with no options
Renegotiate, pay the gap, or cancel
sections: Why This Matters in a Rising Market

When offers are climbing quickly, the contract price can outpace recent comparable sales, which is exactly what an appraiser relies on. An appraisal contingency keeps a buyer from being locked into a price the lender won't fully finance.
Some buyers waive this contingency to compete for a home, but doing so means committing to cover any gap between the appraised value and the price out of pocket, or risk losing their earnest money.
What Happens With a Low Appraisal

First, your agent will often request a reconsideration of value if there's evidence the appraiser missed relevant comps. If that doesn't move the number, the appraisal contingency lets you go back to the seller to renegotiate.
Sellers aren't required to lower their price, so the outcome often comes down to negotiation, how much cash the buyer can bring, or ultimately whether either side is willing to walk.
faqs: What is an appraisal gap?
It's the difference between your agreed purchase price and the lower value the appraisal comes back at.
Can I ask for a second appraisal?
You can't typically order a brand-new appraisal for the same loan, but your agent can request a reconsideration of value with additional comps.
Should I waive my appraisal contingency?
Only if you're prepared to cover a potential value gap in cash; your agent can help you weigh the risk against the competition.
Does the seller ever cover the appraisal gap?
Occasionally, especially if they're motivated to keep the deal together, but it's negotiated case by case and never guaranteed.

h1: What Is a Home Sale Contingency?
title: What Is a Home Sale Contingency? | Your Realty Link
meta: A home sale contingency makes a home purchase depend on the buyer first selling their current home. See how Central Indiana sellers weigh this clause.
hero_sub: For buyers who need to sell before they can buy, and the clause that ties the two deals together.
definition: A home sale contingency is a clause making a buyer's purchase of a new home dependent on successfully selling their current home by a specified date.
qa_lead: If you need the proceeds or equity from your current house to buy the next one, a home sale contingency ties the two transactions together, protecting you from being on the hook for two mortgages, or none at all if your sale falls through. Sellers weigh these carefully since they add uncertainty and often a longer timeline to the deal.
qa_facts: Buyers who need their current home's sale to close first
A kick-out clause letting sellers keep marketing
Selling first, then buying, to avoid it
sections: Why Sellers Are Cautious

A home sale contingency introduces a chain: if the buyer's own home doesn't sell in time, the deal you're counting on can collapse too. Many sellers, especially in a competitive market, prefer offers without one.

To manage that risk, sellers often negotiate a kick-out clause, which lets them keep marketing the home and accept a better offer if one comes along, giving the contingent buyer a set window to remove their contingency or step aside.
When It Makes Sense Anyway

For buyers who can't qualify for two mortgages at once or don't want to carry both, a home sale contingency can be the only realistic path forward, especially when paired with a strong, already-listed home.
Your agent can help you weigh this against alternatives, like a HELOC or bridge financing, or simply listing and selling first before writing an offer.
faqs: What is a kick-out clause?
It lets the seller keep the home on the market and accept a better offer, giving the contingent buyer a limited time to remove their contingency or lose the deal.
Are home sale contingencies common in a hot market?
They're harder to get accepted when sellers have multiple offers, since many prefer certainty over a linked sale.
Is there an alternative to a home sale contingency?
Some buyers sell first and rent back temporarily, or use short-term financing, to make a stronger, non-contingent offer.
Does my current home need to be under contract already?
Requirements vary by offer; some sellers accept a contingency once your home is listed, others require it already under contract.

title: What Is Proof of Funds? | Your Realty Link
meta: Proof of funds is documentation showing you have the cash for a down payment, closing costs, or an all-cash purchase. See when Indiana sellers ask for it.
hero_sub: The paperwork that shows a seller your offer isn't just words.
definition: Proof of funds is a bank statement, brokerage statement, or lender letter showing you have the money available for a down payment and closing costs, or the full purchase price on an all-cash deal.
qa_lead: Sellers, especially in competitive situations, often want more than your word that you can close. Proof of funds is the document that backs it up: recent account statements or a lender letter showing the money is really there. On a cash offer, it usually replaces the loan approval a financed buyer would provide.
qa_facts: Recent bank or brokerage statement, or lender letter
Sellers and listing agents, often before accepting an offer
Cash offers and competitive multiple-offer situations
Usually within the last 30 to 60 days
sections: When You'll Need It

Proof of funds is standard for any all-cash offer, since there's no lender approval to lean on. It's also increasingly requested alongside financed offers, both to show your down payment is real and to strengthen your offer in a competitive market.
Investors making investment offers are asked for it especially often, since sellers want confidence the deal will actually close.
What It Typically Shows

Most documentation is a recent statement from a bank, brokerage, or retirement account showing a balance that covers the purchase, sometimes combined with a letter from your bank or lender confirming the funds.
Sensitive details like full account numbers are usually redacted; the goal is simply to confirm the money exists and is accessible, not to share your full financial history.
faqs: Is proof of funds the same as a pre-approval letter?
No, a pre-approval letter is from a lender about a loan; proof of funds shows actual cash available, whether or not a loan is involved.
How recent does my documentation need to be?
Sellers typically want something dated within the last 30 to 60 days, though exact expectations can vary by offer.
Do I need proof of funds for a financed purchase?
Often yes, at least for your down payment and closing costs, alongside your loan pre-approval.
Can I redact information before sharing it?
Yes, it's standard to black out account numbers and unrelated balances, showing only what's needed to confirm the funds.

h1: What Is an Earnest Money Receipt?
title: What Is an Earnest Money Receipt? | Your Realty Link
meta: An earnest money receipt confirms your good-faith deposit was received and who is holding it. Learn how this works for Central Indiana home purchases.
hero_sub: The paper trail that proves your deposit landed where it's supposed to be.
definition: An earnest money receipt is written confirmation that a buyer's good-faith deposit has been received and is being held, typically by the title company or listing brokerage, stating the amount and who holds it.
qa_lead: After you submit earnest money along with your offer, you should get a receipt back confirming it was actually received, how much, and who's holding it, usually the title company or listing broker's trust account. Keep this document; it matters if there's ever a question about your deposit at closing or in an earnest money dispute.
qa_facts: Amount received and who is holding it
Title company or listing brokerage trust account
Documents your deposit if a dispute or question arises
sections: Why This Document Matters

Earnest money can be a meaningful sum, so having written proof it was deposited and where it sits protects you. Without a receipt, there's no clear record confirming the funds were actually received as agreed.
At closing, the amount on your earnest money receipt is credited back to you against your cash to close, so it directly affects the final number you bring.
Who Holds the Money

In Central Indiana, earnest money is most often held by the title company handling the closing, though some contracts route it through the listing brokerage instead. Either way, the funds sit in a neutral trust account, not with the buyer or seller directly.
The receipt should identify exactly who is holding the deposit, which matters if a later disagreement over release of the funds comes up.
faqs: When should I receive my earnest money receipt?
Typically within a few business days of your deposit being submitted, once the holder confirms it was received.
What if I never get a receipt?
Ask your agent to follow up with the holder promptly, since this document is your proof the deposit was actually received.
Is earnest money the same as a down payment?
No, earnest money is a good-faith deposit credited toward your purchase at closing; the down payment is a separate, usually larger, amount.
Can I get my earnest money back if the deal falls through?
It depends on why the deal ended; a valid contingency generally protects your deposit, but breaching the contract can put it at risk.

title: What Are Seller Concessions? | Your Realty Link
meta: Seller concessions are funds a seller agrees to put toward a buyer's closing costs, negotiated into the contract. See how they work in Central Indiana.
hero_sub: Money the seller agrees to put toward your closing costs, instead of, or alongside, a lower price.
definition: Seller concessions are funds a seller agrees to contribute toward a buyer's closing costs or prepaid expenses, negotiated as part of the purchase agreement.
qa_lead: Rather than lowering the price, a seller can agree to cover some of your closing costs directly, which is often called a concession. It's negotiated into the purchase agreement and can help a buyer bring less cash to closing, though lenders cap how much a seller can contribute based on your loan type and down payment.
qa_facts: Closing costs and prepaid items, not the price itself
Buyers, by reducing cash needed at closing
Capped by loan type and down payment percentage
The purchase agreement or a later counteroffer
sections: How Seller Concessions Work
A buyer can ask for concessions in their initial offer or negotiate them in later rounds, often as a trade-off for accepting the seller's asking price rather than negotiating it down directly.
Concessions typically go toward closing costs, prepaid taxes and insurance, or a home warranty, not toward the buyer's down payment itself.
Why Sellers Agree to Them
Sellers sometimes prefer to hold their headline price steady while offering concessions instead, especially if a lower sale price could affect neighborhood comps for future sales.
Loan programs, especially FHA and VA loans, set specific limits on how much a seller can contribute, so your lender needs to confirm the concession amount fits within those guidelines.
faqs: Do seller concessions lower my loan amount?
No, they cover costs at closing rather than reducing the purchase price your loan is based on.
Is there a limit to how much a seller can contribute?
Yes, lenders cap concessions as a percentage of the purchase price, and the cap varies by loan type and down payment.
Can concessions be used for a down payment?
Generally no, seller concessions are meant for closing costs and prepaids, not the buyer's own down payment.
Are seller concessions common in Central Indiana?
They come and go with market conditions; buyers are more likely to see them offered when homes are taking longer to sell.

title: What Is an Option Period? | Your Realty Link
meta: An option period is a negotiated window letting a buyer cancel a contract for any reason. See how Indiana buyers use inspection contingencies instead.
hero_sub: A flexible cancellation window some contracts allow, and how Indiana buyers usually get the same protection a different way.
definition: An option period is a short, negotiated window during which a buyer can cancel a purchase contract for any reason, sometimes in exchange for a small non-refundable fee paid to the seller.
qa_lead: You may hear the term option period from buyers or agents who've worked in states like Texas, where it's a standard part of the contract. Indiana doesn't use this exact structure; instead, buyers here get similar flexibility through an inspection contingency, which lets you walk away or negotiate based on what an inspection turns up.
qa_facts: States like Texas, as a standard contract term
Short window, small fee, cancel for any reason
Helps buyers moving from other states understand local contracts
sections: How an Option Period Works Elsewhere

In states that use this structure, a buyer pays a modest, often non-refundable fee for a short period, commonly a week or two, during which they can cancel the contract for essentially any reason and still get their earnest money back.
It's a broader right than a typical inspection contingency, since the buyer doesn't have to justify the cancellation with specific findings.
What Central Indiana Buyers Use Instead
Indiana's standard MIBOR purchase agreements rely on contingencies tied to specific conditions, most notably the inspection contingency, rather than a general-purpose option period.

The practical effect is similar: buyers get a defined window to evaluate the home and back out if something concerns them, though the Indiana version is framed around the inspection findings rather than an unrestricted right to cancel.
faqs: Does Indiana have an option period?
Not as a standard contract feature; Indiana buyers typically rely on the inspection contingency for similar flexibility.
Is an option fee the same as earnest money?
No, an option fee, where used, is typically separate and often non-refundable, unlike earnest money, which is usually credited or returned.
Should I ask for an option period if I'm buying in Indiana?
It's not a standard local practice; talk to your agent about how the inspection contingency achieves a similar result here.
Why would I hear this term if I'm not from Texas?
Buyers relocating from option-period states sometimes ask about it out of habit; your agent can explain the Indiana equivalent.

h1: What Is an Earnest Money Dispute?
title: What Is an Earnest Money Dispute? | Your Realty Link
meta: An earnest money dispute happens when a buyer and seller disagree over who keeps the deposit after a deal falls apart. Here's how Indiana typically handles it.
hero_sub: When a deal falls apart, whose money is it? Here's how these disagreements typically get resolved.
definition: An earnest money dispute is a disagreement between a buyer and seller over who is entitled to keep the earnest money deposit after a real estate contract falls through.
qa_lead: Most deals close without any issue, but if a contract falls apart and both sides believe they're owed the earnest money, that's a dispute. In Indiana, whoever is holding the deposit, often a title company, generally can't release the funds until both parties agree in writing or a court resolves it.
qa_facts: Who holds funds during a dispute
The title company or brokerage, neutrally
Written mutual release, or a court decision
Whether a contingency justified canceling the contract
Clear contract terms and documented deadlines
sections: Why Disputes Happen

Most disputes come down to disagreement over whether a buyer had a valid contingency to cancel the contract, or whether they simply changed their mind after a deadline had passed. The holder of the funds isn't in a position to judge who's right; they just wait for both sides to agree.
Clear documentation matters here, which is one reason your earnest money receipt and any written contingency notices are worth keeping.
How These Get Resolved

The most common path is a mutual release, where both parties sign an agreement dividing or assigning the funds, often after some negotiation. If that fails, either side can pursue mediation or small claims court, though this is a last resort most buyers and sellers prefer to avoid.

Working with an experienced agent and title company from the start helps prevent disputes, since deadlines and contingency language are tracked carefully and communicated as issues arise, not after the fact.
faqs: Can I get my earnest money back automatically if a deal falls through?
Only if you canceled properly under a valid contingency and within its deadline; otherwise release usually requires mutual agreement.
Who decides an earnest money dispute?
Neither party alone; the funds stay with the neutral holder until both sides sign a release or a court orders otherwise.
How long can a dispute take to resolve?
It varies widely, from a quick mutual agreement to a longer process if the parties end up in mediation or court.
Does the title company keep the money if there's a dispute?
No, the title company simply holds it neutrally; they don't have authority to award it to either side on their own.

h1: What Is Dual Agency in Real Estate?
title: What Is Dual Agency in Real Estate? | Your Realty Link
meta: Dual agency happens when one agent represents both buyer and seller. Learn how it works under Indiana's limited agency rules and how to protect your interests.
hero_sub: One agent, two sides of the table, and a lot less advocacy for you.
definition: Dual agency is when a single real estate agent or brokerage represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction, limiting how fully either side can be advised.
qa_lead: Dual agency happens most often when a buyer falls for a home listed by their own agent's brokerage. Indiana licensing law calls this arrangement limited agency, and it only happens with written, informed consent from everyone involved.
qa_facts: Written, from both buyer and seller
Neutral - no full representation for either side
You can decline and request a different agent
sections: How Dual Agency Comes Up

Dual agency usually starts small: a buyer working with an agent falls for a home that same brokerage happens to have listed. Rather than send the buyer elsewhere, the brokerage may offer to represent both sides, with the individual agent stepping into a neutral role.

Because the agent now owes duties to two clients with opposing goals, they legally cannot push for the highest price for the seller while also pushing for the lowest price for the buyer. Both parties have to agree to this trade-off in writing before it happens.
What You Give Up

A neutral agent cannot share what a buyer is truly willing to pay or what a seller would truly accept, and cannot advise either side on negotiation strategy the way a fully dedicated buyer's agent or listing agent would. You still get basic honesty and disclosure, just not full advocacy.
If full representation matters to you, you can ask for a different agent inside the same brokerage, sometimes called appointed agency, or work with a completely separate company instead.
faqs: Is dual agency legal in Indiana?
Yes, but only with written, informed consent from both the buyer and the seller, and only after the arrangement is fully disclosed.
Can I say no to dual agency?
Yes. You can ask for a different agent within the brokerage or choose a separate agency so you keep full representation.
Does a dual agent still have to be honest with me?
Yes, basic honesty and disclosure still apply, but the agent cannot advocate fully for either side or share confidential negotiating positions.
Do I still need a representation agreement in a dual agency deal?
Yes. A Buyer Representation Agreement still applies on the buyer side, and any fee-sharing the seller agrees to cover is spelled out in writing, not assumed.

h1: What Is Limited Agency in Indiana Real Estate?
title: What Is Limited Agency in Indiana? | Your Realty Link
meta: Limited agency is Indiana's licensing term for one agent representing both buyer and seller. Learn how it works, what it limits, and how to protect yourself.
hero_sub: The official Indiana term for representing both sides of one deal, and what it costs you in advocacy.
definition: Limited agency is Indiana's licensing term for an agent or brokerage representing both the buyer and seller in one transaction, staying neutral instead of fully advocating for either side.
qa_lead: Indiana law uses limited agency where many other states say dual agency. It means the same thing: one agent, two clients, and reduced advocacy for both, allowed only with everyone's written consent.
qa_facts: Dual agency in most other states
Disclosure and written consent from both parties
Appointed agency or a separate agent entirely
sections: When Limited Agency Applies

You will most often see limited agency disclosed the moment a buyer asks to tour a home listed by the same brokerage that represents them. The disclosure has to happen before the limited agency relationship begins, not after an offer is already on the table.

Once both sides consent in writing, the agent, or agents if the brokerage assigns one to each side, can no longer fully advocate for either the buyer or the seller, only facilitate the transaction fairly.
Your Options Under Limited Agency

You are never required to accept limited agency. Many brokerages, including Your Realty Link, can appoint a different agent within the office to represent just you, preserving full advocacy for both the buyer and the seller.
If full, undivided representation matters to you, it is worth asking upfront how a brokerage handles this situation before you sign a buyer's agency agreement.
faqs: Is limited agency the same as dual agency?
Yes. Limited agency is simply Indiana's official licensing term for what most states call dual agency.
Do I have to agree to limited agency?
No. You can request a different agent within the brokerage or work with an entirely separate company to keep full representation.
What does an agent still have to do for me under limited agency?
They still owe basic honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure, but cannot fully advocate for your side of the negotiation.
Does limited agency change what I pay?
Not automatically. A signed representation agreement still spells out compensation, and any amount the seller agrees to cover is documented in writing.

h1: What Does a Transaction Coordinator Do?
title: What Does a Transaction Coordinator Do? | Your Realty Link
meta: A transaction coordinator manages paperwork, deadlines, and communication after a contract is signed. Learn what this role covers from contract to closing.
hero_sub: The behind-the-scenes person making sure nothing slips through the cracks between contract and closing.
definition: A transaction coordinator is a support professional who manages paperwork, deadlines, and communication to keep a real estate deal on track, working alongside your agent rather than in place of them.
qa_lead: Once a purchase agreement is signed, dozens of deadlines start ticking at once. A transaction coordinator tracks those dates and documents so your agent can stay focused on strategy and negotiation instead of chasing paperwork.
qa_facts: Administrative support, not a licensed advisor
Your agent and the other side's agent
sections: What a Transaction Coordinator Handles

A transaction coordinator keeps the file organized, making sure signatures are collected, deadlines for inspections and financing are tracked, and everyone involved, including the lender and title company, has what they need on time.
They typically do not negotiate on your behalf or give you advice about price or strategy. Those decisions stay with your buyer's agent or listing agent.
Why This Helps You
A missed deadline in a real estate contract can mean losing an earnest money deposit or a contingency right, so having someone dedicated to tracking dates reduces that risk considerably.
It also frees up your agent's time for the parts of the deal that actually require their judgment and experience, like pricing strategy and negotiation.
faqs: Do I pay the transaction coordinator directly?
Usually not. Coordinator fees are typically built into brokerage operations or paid by the agent, not billed to you separately.
Is a transaction coordinator a licensed agent?
Not necessarily. Many hold a real estate license, but they operate in an administrative capacity rather than as your advocate.
Will I talk to the transaction coordinator or my agent?
Both. Your agent still handles strategy and negotiation, while the coordinator often reaches out directly about paperwork and deadlines.
Does every transaction have a coordinator?
Not every brokerage uses one, but many teams, including ours, rely on a coordinator to keep larger transaction volumes on schedule.

title: What Is a Buyer's Agent? | Your Realty Link
meta: A buyer's agent represents only the buyer's interests during a home purchase. Learn what they do, how they're paid, and why a signed agreement matters.
hero_sub: The person whose job is to look out for you, and only you, from the first showing to closing day.
definition: A buyer's agent is a licensed real estate agent who represents the buyer's interests exclusively, helping them find homes, negotiate offers, and navigate the process through closing.
qa_lead: A buyer's agent works for you, not the seller. Their duty of loyalty runs to the buyer once you sign a buyer's agency agreement, which spells out how long they represent you and how they are compensated.
qa_facts: Negotiated in writing, sometimes covered by the seller
sections: What a Buyer's Agent Does For You

Beyond unlocking doors, a buyer's agent researches comparable sales, helps you understand a home's condition and value, structures a competitive offer, and negotiates on your behalf through inspection, appraisal, and closing.
Because their duty runs to you, they can share information with you that a listing agent legally cannot, like honest opinions about a home's flaws or how much room there may be to negotiate.
The Buyer Representation Agreement

Since 2024, buyer's agents nationwide are required to have a signed representation agreement in place before touring homes with a client. It sets out the length of the relationship, the agent's duties, and how compensation works.

Buyer representation is not automatically free. The agreement spells out the fee, and in many Central Indiana deals the seller agrees to cover some or all of it as part of the offer, but that is negotiated case by case, not guaranteed.
faqs: Do I have to sign something before touring homes?
Yes, most brokerages require a written Buyer Representation Agreement before showing you homes in person.
Is working with a buyer's agent free?
Not automatically. A written agreement sets the fee, and the seller sometimes agrees to cover it as part of the deal, but that is negotiated, not guaranteed.
Can a buyer's agent also represent the seller?
Only in a dual agency or limited agency arrangement, and only with informed written consent from both sides.
How long does a buyer's agency agreement last?
It varies by agreement, often a set number of months, and is spelled out in the contract you sign.

title: What Is a Listing Agent? | Your Realty Link
meta: A listing agent represents the seller, handling pricing, marketing, and negotiation for a sale. Learn what they do and how they differ from a buyer's agent.
hero_sub: The agent whose job is getting your home sold, for the right price, with the fewest headaches.
definition: A listing agent, also called a seller's agent, represents the seller's interests, handling pricing strategy, marketing, showings, and negotiation through closing.
qa_lead: A listing agent's duty of loyalty runs to the seller, formalized through a listing agreement that sets the price strategy, marketing plan, and commission before the home ever hits the MLS.
sections: What a Listing Agent Does

A listing agent starts with pricing strategy, often building a comparative market analysis to help set a competitive list price, then coordinates photography, staging advice, and marketing across the MIBOR MLS and other channels.
As offers come in, the listing agent presents them to the seller, negotiates terms on the seller's behalf, and manages the transaction through inspection, appraisal, and closing.
Listing Agent vs Buyer's Agent

A buyer's agent and a listing agent sit on opposite sides of the same transaction, each with a duty of loyalty to a different client. If a buyer doesn't have their own agent, the listing agent still cannot advocate for that buyer the way their own agent would.
When one agent or brokerage ends up representing both sides, that becomes dual agency and requires written consent from everyone involved.
faqs: How is a listing agent paid?
Typically through a commission set in the listing agreement, paid at closing out of the sale proceeds.
Can a listing agent also work with buyers?
Yes, many agents work with both buyers and sellers, though not usually both sides of the same transaction unless it becomes a disclosed dual agency.
What's the difference between a listing agent and a Realtor?
Listing agent describes the role in a transaction, while Realtor refers to membership in the National Association of Realtors and its code of ethics.
Do I need a listing agent to sell my home in Indiana?
No, but a listing agent brings pricing expertise, marketing reach, and negotiation experience that most owners selling on their own do not have access to.

title: What Is a Managing Broker? | Your Realty Link
meta: A managing broker supervises a brokerage's agents and ensures the office follows Indiana real estate law. Learn why this role matters to buyers and sellers.
hero_sub: The licensed broker responsible for every agent in the office, and your resource if something goes wrong.
definition: A managing broker is the licensed broker responsible for supervising a real estate brokerage's agents and ensuring the office operates within Indiana real estate law.
qa_lead: Every Indiana brokerage operates under a managing broker, who oversees agent conduct, contracts, and trust accounts. At Your Realty Link, Janet Giles-Schultz serves as Principal Broker, providing that oversight for our team of agents.
qa_facts: Indiana Real Estate Commission licensing law
Agent conduct, contracts, and trust accounts
sections: What a Managing Broker Oversees

The managing broker reviews contracts and disclosures, maintains the brokerage's trust or escrow accounts, and makes sure every licensed agent in the office is operating within Indiana real estate law and MIBOR MLS rules.
They also handle training, mentorship, and, when needed, resolving disputes between agents and clients before they become bigger problems.
Why the Managing Broker Matters to You

If you ever have a concern about how your transaction is being handled that your individual agent can't resolve, the managing broker is the person with the authority and legal responsibility to step in.
It's also worth asking who the managing broker is when you're comparing brokerages. Experienced oversight tends to mean fewer surprises during your transaction.
faqs: Is a managing broker the same as a broker-owner?
Not always. A managing broker holds the supervisory license required by law, and in many brokerages that person also owns the company, but not in every case.
Can I contact the managing broker directly?
Yes. Most brokerages, including ours, welcome direct contact if you have a concern your agent hasn't been able to resolve.
Does every real estate office have a managing broker?
Yes, Indiana law requires every licensed brokerage to have a designated managing broker responsible for supervision.
Who is the managing broker at Your Realty Link?
Janet Giles-Schultz serves as Principal Broker, overseeing our agents and transactions across Central Indiana.

title: What Is a Realtor? | Your Realty Link
meta: A Realtor is a licensed agent who belongs to the National Association of Realtors and follows its code of ethics. Learn how this differs from a general agent.
hero_sub: Not every real estate agent is a Realtor, and the difference is more than a trademark.
definition: A Realtor is a licensed real estate professional who belongs to the National Association of Realtors and agrees to abide by its code of ethics, on top of standard state licensing requirements.
qa_lead: Realtor is a trademarked membership title, not a job title. In Central Indiana, most agents who use it also belong to the local MIBOR Realtor Association, which grants access to the regional MLS.
qa_facts: Agreeing to the NAR Code of Ethics
sections: Realtor vs Real Estate Agent

Every Realtor is a licensed real estate agent, but not every licensed agent is a Realtor. The title requires paying dues to join the National Association of Realtors and formally agreeing to its code of ethics, which covers honesty, fair dealing, and cooperation with other members.
Locally, that membership runs through MIBOR, the Realtor association serving Central Indiana, which also operates the regional MLS most agents use to list and search homes.
Why the Realtor Distinction Matters
The code of ethics gives you an extra layer of accountability beyond state licensing law, including a formal process for filing a complaint if a Realtor doesn't live up to its standards.
At Your Realty Link, Principal Broker Janet Giles-Schultz and our team hold MIBOR membership, so you're working with agents who have agreed to that added standard.
faqs: Are all real estate agents Realtors?
No. Realtor is a membership title through the National Association of Realtors, not a requirement to hold a real estate license.
What does the code of ethics actually cover?
It covers duties like honesty, fair dealing, proper handling of client funds, and cooperation with other Realtor members, with a formal complaint process if it's violated.
Do I need a Realtor or just a licensed agent?
Either can legally represent you, but Realtor membership adds an extra layer of ethical accountability many buyers and sellers value.
Is MIBOR the same thing as the MLS?
Not exactly. MIBOR is the Realtor association; it operates the regional MLS that member agents use to list and search properties.

h1: What Is Fiduciary Duty in Real Estate?
title: What Is Fiduciary Duty in Real Estate? | Your Realty Link
meta: Fiduciary duty is the legal obligation your agent owes to act with loyalty, honesty, and care. Learn what this means for buyers and sellers in Indiana.
hero_sub: The legal backbone that makes your agent work for you, not just with you.
definition: Fiduciary duty is the legal obligation a real estate agent owes their client to act with loyalty, honesty, and reasonable care, always putting the client's interests first.
qa_lead: Once you sign a representation agreement with a buyer's agent or a seller signs a listing agreement, that agent owes a set of fiduciary duties built around loyalty, disclosure, and confidentiality.
qa_facts: The client who signed the representation agreement
A signed buyer or listing agreement
sections: The Duties Your Agent Owes You

Fiduciary duty generally breaks down into loyalty, putting your interests first, reasonable care and diligence, disclosure of material facts, confidentiality of what you tell them, and proper accounting of any funds handled on your behalf.
These duties are why your agent can't casually mention your top offer price to the other side, or the seller's rock-bottom acceptable number to you, once they represent you.
When Fiduciary Duty Gets Complicated
In a dual agency or limited agency situation, an agent's duty to each side is necessarily reduced, since full loyalty to both a buyer and a seller in the same deal isn't legally possible.
That's part of why Indiana law requires written, informed consent before an agent can represent both sides, so you know exactly what level of advocacy you're getting.
faqs: What happens if an agent breaks fiduciary duty?
It can lead to a complaint with the Indiana Real Estate Commission or MIBOR, and in serious cases, legal liability for the agent or brokerage.
Does a transaction coordinator owe me fiduciary duty?
Generally no. A transaction coordinator handles administrative tasks and typically is not acting as your licensed advocate the way your agent does.
Do I need a signed agreement for fiduciary duty to apply?
Yes, generally. Fiduciary duty attaches once you have a signed buyer's agency agreement or listing agreement in place.
Is fiduciary duty the same for buyers and sellers?
The core duties are similar, but they apply to whichever side the agent represents, protecting that client's interests specifically.

title: What Is an Easement? | Your Realty Link
meta: An easement gives someone else a legal right to use part of your property, often for utilities or access, while you keep ownership. Here's what that means.
hero_sub: A legal right for someone else to use part of your land, without taking away your ownership of it.
definition: An easement is a legal right that allows another party, such as a utility company or a neighbor, to use a specific part of a property for a defined purpose, even though someone else owns the land.
qa_lead: An easement lets someone else use part of your property for a specific purpose, like running utility lines or crossing to reach a landlocked parcel, while you keep ownership. Most easements are recorded in the deed or shown on a survey and transfer automatically to future owners.
sections: Common Types of Easements

Utility easements let power, water, gas, or cable companies install and maintain lines across a yard, usually along a rear or side property line. Access easements, sometimes called right-of-way easements, allow a neighbor to cross one property to reach their own when there's no other road frontage. Drainage easements protect a natural or engineered path for stormwater to flow through a subdivision.
Because these rights run with the land, they typically remain in place no matter who owns the property, which is why a title search and survey are so important before closing.
How Easements Show Up During a Sale

Most easements are discovered during the title search or noted on a recorded plat, and a current survey will show exactly where they sit relative to structures. An easement usually isn't a dealbreaker, but buyers should understand what it limits, such as where a fence, pool, or addition can go.
If an easement seems to have been created informally, without ever being recorded, that's a different situation worth discussing with a title company or real estate attorney before closing.
faqs: Can I build on an easement on my property?
Generally no, or only with restrictions. The easement holder has the right to access that area, so structures placed there can sometimes be required to move.
Does an easement lower my property's value?
It can affect how much of the lot is usable, but common utility and drainage easements are routine and rarely change value much on their own.
Is an easement the same as an encroachment?
No. An easement is a legal right to use part of a property, while an encroachment is a structure that has physically crossed a boundary line without permission.
Who removes an easement?
Easements typically end only by agreement, expiration of their stated purpose, or a legal release recorded with the county, not simply when a home sells.

title: What Is a Property Lien? | Your Realty Link
meta: A lien is a legal claim against a property for unpaid debt, and it generally must be resolved before a home can be sold. See how liens affect Indiana closings.
hero_sub: A legal claim against a property that typically has to be cleared before ownership can change hands.
definition: A lien is a legal claim placed against a property to secure payment of a debt, such as a mortgage, unpaid taxes, or a contractor's bill. It gives the creditor a right to the property's value until the debt is satisfied.
qa_lead: A lien attaches to a property, not just to the owner, so it generally has to be paid off or released before title can transfer to a new buyer. The title search is how liens get discovered before closing, giving everyone time to resolve them.
qa_facts: Usually must be resolved before closing
sections: Common Types of Liens

A mortgage lien is the most familiar example. It's created the moment a buyer takes out a loan, and it's released once the loan is paid off. Tax liens arise from unpaid property taxes or income taxes and can take priority over other claims. Mechanic's liens, sometimes called construction liens, let unpaid contractors or suppliers place a claim on a property they worked on, and judgment liens come from a court ruling in a lawsuit against the owner.
Indiana counties record liens with the county recorder, which is exactly what a title company checks during the title search.
How Liens Get Resolved Before Closing

Most liens are paid off out of the seller's proceeds at closing, and the title company handles getting the release recorded. If a lien is larger than expected, or contested, it can delay or derail a closing until it's sorted out.
This is one reason title insurance matters: it protects the buyer and lender if a lien turns up later that wasn't caught during the search.
faqs: Can I sell a house with a lien on it?
Often yes, as long as the lien is paid off or otherwise resolved at closing, typically from the sale proceeds.
How do I find out if a property has a lien?
A title search performed by a title company or attorney will surface recorded liens; a preliminary check can also be done through the county recorder's office.
What happens if a lien isn't caught before closing?
This is rare when title insurance is in place, since the policy is designed to cover valid claims that surface after closing.
Is an HOA lien the same as a mortgage lien?
Both are liens, but an HOA lien secures unpaid association dues while a mortgage lien secures the home loan; either can affect a sale if unresolved.

title: What Is a Property Survey? | Your Realty Link
meta: A property survey shows a home's legal boundaries, structures, and easements. Learn when Central Indiana buyers need one and what it can reveal before closing.
hero_sub: A precise drawing of where a property actually begins and ends, and what sits on it.
definition: A survey is a drawing, prepared by a licensed surveyor, that shows a property's legal boundaries, along with structures, easements, and other features located on or near the lot.
qa_lead: A survey tells you exactly where your property lines fall, which matters for fences, additions, and driveways. It can also reveal an encroachment or an easement that wasn't obvious from a walkthrough.
qa_facts: New construction, unusual lots, some lenders
sections: What a Survey Actually Shows

A typical boundary or mortgage survey marks the corners and lines of a lot, along with the footprint of the house, garage, fences, decks, and driveways relative to those lines. It also plots any recorded easements, so a buyer can see, for example, exactly how much of the backyard sits under a utility easement.

Some transactions call for a more detailed ALTA/NSPS survey, which adds items like zoning setbacks and flood zone data, and is more common on larger or commercial-adjacent properties than on a typical suburban resale.
When a Survey Is Worth Ordering

Older Central Indiana neighborhoods, rural parcels, and properties with fences or additions that look like they might cross a line are all good candidates for a fresh survey, since an outdated one may not reflect current improvements. New construction almost always comes with a current survey from the builder or municipality.
A survey isn't automatically required for every resale, so buyers who want one should ask early, since scheduling and turnaround time can affect the closing timeline.
faqs: Do I need a survey to buy a house in Indiana?
Not always. Many resales close without a new survey, though a lender, title company, or buyer's attorney may require or recommend one depending on the property.
How is a survey different from a home inspection?
A survey maps legal boundaries and structures on the land; a home inspection evaluates the condition of the house itself.
Who pays for a survey?
This is negotiable between buyer and seller and varies by transaction, so ask your agent how it's typically handled locally.
What if a survey finds a fence in the wrong spot?
It becomes a conversation between the parties, sometimes resolved with a boundary line agreement, moving the fence, or simply disclosure and acceptance by the buyer.

title: What Is a Title Search? | Your Realty Link
meta: A title search reviews public records to confirm a seller can legally transfer clear ownership. See how it protects Central Indiana buyers before closing.
hero_sub: A behind-the-scenes records check that confirms the seller actually has the right to sell.
definition: A title search is a review of public property records, usually performed by a title company or attorney, to trace a property's ownership history and identify any liens, judgments, or other claims that could affect the sale.
qa_lead: Before you close, a title search digs through county records to confirm the seller has clear ownership and to uncover any liens or claims that need to be resolved first. The results are summarized in a title commitment before closing.
qa_facts: Title company or real estate attorney
A title commitment and title insurance
sections: What the Search Actually Uncovers

A title examiner traces the chain of title back through prior owners, checking county recorder and court records for anything that could cloud ownership: unpaid liens, unresolved judgments, missing signatures on old deeds, or unreleased mortgages that were paid off but never formally cleared from the record.
In Central Indiana, this work is typically done at the county level where the property sits, which is why closings on properties with unusual histories can occasionally take a little longer to clear.
From Search to Title Insurance

Once the search is complete, the title company issues a title commitment listing any issues, called exceptions, that need to be cleared before closing. Resolving those exceptions is what allows the title company to issue title insurance, which protects the buyer and lender against title problems that weren't caught during the search.
faqs: How far back does a title search go?
Practices vary, but examiners often review several decades of records to build a reliable chain of ownership.
Who orders the title search?
