The title company or closing attorney handling the transaction typically orders and manages the search.
What happens if the search finds a problem?
Most issues, like an old unreleased lien, can be cleared with paperwork before closing; more complex title defects may take longer to resolve.
Is a title search the same as title insurance?
No. The search is the investigation; title insurance is the policy that protects against claims the search didn't catch.

title: What Is a Quitclaim Deed? | Your Realty Link
meta: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the signer has in a property, with no guarantee the title is clear. See when Indiana buyers and sellers use one.
hero_sub: A simple deed for transferring interest between people who already trust each other, not a typical home sale.
definition: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever ownership interest the person signing it has in a property, without making any promise about whether that title is clear or valid.
qa_lead: A quitclaim deed hands over the signer's interest in a property as-is, with no promises about clear title, which is why it's rarely used for typical arm's-length purchases. It shows up far more often in family transfers, divorces, and fixing a name on the chain of title.
qa_facts: Title insurance for the recipient's protection
sections: When a Quitclaim Deed Makes Sense

Because a quitclaim deed offers no guarantee about the state of the title, it works best between parties who already know and trust each other and understand exactly what they're getting. Common examples include a parent adding a child to a deed, one spouse transferring their interest during a divorce, or correcting how a name is spelled in prior recorded documents.
It's generally not the right tool for a typical home purchase from a stranger, since a buyer paying market value wants the stronger protection of a warranty deed.
What It Doesn't Protect Against

Signing or receiving a quitclaim deed doesn't clear existing liens or fix title problems; it simply passes along whatever interest, good or bad, the signer actually has. If there's any question about the title's history, running a title search or purchasing title insurance is still worthwhile even in a quitclaim situation.
faqs: Is a quitclaim deed less official than other deeds?
No, once properly signed and recorded it is a legally binding transfer; it simply carries no warranty about the title's condition.
Can I get a mortgage with a quitclaim deed?
It depends on the lender and situation; because there's no title warranty, some lenders want additional title work before financing.
Does a quitclaim deed remove someone from a mortgage?
No. It only affects who is on the title; the mortgage loan obligation stays with whoever originally signed the loan documents unless the lender agrees otherwise.
Should I get title insurance with a quitclaim deed?
It's often a good idea, since a quitclaim deed itself provides no protection if a title problem surfaces later.

title: What Is a Warranty Deed? | Your Realty Link
meta: A warranty deed is the seller's legal guarantee that the title is clear, and a promise to defend it. See why it's standard in most Central Indiana home sales.
hero_sub: The seller's formal promise that the title is clear, and that they'll stand behind it.
definition: A warranty deed is a deed in which the seller guarantees they hold clear title to the property and promises to defend that title against claims from others.
qa_lead: A warranty deed gives the buyer the strongest form of protection at closing, because the seller is legally promising the title is clear and backing that promise up. It's the standard deed type in most Indiana residential sales, unlike a quitclaim deed, which offers no such guarantee.
qa_facts: Title insurance and a title search
sections: General vs. Special Warranty Deeds

A general warranty deed is the broadest promise: the seller guarantees the title against claims from any point in the property's history, even from before they owned it. A special warranty deed only guarantees the title for the period the seller personally owned the property, which is common with bank-owned or estate sales where the seller doesn't want to vouch for history before their ownership.
Most Central Indiana resales use a general warranty deed, which gives buyers the most confidence in the transfer.
How It Works With Title Insurance

A warranty deed is a promise from the seller, but promises are only as good as the seller's ability to keep them, which is why title insurance is used alongside it. The title search and insurance policy back up the deed's warranty with an actual financial guarantee if a covered title problem shows up later.
faqs: Is a warranty deed required in Indiana?
It's not legally required, but it's the standard and generally preferred deed type for typical purchase transactions.
What's the difference between a warranty deed and title insurance?
The deed is the seller's personal promise about the title; title insurance is a separate policy that financially protects the buyer and lender if a title problem surfaces.
Who prepares the warranty deed?
Typically the closing attorney or title company handling the transaction prepares and records it.
Does a warranty deed protect against every possible title issue?
It covers claims within the scope of its warranty, but it's not a substitute for a title search and title insurance, which address issues that may not be obvious to the seller.

h1: What Is a Chain of Title?
title: What Is a Chain of Title? | Your Realty Link
meta: A chain of title is the recorded ownership history of a property, passed from one owner to the next. Learn how gaps can affect a Central Indiana closing.
hero_sub: The paper trail of every owner a property has ever had, linked one deed to the next.
definition: A chain of title is the documented sequence of ownership transfers for a property, showing how it passed from one owner to the next over time through recorded deeds.
qa_lead: The chain of title has to be unbroken for a seller to prove they can legally transfer the property. A title search is how a title company verifies that chain and catches any gaps before closing.
sections: How the Chain Gets Built

Every time a property changes hands, the deed is recorded with the county, creating one more link in the chain. Over decades, a property might pass through inheritance, divorce, foreclosure, or a dozen ordinary sales, and each transfer needs to be properly documented for the chain to stay clean.
Title examiners piece this history together during the title search, working backward from the current owner.
What Happens When There's a Gap

A missing signature, an heir who was never formally released from an inherited interest, or a deed that was never recorded can all create what's called a cloud on title. These issues usually get resolved with additional paperwork, like an affidavit or a corrective deed, though a more serious gap can occasionally require a court action to clear.
This is exactly the kind of problem title insurance is designed to protect against if it isn't caught in time.
faqs: What causes a broken chain of title?
Common causes include unrecorded deeds, missing heir signatures, clerical errors, or a deed that was never properly executed.
Can I still buy a home with a title gap?
Often yes, once the gap is resolved through corrective paperwork or, in more complex cases, a legal action to clear the title.
Who fixes a chain of title problem?
The title company or a real estate attorney typically identifies the fix needed, which the seller usually has to complete before closing.
Does title insurance protect against chain of title issues?
Yes, it's one of the main risks title insurance is designed to cover if a covered issue surfaces after closing.

title: What Is an Encroachment? | Your Realty Link
meta: An encroachment is when a structure crosses onto a neighbor's property or a setback line. Learn how it's found and resolved before an Indiana closing.
hero_sub: When a fence, shed, or driveway crosses a line it isn't supposed to.
definition: An encroachment occurs when a structure, such as a fence, shed, driveway, or roof overhang, physically extends across a property's boundary line onto a neighboring lot or into a required setback.
qa_lead: An encroachment means something physical, like a fence or a shed, sits over the property line. A survey usually reveals it, and while it's not always a dealbreaker, it typically needs to be addressed before closing.
qa_facts: A physical structure crossing a line
An easement, which is a use right
sections: How Encroachments Get Discovered

Most encroachments turn up on a current survey, which compares the actual footprint of structures against the recorded property lines. A visual walkthrough often can't catch a fence that's a foot or two over the line, especially on older lots where boundaries were staked out decades ago.
Encroachments can also be a symptom of an outdated survey being relied on, which is one reason buyers on older or irregular lots sometimes order a fresh one.
How They Get Resolved

Options range from a simple agreement between neighbors acknowledging the situation, to physically moving the structure, to a formal boundary line adjustment recorded with the county. In many cases, a minor encroachment like a foot of fence doesn't stop a sale, as long as it's disclosed and the buyer accepts it.
An encumbrance more broadly includes encroachments along with other claims that can affect a property's title or use.
faqs: Does an encroachment kill a home sale?
Not usually. Minor encroachments are often resolved through disclosure, a written agreement, or a boundary adjustment rather than stopping the sale.
Who has to fix an encroachment?
It depends on the situation and what the parties agree to; sometimes the structure is moved, sometimes it's addressed through a recorded agreement instead.
Can a neighbor's shed on my land become theirs over time?
Indiana law recognizes adverse possession in limited circumstances, but it's fact-specific and worth discussing with a real estate attorney rather than assuming.
How do I know if I have an encroachment?
A current survey is the most reliable way to confirm whether a structure crosses a property line.

title: What Is a Title Encumbrance? | Your Realty Link
meta: An encumbrance is any claim or restriction on a property, from liens to easements and deed restrictions. Learn what can encumber title before closing.
hero_sub: An umbrella term for anything attached to a property that can affect its use, value, or transfer.
definition: An encumbrance is any claim, restriction, or interest attached to a property that can affect its use, value, or ability to transfer, including liens, easements, deed restrictions, and encroachments.
qa_lead: Encumbrance is the broad umbrella term covering anything that clouds a clean title, from a lien for unpaid debt to an easement or deed restriction limiting how the land can be used. A title search identifies them so they can be addressed before closing.
sections: Financial vs. Non-Financial Encumbrances

Some encumbrances involve money, like a lien for an unpaid mortgage, tax bill, or contractor invoice, and those usually get paid off at closing. Others don't involve debt at all: an easement lets someone else use part of the land, a deed restriction limits how it can be used, and an encroachment is a structure sitting over a line.
Not every encumbrance is a problem. Plenty of properties have a routine utility easement or a longstanding deed restriction that simply gets disclosed and doesn't affect the sale.
How Encumbrances Get Handled at Closing

The title search surfaces encumbrances so the title company can list them on the title commitment as exceptions. Financial encumbrances typically need to be paid off or released; non-financial ones are usually just disclosed, accepted, or occasionally negotiated between buyer and seller before closing.
faqs: Is an encumbrance always a bad thing?
No. Many encumbrances, like a standard utility easement, are routine and don't meaningfully affect a property's use or value.
How do I find out what encumbers a property?
A title search performed before closing will identify recorded encumbrances such as liens, easements, and deed restrictions.
Can a property be sold with an encumbrance still attached?
Yes, in many cases, especially non-financial ones like easements, as long as it's properly disclosed to the buyer.
What's the difference between a lien and an encumbrance?
A lien is one specific type of encumbrance tied to a debt; encumbrance is the broader category that also includes easements, restrictions, and encroachments.

title: What Is a Title Commitment? | Your Realty Link
meta: A title commitment outlines exactly what a title company will insure and what must be cleared first. See how it fits into a Central Indiana closing timeline.
hero_sub: The title company's promise to insure, once a short list of items gets cleared up first.
definition: A title commitment is a document issued by a title company after the title search, outlining the terms under which it will insure the title and listing any issues that must be resolved before closing.
qa_lead: Once the title search is done, the title company issues a commitment spelling out what it will insure and what still needs to be cleared, such as an outstanding lien. Reviewing it early gives everyone time to resolve issues before closing day.
sections: What's Inside a Title Commitment

A title commitment is typically organized into sections: one confirming the basic details of the transaction, like the buyer, seller, and property; and another listing exceptions, meaning any liens, easements, or other issues found during the title search that need to be addressed, or that will simply remain as standard exclusions from coverage.
Buyers and their agents should review the commitment closely, since it's the clearest picture of anything unusual attached to the property before closing.
From Commitment to Final Policy

Once the required items on the commitment are resolved, such as paying off a lien or recording a missing document, the title company issues the actual title insurance policy at closing. The commitment is essentially a preview of that policy, giving everyone a chance to fix problems before it's finalized.
faqs: When do I receive a title commitment?
It typically arrives after the title search is complete and well before closing, giving time to resolve any issues it identifies.
Who should review the title commitment?
Buyers, along with their agent and, where used, their attorney, should review it to understand any exceptions listed.
Is a title commitment the same as title insurance?
No. The commitment is a promise to insure once conditions are met; the actual policy is issued at closing.
What if the commitment lists a problem I don't understand?
Ask your title company or real estate attorney to explain it; most exceptions are routine, but it's worth understanding each one.

title: What Is a Deed Restriction? | Your Realty Link
meta: A deed restriction is a private rule written into a property's deed that limits how the land can be used. See how it differs from HOA rules and zoning.
hero_sub: A private rule baked into the deed itself, controlling how a property can be used long after the original owner is gone.
definition: A deed restriction is a limitation written directly into a property's deed that controls how the land can be used, and it generally binds all future owners, not just the person who agreed to it.
qa_lead: A deed restriction is a private limit on how land can be used, recorded right in the deed, so it runs with the property from one owner to the next. It's different from an HOA rule or public zoning, though all three can apply to the same property.
qa_facts: Land use, building type, minimum size
sections: How Deed Restrictions Differ From HOA Rules and Zoning

Zoning is a public rule set by the city or county, applied broadly across an area. An HOA's rules, sometimes called covenants, conditions, and restrictions, are private but managed by an association that can amend or enforce them over time. A deed restriction is also private, but it's written directly into a specific property's deed, which can make it harder to change and, in some cases, older than any HOA covering the same neighborhood.
A single property can be subject to all three at once, which is why it's worth understanding which rules actually apply before assuming a plan for the land is workable.
What Happens If a Restriction Is Violated

Because a deed restriction runs with the land, it can typically be enforced by a neighbor, a homeowners association, or whoever holds the right to enforce it, sometimes years after the original restriction was created. Removing or modifying one usually requires a formal release or, in some cases, a court action, so it isn't something a new owner can simply choose to ignore.
faqs: How do I find out if a property has deed restrictions?
They show up during the title search and are typically referenced in the property's recorded deed history.
Can a deed restriction ever expire?
Some are written with an expiration date or sunset clause, but many are intended to run indefinitely unless formally released.
Is a deed restriction the same as an HOA rule?
No. A deed restriction is tied to the specific deed; HOA rules come from the association's separate governing documents, though both can apply to the same home.
Can I challenge or remove a deed restriction?
Sometimes, through a recorded release or a court action, but it depends on the specific restriction and who has standing to enforce it, so legal advice is usually worthwhile.

title: What Is Joint Tenancy? | Your Realty Link
meta: Joint tenancy lets co-owners hold equal shares in a home with rights of survivorship. Learn how it works for Central Indiana buyers taking title together.
hero_sub: A way for co-owners to hold title so a share passes automatically to the others, not through probate.
definition: Joint tenancy is a way for two or more people to hold title to a property together, with equal ownership shares and a right of survivorship, meaning a deceased owner's share passes automatically to the surviving owners.
qa_lead: In a joint tenancy, co-owners hold equal shares, and if one owner dies, their share passes directly to the surviving owners rather than through probate. It's a common choice for co-buyers, though married Indiana couples may also consider tenancy by the entirety.
sections: How Joint Tenancy Works

When people take title as joint tenants, each holds an equal, undivided interest in the whole property, and none of them owns a specific physical portion of it. The defining feature is the right of survivorship: if one joint tenant passes away, their interest transfers automatically and immediately to the remaining joint tenants, bypassing probate entirely.
This differs from tenancy in common, where owners can hold unequal shares and each share passes according to a will or the state's inheritance laws rather than automatically to the co-owners.
Things to Consider Before Choosing It

Because survivorship is automatic, joint tenancy isn't always the right fit for co-owners who want their share to go to their own heirs rather than to the other owners. It also means all owners generally need to agree to major decisions, like selling or refinancing, since each holds an interest in the whole property.
Buyers deciding how to take title, especially unmarried co-buyers or investment partners, often find it worthwhile to talk it through with a real estate attorney before closing.
faqs: Can joint tenancy be changed after closing?
Yes, owners can typically change how title is held later, though it usually requires a new deed to be prepared and recorded.
What happens if joint tenants split up or have a falling out?
The ownership structure doesn't automatically change, so co-owners typically need to agree on next steps, such as one buying out the other or selling the property.
Is joint tenancy the same as tenancy in common?
No. Joint tenancy includes automatic survivorship and equal shares; tenancy in common allows unequal shares and no automatic survivorship.
Does joint tenancy avoid all estate taxes?
It can help a share bypass probate, but it doesn't automatically address estate tax questions, which depend on the individual situation.

h1: What Is Tenancy by the Entirety?
title: What Is Tenancy by the Entirety? | Your Realty Link
meta: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of joint ownership for married couples with automatic survivorship rights. See how Indiana treats it and what it protects.
hero_sub: A form of joint ownership just for married couples, treating them as a single legal owner.
definition: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of joint property ownership available only to married couples, in which the law treats them as a single legal owner with automatic rights of survivorship.
qa_lead: Tenancy by the entirety works like joint tenancy with survivorship, but it's reserved for married couples and treats them as one legal owner. Indiana recognizes this form of ownership, and it can offer some protection from a creditor pursuing only one spouse individually.
qa_facts: Yes, automatic to the surviving spouse
Can shield the home from one spouse's separate creditors
Divorce, death, or a new deed by both spouses
sections: How It Differs From Joint Tenancy

Like joint tenancy, tenancy by the entirety includes a right of survivorship, so the surviving spouse automatically owns the whole property when the other spouse passes away, without probate. The key difference is that it's limited to married couples and treats them as a single legal unit, which is where its added creditor protection generally comes from: in many cases, a creditor with a claim against only one spouse cannot force a sale of property held this way.
That protection isn't unlimited, and it generally doesn't apply to debts both spouses took on together, like a shared mortgage.
What Happens if the Marriage Ends

Divorce typically converts a tenancy by the entirety into a tenancy in common, since the legal basis for treating the couple as a single owner no longer applies. Couples going through a divorce often need a new deed or a court order to formally divide or reassign the property, which is worth coordinating with a real estate attorney alongside the divorce proceedings.
faqs: Do all married couples automatically get tenancy by the entirety in Indiana?
Not automatically. How title is held depends on what's written into the deed, so married buyers should confirm this with their closing attorney or title company.
Does tenancy by the entirety protect against all debts?
No. It mainly offers protection from a creditor pursuing only one spouse individually, not from debts both spouses owe jointly, such as a shared mortgage.
What happens to the property if one spouse dies?
The surviving spouse automatically becomes the sole owner, without the property having to go through probate.
Can unmarried co-owners use tenancy by the entirety?
No, it's only available to married couples; unmarried co-owners typically choose joint tenancy or tenancy in common instead.
